Besides supporting long-term strategic research at institutes, NTNF would also fund industrial R&D projects initiated by finns and carried out by them alone or in collaboration with in stitutes.

To prevent the use of this «industrial R&D» support from being dominated by a few large firms in each sector, positive 5. Periodic reassessment and updating of the industrial and technological stråside 200

steps should be tåken to ensure wider involvement. For example, the number of applications accepted by NTNF from any one finn could be limited, and the procedure for applying simplified (see 34 below). 11. While it is extremely important to en courage proposals of high quality from firms, care must be tåken to ensure that overemphasis of this point does not mi litate against small firms' applications. 12. While high quality proposals are clearly essential, of even greater importance is the quality and utility of the R&D car ried out, and particularly its transfer into industrial application. It is clear from this report that assessment in this area has been rather lacking (section 13.2.3). 13. This implies the need for more careful monitoring of on-going research pro grammes and projects, and for mecha nisms to assess the degree of success in implementing research results in in dustry. This «quality control» function could be carried out by NTNF committees and by institute boards. Per haps some of the techniques utilized in this study might be adopted. 14. The establishment of a coherent stra tegy within the research institutes (and by NTNF with respect to the institutes) should go some way towards resolving the confusion that currently exists con ceniing the role and functions of instu tes (section 13.3.1). In particular, it should clarify their function with res pect to long-term «strategic» research. 15. It is suggested in this report that the above function, along with those of «in dustrial research and development» and «special help for small firms», should be administratively separated, with each receiving separately designated funding. Institutes and firms would then no lon ger compete directly for funds, as they do at present, often to the disad vantage of the firms (particularly smal ler ones). Moreover to avoid the poten tial conflicts of interest currently asso ciated with NTNF trying to fulfill two roles at the same time — that is, funding R&D, and being responsible for NTNF institutes — a formal legal separation between NTNF and the institutes should perhaps be considered. 16. The present rather unwieldy system of 20 NTNF committees could be greatly reduced to a small number of «industrial R&D committees» so chosen that they correspond more closely with today's (and tomorrow's) technological needs. Since these committees would only con sider applications from firms and not institutes, and since the number of app lications accepted from each finn might be limited (see 10 above), their workload would be considerably less than that for the present committees. The member ship of these new committees could therefore be kept very small. In addition, the use of overseas experts might be considered in order to avoid possible con flicts of interest. 17. In selecting between projects submitted to NTNF industrial R&D committes, the key criterion should be the likely industrial benefit of the proposed work, rather than whe ther it is technologically «interesting». 18. For those firms successful in obtaining project grants, the choice as to whether or not to use the institutes for carrying out some of the work would remain with them. 19. If a firm did choose to sponsor work at an institute, financial provision could be made in the grant to encourage the transfer of technology through the movement of people. For example, the finn might be encouraged to send some of its staff to work at the institute in the early stages of the project, helping to specify exactly what was required. In addition, towards the end of the project, institute staff might be required to spend some time at the finn implementing the project re sults (see 28 below). 20. However, the present scale of NTNF support for R&D carried out in industry is so small that its effects are little more than marginal. One ultimate aim of a national industrial strategy would be to move away from providing large subsi dies for declining industries, and to wards backing potentially important new industries on the one hand, and en couraging (for example, through re training schemes) moves away from in dustrial sectors that are likely to be threatened in the f uture b e f o r e firms run into financial difficulties on the other. In short, there would be more of a «preventative medicine» approach, with procurement policy again playing a key role. 21. In order to fulfill the increased strategic role assigned to them, several institutes might require considerable reorientaside 201

a key role. 21. In order to fulfill the increased strategic role assigned to them, several institutes might require considerable reorientaside 201

tion. Institutes incapable of adapting themselves sufficiently might have to be phased out, or at least encouraged to perf orm different, less research-oriented functions (such as organizing training courses, providing assistance to small firms, and carrying out development work), while staff were being retrained to work in more strategically important areas of technology. 22. This raises the question of the need for constant regeneration of institute staff. Skills and attitudes geared to solving yesterday's problems may be inapprop riate to the implementation of f orward looking strategies, particularly if they involve new areas of technology and new markets. 23. As part of this regeneration process, the institutes will need two main types of recruits: new graduates, and engineers or researchers with industrial expe rience. The first of these can best be provided through the very close associa tion and perhaps physical integration of an institute with a local university or regional college. (Involvement in tea ching would also stimulate institute staff, helping them to maintain their re search creativity and to develop new skills.) The second might be achieved through the introduction of a more flex ible salary structure to attract experien ced industrial researchers, even on a short-term basis. 24. The prime function of the technical col lective research infrastructure is that of technology transfer, and, in the Norwegian context, there are three as pects to this. First Norway, being a small country, and perf orming less than 1 % of the total world R&D, clearly needs to import ideas and technologies from abroad. In order to facilitate this pro cess, much greater f unds need to be pro vided for financing institute staff to work overseas for temporary periods in universities and advanced technology firms. 25. Secondly, there is the aspect of the transfer of technology between institu tes, a process which, this report suggests, is highly unsatisfactory (Section 13.3.3). Although it might prove difficult to ar range, there is no doubt that the trans fer of individuals between institutes (even on a temporary basis) could greatly improve this process. Mecha nisms to facilitate such transfers should therefore be actively sought (for example, through the secondment of staff from one institute to another to build up teams for carrying out strategic re search programmes). 26. Thirdly, there is the all-important transfer of technology from the institu tes into industrial use. At present, no very effective mechanisms appear to operate in Norway to f acilitate, or even to monitor, this process. This major weakness in the system might be allevia ted through a combination of measures. 27. In the first case, with strategic research programmes, institutes should be encou raged to recruit, on secondment for one or several years, research staff from user industries. These individuals would, in turn, be actively involved in the later industrial implementation of the re search results. 28. A second mechanism involves the trans fer of industry-sponsored R&D under taken at institutes. The institute might be required to submit a report not at the end but 80% of the way through the project, after which institute staff would spend the remaining 20%. of the time working to implement the results within industry. 29. A third mechanism involves the State Technology Institute (STI). At present, there appears to be little contact bet ween NTNF and the institutes on the one hand and STI on the other, thus restricting the possibilities for diff using new industrial methods and techniques into industry. Consideration should per haps be given to the establishment of a formal body within the Ministry of In dustry linking and co-ordinating the ac tivities of NTNF, the research institutes, and STI. 30. A final mechanism is the encourage ment of long-serving institute staff to undertake «industrial sabbaticals» per haps once every 5 or 6 years. This would increase their awareness of industry's problems. They might, in particular, spend their time on projects involving the implementation of previous re search at their institute. Finns would then be able to use institutes as a «lib rary of skills», temporarily borrowing re searchers on sabbaticals. 31. The collective research system, as cur rently constituted, is being abused by certain firms, some of whom fail to put in their share of the costs of a project for which they have received NTNF sup port. Such abuses could be discouraged

firms, some of whom fail to put in their share of the costs of a project for which they have received NTNF sup port. Such abuses could be discouraged

side 202

by taking more care to ensure that grants are awarded only for projects to which firms are genuinely committed. By removing the need for firms and in stitutes to compete directly for the same funds, one would end the current bar gaining process in which institutes «soli cit» industrial partners, a process that often results in firms entering projects to which they are only half committed. 32. Another questionable use of the system concerns those firms receiving grants for work that they themselves can aff ord without NTNF help. Greater considera tion should therefore be given by NTNF committees to the ability of firms to carry out R&D without help. 33. Some firms, particularly smaller ones, are unable to use the existing collective research system very effectively. In the competition for funds with institutes and large firms, they are at a severe disadvantage. They need special help. 34. This might be provided by a more tech nically-oriented STI, although this would probably require better co-ordi nation between NTNF and STI than there is at present (see 29 above). In ad dition, the institutes might provide sub sidized services for small firms. Finally, NTNF could make the procedures invol ved in applying for help more simple (with a less complicated application form for small firms) and more flexible (by håving more than one application date each year). It could also provide a «sign-posting» service to inf orm firms of all the f acilities and types of help avail able. 35. Successful innovation depends as much on non-technical factors (such as good management, forecasting of user-needs, and marketing) as it does on technical ones. At present, NTNF, when deciding which projects to fund, rather neglects these non-technical considerations. The ability of the firm concerned to supply the necessary non-technical skills should be incorporated as one of the cri teria in the selection precedure for pro jects. 36. In addition, institutes could begin to build up non-technical support services, perhaps through co-operation with a university or college, or through «swap» arrangements with firms. 37. By virtue of the unique opportunity af forded by North Sea oil, Norway has the resources required to implement these various measures. With a strengthened and evolving R&D capability, Norwe gian industry and indeed the country as a whole could enter the 2 lst century with optimism. 1. INTRODUCTION The crucial and increasing importance of research and development (R&D) and of innovation in general in strengthening and maintaining the international competitive ness of a nation's industry is by now firmly established. Although the need to develop an industrial R&D capability had been re cognized in Norway for some time, it was only at the end of the Second World War that the first steps were tåken in this direc tion. The Royal Norwegian Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (NTNF) was set up shortly afterwards in 1946. Of the various mechanisms available for state sup port of R&D, Norway has chosen to concen trate particularly on that of «collective re search», with centralized f acilities funded by the government at institutes carrying out research for the benefit of (and partly paid for by) industry and public agencies. Over the 35 years of its existence, NTNF has grown significantly in both size and complexity, establishing a large network of committees to determine and administer the distribution of research resources, as well as running its own research institutes. In addi tion, various other mechanisms for the sup port of R&D have been set up outside NTNF. The total system for the support of R&D has, however, become rather complex and inflexible, and one apparent conse quence of this is that many firms are increa singly experiencing difficulty in using the system. This is one important reason for assessing NTNF and its relationship to other mechanisms for the support of R&D. A second main reason for carrying out such a study concerns the changes in the structure of the Norwegian economy, and in the nature of firms, many of which now have their own R&D capability. This gives rise to the question of whether the NTNF system as presently constituted is still ap propriate to current industrial needs. Thirdly, the retirement of Robert Major, NTNF's Director for the first 34 years, and the question of who should succeed him, gave rise to a debate over the aims of NTNF — for example, over the relative emphasis that should be given to long-term research compared with shorter-term development work, and whether it was wise for NTNF to operate both as a funding agency and an

given to long-term research compared with shorter-term development work, and whether it was wise for NTNF to operate both as a funding agency and an

side 203

organization actually carrying out research in its own institutes. Finally, the collective research system was set up in Norway to provide national centres of excellence in key technological areas. Over recent years, the extent to which the research institutes are successf ul in provid ing such centres of excellence has come to be questioned. However, until now there has been little systematic data available on the performance of institutes in order to resolve this question. The Industriforskningsutvalget was set up to consider these and other questions. They decided to commission the Science Po licy Research Unit (SPRU) to provide an «outsider's» assessment of the Norwegian R&D system. In addition, other studies (on the historical development of NTNF, and on international comparisons with other col lective research systems) were carried out by NAVF's Utredningsinstitutt. It was inten ded that all these commissioned studies should provide the background information required to enable the Commission to iden tify the strengths and weaknesses of Nor way^ collective research system, and hence to put forward proposals to improve it. 2. THE SPRU WORK — AIMS AND METHODS This work has five principal elements: (1) To examine the structure, organization, and operational mechanisms for resource allocation in NTNF, concentrating in parti cular on a sub-section of the wider system consisting of two industrial sectors — me chanical engineering and electronics. This involves following the flow of money from two NTNF Committees, the Mechanical En gineering (VF) and Electronics (TE) Com mittees. Much of this money passes to insti tutes and firms, and these therefore corres pond to the second and third aspects of our work. (2) To study four institutes, the Central In stitute for Industrial Research (SI), the Foundation of Scientific and Industrial Re search at the Norwegian Institute of Tech nology (SINTEF), Rogaland Research Insti tute (RF), and the Norwegian Defence Re search Establishment (FFI), and in particu lar their work in the areas of mechnical engineering and electronics. This involves looking at the inputs and the various out puts from the institutes, especially the bene fits to industry. The four institutes each provide a slightly different model for collec tive research. SI is a large, centralized NTNF institute, while SINTEF is very clo sely associated with the Technical Univer sity at Trondheim. RF is a regional insti tute, linked to Rogaland District College, and FFI is concerned with providing tech nology for a single user, the Ministry of De fence. By considering the different organi zational and funding patterns along with the various outputs, it should be possible to identify the major advantages and disad vantages associated with each model. (3) To look at firms in the mechanical engi neering and electronics sectors, and the in terface between them and the system for state support of R&D. The firms fall into one of two categories. First, there are those that have obtained help from NTNF and/or the institutes in carrying out R&D. Which are they? What sorts of help have been pro vided? And how successful has the help been? Secondly, there are firms that have not obtained any support. Again, which are they? And what are the reasons why they have not received help? (4) To examine the relationship of NTNF to other mechanisms for the support of R&D. There exist at present a great variety of mechanisms for the support of industrial research and development in Norway. These include: — NTNF; — the Industrial Fund and its constituent parts: the Development Fund or «Risk Bank», and the Innovation Plan; — STI; — INKO; — Branch Associations and their research institutes; — various special initiatives coming under NTNF (e.g. the Ship Plan, microprocessors). Some of the main channels for the flow of money through all these various mecha nisms are shown in simplified form in Fi gure 1 below. (This diagram does not show the two other Research Councils, NLVF and NFFR, nor the Government Research Insti tutes.) In this study, wc are concerned prin cipally with only a part of the overall sys tem, this sub-section being shown in Figure 2. (5) To comment generally on the structure of R&D support mechanisms, the approp riateness of that structure to current R&D needs, and the effectiveness with which the money currently allocated by NTNF to in stitutes and industry is used. ible improvements to the system. One such change in which the Commission was parti cularly interested was the possibility of establishing a more formal system for conti nuously monitoring and improving the per formance of NTNF and the wider R&D sys tem, if this was seen to be necessary. It must be emphasized that this report, håving been produced in a relatively short period of time by a foreign research group, with limited experience and knowledge of the Norwegian economy and society, can only be regarded asa discussion do cume n t . Certainly, there are advantages in bringing to bear a f resh independent view on the strengths and weaknesses of the R&D system. But against this needs to be counterbalanced the lack of detailed know ledge about Norway; and because of this wc have tried wherever possible to base our conclusions on a «distillation» of the views held by those wc have interviewed, and to avoid imposing our own cultural and politi cal stereotypes on the system. The aim of the study is, of course, to pinpoint certain areas where changes might be considered, but wc would not want to give the impres sion that these are in any way to be seen as definite recommendations. The methods used to obtain information and data relevant to the five tasks distin guished above can be summarized briefly as follows. Tasks (1), (2) and (3) required statis tical information from NTNF, the institu tes, and firms, on the inputs and outputs (and particularly the flows of money) for each. In addition, task (2) involved the use of structured interviews with researchers in institutes on the nature of their work, their contact with industry, and their perceptions of the benefits gained by firms. These typi cally took over 2 hours, 90 staff in total being interviewed at the four institutes. Si milarly, for task (3) structured interviews, generally with the Technical Director (or the Managing Director in the case of smal ler firms) were carried out with over 70 firms to establish the nature and extent of the finn's R&D efforts, its contact with NTNF and institutes, and the benefits derived from that contact. Information for task (4) came from interviews with firms and with about 10 other interested parties, such as repre sentatives of the State Technology Institute (STI), Branch Associations, industrial co operatives (for example, TESA in Rogaland), County planners, etc. Finally, for task (5), interviews were first held with senior people associated with NTNF and with the Direc tors of the four institutes covered in the study. On the basis of this (and the survey of previous work concerning the area of collec tive research), certain key issues were iden tified, and again institute researchers and firms were questioned about these in the interviews. The structure of this report can be briefly described as follows. There are three main parts, the first of which is largely descrip tive. In Section 3, wc examine the demand for industrial R&D, discussing the rela tionship of R&D to innovation and indu strial policy, the nature of the innovation process, and the role of collective research systems. Particular attention is paid to some of the critical issues that can arise with such systems. This is followed by a description of some of the R&D needs of Norwegian firms, particularly those in the two industrial sec tors with which wc are concerned. Section 5 then outlines the methods by which NTNF has attempted to meet those needs. The second part of the report (Sections 6 to 12) contains the bulk of the assessment that wc have carried out of a subsection of the Norwegian collective research system. Sections 6, 7 and 8 focus on the research efforts of SI, SINTEF, and Rogalandsforsk ning, and provide a number of case-studies of their longer-term research programmes. For each of these, wc attempt to assess the degree of success of the research, and to identif y the f actors that have contributed to the success or failure of the work. Section 9 looks at who uses the institutes, and descri bes some of the services the latter offer to industry. One such service is the carrying out of sponsored R&D projects for firms, and Section 10 evaluates ho w successful these have been. On the basis of Sections 6 to 10, certain conclusions can be drawn about the relative strengths and weaknesses of the institutes, and these are examined in Section 11. Lastly, Section 12 considers the views of industry on the degree to which NTNF and institutes in general are success ful in meeting their R&D needs. The final part of the report (Section 13) brings together some of the main findings from earlier sections, and identifies areas where institute researchers and/or firms be lieve that improvements are needed in Nor way^ system for the support of industrial R&D. Some possible changes are then dis cussed. Since FFl's prime responsibility is for research and de velopment aimed at strengthening Norway's def ence capability rather than for the sup port of R&D in industry, FFI has been trea ted separately from the other institutes. A description and analysis of the major cha racteristics of FFI with regard to the perfor mance of R&D and its relationship with industry can be found in Appendix 1. 3. THE DEMAND FOR INDUSTRIAL R&D AND THE ROLE OF COLLECTIVE RESEARCH 3.1 Innovation, industrial policy, and economic development. Why is industrial research and develop ment needed? In order to answer this, one needs to examine the relationship of R&D to the wider process of industrial innova tion, and this in turn must be set in the context of national industrial policy and the need for economic development. In this section, wc shall first look briefly at the role of industrial innovation and its relationship to industrial and economic po licy. Wc shall then consider in some detail the nature of the innovation process. This will be followed by a discussion of the part that can be played by collective research systems, together with an identification of some of the problems than can arise with collective research. There are f ew who would dispute that eco nomic and social progress in the advanced countries has depended heavily on conti nuous improvements in industrial ef f iciency and competitiveness, often brought about through new technology. And despite va rious predictions about the coming of the «post-industrial society», it sees clear that such continuous improvements or «innova tions» will continue to be crucially impor tant in the future as developed countries face the dual challenge of increasing compe tition from the newly industrialised count ries and changing patterns of demand from consumers for new or improved products and services. In Norway, there is in addition the particular challenge and opportunity of North Sea oil and gas. The challenge is to maintain industrial competitiveness with a high-value currency. The opportunity is to build on the resources, the activities, and the linkages created by the oil and gas. In Norway, as in all industrially advanced countries, what are therefore needed are conscious policies to encourage the develop ment of skills and technology, just at there are conscious policies for health, housing, and investment, for example. Unfortuna tely, however, the guidelines for such go vernment policies have in the past received too little attention from scholars and policy analysts. Nonetheless, it is possible to say something about the elements of such poli cies. One such crucial element is the recog nition that most of the essential ingredients for successful innovation must be found in manufacturing firms themselves. These vi tal ingredients include professionally trai ned management, technical skills, R&D ac tivity coupled to production and marketing activity, incentives to think beyond imme diate profitability to the development and improvement of the next generation of products, and flexibility in organisation and the deployment of skills. Both government and private institutions that finance and regulate industrial activity can influence these ingredients, in particular, by adequate provision for education and training, by in centives to encourage longer time-horizons in decision-making, and by ensuring that incompetence in management and deficien cies in skills are quickly identified and re medied. At the same time, there are other activities capable of promoting innovation for which governments have a more direct responsibility. One of the most important of these is a government-financed infrastruc ture for knowledge creation and diffusion, on which industrial firms can draw. This inf astructure includes not only the univer sities, but also goverment-supported institu tes that undertake either long-term re search or «generic research» (that is, re search cutting across scientific disciplines and håving potential applications in a wide range of industries), as well as giving help to firms (very often smaller firms) without the required technical skills. This report is mainly about collective re search institutes in Norway, but at the same time many of the other factors mentioned above must also be kept in mmd, in particu lar the financial and skill requirements for full-scale innovation and the degree to which they already exist in industry; and the links between policies for R&D, innova tion, industry and international competiti vess. 3.2 The industrial innovation process. So what exactly is «industrial innovation», and under what conditions is it likely to be sucessful? Althoug there exists, as yet, no satisfactory «theory» of industrial innova tion, wc can nevertheless offer a general

is it likely to be sucessful? Althoug there exists, as yet, no satisfactory «theory» of industrial innova tion, wc can nevertheless offer a general

FIGURE 3 MODEL OF THE INNOVATION PROCESS Source: The Management Specialist, Vol. 1 (7), p. 16, 1977 description of the innovation process, and even, on the basis of results from a growing number of empirical studies, say something about the factors associated with success and failure in innovation. Figure 3 provides a rather simplified «model» of industrial in novation. It shows a highly interactive pro cess involving the linkage of technological know-how to a range of perceived societal and market needs via the intermediary of the innovating finn or unit. It would be out place here to offer a detail ed listing or analysis of factors associated with success and failure in innovation, and instead the reader is ref erred to Appendix 2 which summarizes and compares the results of nine major studies of industrial innova tion in a number of countries. For our pur poses, wc can propose a three-input model of the innovation process: — financial inputs; — market information and management expertise: — technical information and expertise. It is probably true to say that today most governments are increasingly becoming in volved in helping to provide all three inputs. To take the first of these, there exists in all the advanced nations a battery of measures for the direct financial support of industrial R&D, while a number of governments are also experimenting with the indirect measu res of innovation-oriented procurement. Ås for the second input, in most countries, there are now systems for the provision of, for example, information on export markets. However, it is with the third input — tech nical information and expertise — that col lective research systems are most concer ned, either as a provider of new technology, or as a channel for communicating informa tion on existing technology to potential users. The latter is particularly important since the evidence on factors affecting suc cess and failure in innovation points over whelmingly to the crucial importance of good communication with external sources of expertise and technical information in encouraging successful innovation. Simply establishing a comprehensive net work of sources of technical information and assistance is, however, not sufficient, and the process of techology transfer itself is fraught with difficulties and uncertainties. 1 There are two main problems. First, the pro cess requires extremely careful manage- ') See, for example, R. ment; left to its own devices, it will not simply «happen». What the innovation literature does point to is the key role played by individuals in technology transfer; suc cessful transfer is more often a matter of agents rather than of agencies. Secondly, the factor that perhaps most consistently differentiates successful inn ovators from those who fail, is their relative degree of understanding of the needs of the user; successful innovators have a much more thorough and imaginative understan ding of users needs than those who fail. This implies the need for companies dra wing upon collective research organisations in the development of new products to make the latter aware of the requirements of the eventual user; the literature is full of ex amples of projects undertaken by external R&D organisations that result in very ele gant technical solutions which are comple tely inappropriate to the requirements of the market-place. Similar problems can arise when firms attempt to enlist external technical aid in tackling problems associa ted with their own production processes. To avoid such problems, one needs to establish ef ficient and on-going communication links between the two organisations. What other f actors influence success and failure in the innovation process? First, there is a great deal of evidence to support the contention that many would-be innova tive small firms suf fer from a scientific and technological «information gap». This gap is made worse by the inability of many small firms to employ, on a full-time basis, quali f ied scientists and engineers. (This does not apply to the highly innovative small firms in rapidly evolving areas of technology such as electronics and computing.) Thus, it would seem that collective industrial research has an especially important role to play in assi sting the innovation endeavours of smaller firms. Since this can be a costly and labour intensive process, this is clearly one area for governmental intervention in the innova tion process. Lastly, it is probably true to say that most innovations fail due to problems of manage ment and marketing, rather than through technical problems. Access to technology (ei ther in-house, or external) is certainly a prime condition for entering the innovation race in the first place: techological know how is an «enabling condition» without which innovation, however well or poorly managed, could not begin to occur. How ever, it is only one condition. Other fac tors, including good management and mar keting, are also vitally important. Now, while governments can do a great deal (via demand, regulatory action, taxation policy, subsidies, technology-supply, etc.) to create a set of environmental conditions favou rable to industrial innovation, their ability to aff ect directly the transf ormation process within the firm (that is, the process for transforming technology into a successful new product or process) in limited. A no table, and laudable, trend in collective indu strial research, evident in certain counties, is the willingness of research organisations to become increasingly involved in this in ternal transformation process, through the provision of non-technical services in such areas as market research and forecasting, and management training. In other words, collective research organisations are becom ing involved in the wider process of indu strial innovation rather than just industrial R&D. However, at the same time it must be recognised that collective industrial re search organisations can only enha n c e the innovative potential of individual firms; they can never substitute entirely for a lack of such potential. 3.3 The role of collective industrial research. In most of the advanced market econo mies, the scientific and technological mf ras tructure plays a key role in the performance of national research and development work. This is illustrated in Table 1, which lists the relative contributions of industry, public and non-profit-making organisations, and higher education (the latter two categories comprising «the mf rastructure») to national R&D in the EEC countries, the USA, Japan and Israel during 1967 and 1975. It can be seen that the signif icance of the infrastructure varies considerably between countries. Despite these national differen ces, however, it seems that governments are laying increasing emphasis on utilising the infrastructure as an adjunct to national innovation policies. 1 This is evident even in the USA, where President Carter's Domestic Policy Review of 1979 included statements concerning the need to improve university/ industry interactions, and the intention to establish a number of govemment-funded industrial research organisations. In this study, wc are particularly concer ned with that aspect of the infrastructure that falls under the heading of co 1 1 cc - tive industrial research, and which can be defined as: «all establishments and activities designed to promote tecnnical progress in a branch of a particular industrial sector or a particular scientific or technical discipline which is being developed in industry.» Justification for the establishment of a system of collective industrial research de rives essentially from a failure of market mechanisms in three areas: (1) Fe w firms will wish to participate on an individual basis in those types of re search which do not offer it a competitive advantage, but which can nevertheless raise the general level of performance of all com panies in its sector. (2) While a marked feature of the twenti eth century industrial scene has been the growth in industry-based R&D, few but the largest high-technology firms perform long-term, fundamental research. (3) Many small firms — especially in tra ditional areas of industry — contain little or no in-house R&D expertise, and can expe rience great difficulties in gaining access to scientific and technological information and advice. This sets them at a marked dis advantage in relation to their larger coun terparts. Not all industries subscribe to collective research, although this varies to some ex tent with the local industrial environment. In certain highly competitive areas of in dustry, collective research may be impos sible, especially when technology is an im portant factor in the competition. The pre sence of multinationals or large dominating organisations in a sector can also preclude collective research activities. In fact, in most countries, collective industrial research or ganisations exist to service the traditional and often highly fragmented sectors of in dustry. Despite this inability to cover all sectors of industry, the indications are that collec tive industrial reseach is generally on the increase; and there is a growing awareness of its potential usefulness to industry at a time of rapid technical and economic change. While governmental involvement in determining the size and direction of collec tive research varies a great deal from country to country — it is negligible in the United States, low in France, growing in the UK, high in West Germany, Japan, and Sweden — nevertheless there appears to be an increasing recognition of its utility as an arm of government industrial policy. In a number of countries, notably West Ger many, Japan and Sweden, collective indu strial research is in particular an important component of government policy towards small firms. Zegveld, Industrial Innovation and Public Policy; Preparing for the 1980 s and the 19905, Frances Pinter (Publishers) Ltd. London, 1981. 3.4 Collective research: some critical issues. As Table 2 shows, collective research is organised and financed in a variety of ways in different countries. Despite these natio nal differences, however, there are a num ber of important issues common to collec tive research in all countries. The most cri tical of these are discussed briefly below. 3.4.1 Funding of collective research. Clearly the mode and level of funding of collective research will have a significant impact on both its eff ectiveness and its ori entation (long-term or short-term; basic or applied, etc.). The three main modes of base funding for collective research are: — subscription income from industrial membership; — compulsory levy (e.g. parafiscal tax); — direct government grants. Other sources of finance are: — government contracts; — voluntary contributions; — contract research, either for a single firm or on a multi-client basis. In most cases, base funding derives from a combination of two or more of the above sources, and government support is often linked to specific projects or programmes.
