ever source, has the advantages of enabling the collective research organization to insti gate comprehensive programmes of re search (as opposed to individual projects), and to undertake more fundamental, long term research to meet the fut u r e needs of industry. On the other hand, it can lead to research for its own sake, often with little relevance to the more urgent current needs of industry. It can also result in a general climate of complacency within the collective research system. Direct govern ment grants have the advantage of provi ding funds to cover the high cost of services to smaller firms, many of which might otherwise not receive assistance. In a number of countries, contract re search provides an important component of funding for collective research. This often relates to product rather than process deve lopment, and in either case should increase the awareness in collective research organi sations of industry's needs. Governments also provide contract support for specific research programmes or projects, support which is in some cases linked to stated indu strial needs and coupled to direct cash sup port for firms. In other cases, it is in the form of a direct grant for a specific piece of research, which is often defined by the go vernment funding agency. One of the disad vantages of the latter system is that it can result in a strong focus on short-term re search and in a tendency to ignore techni cally backward firms; an advantage is that it provides funding for research directed to wards clearly defined industrial needs. A statutory levy (for example, the parafis cal tax system employed in France) has the advantage of guaranteeing all firms in an industry membership of a collective re search organisation. Too high a level of sta tutory support can, however, result in com placency, lack of creativity, and the formu lation of programmes remote from the needs of industry. 3.4.2 Collective research and government policy. Collective research clearly represents a useful adjunct to government industrial po licy, and it is often explicitly employed as such. The degree to which government in fluences collective research programmes de pends largely on the level of government financial support and the means by which this support is administered. In general, it seems that government support, provi ded it is linked to an over all industrial strategy, can have an integrative effect on an otherwise often fragmented research system. In the Netherlands, individual ministries provide funds to TNO for research in areas of special relevance to government policy. In Sweden, the government, via STU, has a strong say in determining the research pro grammes of the various collective research organisations. In France, in contrast, go vernmental involvement in determining di rections of collective research is relatively small and largely negative — in the form of a veto. In the UK, governmental direction of collective research in achieved via the Re search Requirements Boards, which fund selected projects and programmes in Re search Associations. While collective indu strial research in the USA is largely uncoor dinated, with virtually no governmental in volvement, in West Germany it is closely linked to government policy, and indeed po licy towards small and medium-sized firms is implemented principally through the indus trial research associations. Perhaps the clos est integration of collective research to go vernment policy occurs in Japan. Research performed in the Government Centres, which are attached to specific ministries, is predominantly of a medium to long-term nature and reflects national needs as defin ed by the ministries. The Local and SemiPublic Centres, albeit funded primarily through local sources, nevertheless reflect the strong governmental bias towards assis ting innovation in small and medium-sized firms; their research programmes are gene rally indirectly influenced by the Ministry of International Trade and Industry along paths relevant to central government policy. One of the major potential problem areas associated with the utilisation of coopera tive research as an arm of governmental policy is the involvement of government re presentatives in the decision-making pro cess. There are two aspects to this. The first lies with the possible bureaucratisation, and consequent slowing down, of the decision making process. The second relates to the question of the level of governmental under standing of the needs of industry, and the competence of governments to take strate gic decisions concerning the future direc tion of cooperative research. On the other hand, it is probably true to say that in areas such as energy, health and the environment, governments should take the initiative in instigating programmes of cooperative research in line with central policy. In general terms, it would seem sensible that collective research organisations be inside 213

of cooperative research in line with central policy. In general terms, it would seem sensible that collective research organisations be inside 213

volved in implementing policy initiatives co vering areas of high technical risk, pro grammes of long-term research, and major programmes of industrial regeneration and restructuring, especially when they involve the adoption of new technologies. Finally, where collective research is largely decen tralised, as, for example, in Japan, it would seem particularly well-suited to the imple mentation of regional policy. 3.4.3 Programme selection and the decisionmaking process. While governments can influence natio nal trends in collective research, generally it is true to say that programme decisions are tåken primarily by the collective research organisations themselves. In many cases, the decision-making committee will contain strong industrial representation, although this varies from country to country. The major advantage in håving a significant in dustrial representation is that it does — or should — ensure relevance of the research to the needs of industry. On the other hand, it may result in a focus on short-term, pro blem-solving activities to the detriment of longer-term research. A major problem of committee decision making — often involving a number of com mittees sequentially — is that programmes involving a relatively high element of risk are likely to be rejected. As a consequence, programmes can easily involve simply add ing minor changes to existing technologies or products, and opportunities presented by new areas of research can be lost. Collective research institutes need to for mulate an explicit, long-term strategy to guide programme-selection that is based on both current and future market require ments. It should, however, be flexible and responsive to important, and perhaps unfo reseen, changes in technology, the economic climate and market needs. It must be subject to guidance and to regular evaluation con cerning its continued worth and relevance. Evaluation of collective research is, of course, inherently difficult and, indeed, there are few examples of this, although some attempt has previously been made in the UK, West Germany, and France. Thus, wc see a need for strategic thinking on the part of decision-makers in collective research institutes, and for the formulation of research programmes relating both to go vernment policy and to industry's future, as well as current, needs. At the same time, collective research organisations should be responsive in solving the day-to-day prob lems of industry. It is a question of striking a balance between strategic objectives and of reacting to current needs, which requires a difficult combination of central direction of research coupled with flexibility in the provision of technical and advisory services. Finally, probably the major problem of decision-making with respect to instigating short-term programmes or projects is the time it takes to reach a conclusion. In West Germany, for example, this can take as much as 15 months, which is of ten too long for companies requiring rapid solutions to today's problems. This is a consequence of the rather cumbersome, centralised decis ion-making processes of the AIF. In the UK, where decisions are tåken at the level of the individual research association , they are usually made within about six months. In Sweden, periods as short as six weeks are common, especially for relatively minor pro jects involving small finns. 3.4.4 Identification of users. A crucial problem facing any collective industrial research organisation is that of identifying firms which might benefit from its services, and then convincing them to use these services. Probably about 5% to 10% of firms in a sector will be active inn ovators, and will have been involved with a collective research organisation at one time or another; between 25% to 40% will have the potential for innovating, bur need help in this; the remainder, because of their structure, management style, or whatever, will lack the ability to innovate, and there is little that can be done to change this. From the point of view of the collective research organisation, the second group is most im portant, and it is the identification of these firms that is one of the major tasks. Since the group is quite large, it is unlikely that the research organisation could identif y and directly contact all its members. Conse quently, programmes aimed at this group should have a demonstration component so that the benefits, both of innovation and of the use of collective research, can be brought to other members' notice. Most collective research organisations operate in highly fragmented industries composed of a relatively few large, and very many small, firms, and this presents them with very real problems. For example, out side those countries that employ levies, membership is likely to comprise mainly of the large firms in the sector, which then dominate the programme-selection process. Smaller firms tend to see «programmes» of

to comprise mainly of the large firms in the sector, which then dominate the programme-selection process. Smaller firms tend to see «programmes» of

side 214

research as being less relevant than indivi dual projects, often because of their more general nature, and also because of their long-term perspective. Certainly smaller f irms require a speedy solution to their pro blems — especially those concerned with product development — and are unwilling, and frequently unable, to wait while the wheels of bureaucratic decision-making grind slowly to a conclusion. Thus, while it is clearly necessary to establish comprehensive programmes of col lective research, it is also necessary to main tain a high degree of flexibility with respect to individual problems for smaller firms. The particular problems of smaller firms are, of course, widely recognised and collec tive research in several countries is biased firmly towards solving them, most notably in Japan and West Germany. Some collec tive research organisations also discrimi nate in favour of smaller firms by linking subscription rates to either turnover or employment. Because of the limited ability of most small firms to pay for contract research, services to them tend to be extremely costly for the collective research institutes. This is an area in which governments can — and sometimes do — help by providing funds specifically for services to smaller firms. Ide ally these should cover the initial project def inition and the final technology transfer phases, as well as the actual technical pro blem solving. 3.4.5 Collective research vs. contract research. Not surprisingly, the bulk of the research undertaken by collective industrial research organisations is of a «collective» nature, de signed to solve problems common to the ma jority of member firms. This might be con cerned with establishing standards, improv ing overall efficiency, or helping industry cope with new regulations; it more often relates to process, rather than product, de velopment. Increasingly, however, collective research organisations are becoming invol ved in «contract» research for individual firms — or relatively small groups of firms — often in the area of new product develop ment. Contract research can raise very real problems associated with confidentiality, proprietry rights over research results, and especially patents. It can also lead to dispu tes over the extent to which state-subsidized collective research institutes should com pete in the market for specialized consul tancy and contract work against private consultancy firms. On the other hand, con tract research often brings new people into the collective research organisation, and greatly increases its awareness of industry's more pressing heeds, both of which are desi rable from the viewpoint of the research institutes and industry. Overall, contract re search would appear more appropriate in the case of small firms, which most often require rather rapid solutions to specific problems, although some of their needs can be catered for by private consultancy firms. 3.4.6 Information dissemination. There are a number of aspects to the question of information flows between the collective research system and industry. In the first place, there is the problem of making firms aware of the range of services the research system has to offer. Secondly, there is the need for collective research or ganisations to be aware of the current and f uture needs of the firms they are attemp ting to service, including general technical, economic, and market trends that are likely to affect them in the future. Thirdly, there is the question of the dissemination of infor mation concerning standards, regulatory re quirements, etc. Lastly, there is the question of the final transfer of research results to potential user firms. The latter aspect is particularly crucial in fragmented industries characterised by many small firms. These not only need the information, but require it to be «translated» into a language that they can understand. The process of technology transfer to small firms can, if it is to be achieved satisfacto rily, be labour-intensive, involving the em ployment of «brokers». The broker system has the added advantage of increasing the degree of feedback from industry to the re search organisation. Where government funds are involved, it seems sensible that contracts should expli citly include an allowance for achieving technology transfer. This is particularly ap propriate as an adjunct to small firms po licy. Finally, do-it-yourself laboratories of the type established by TNO in the Nether lands have great potential for stimulating information flows and establishing strong personal contacts between members of col lective research organisations and user firms. 3.4.7 Quality of staff and staff mobility. An important question is that of the

between members of col lective research organisations and user firms. 3.4.7 Quality of staff and staff mobility. An important question is that of the

side 215

quality and mobility of staff in collective research institutes. Many of the more senior staff, for example, will have been with the organization for many years, and will often tend to be conservative in their attitudes towards research and to other services of f ered. It also seems that the «image» of col lective research, especially in traditional areas, is such that organizations experience dif ficulty in attracting high quality resear chers. Certainly there exists a general problem of inducing change in some of the long-established collective research organi zations, which must act to their disadvant age at a time of rapid technological and eeonomic change. The general trend towards more contract research might help to overcome a number of these problems. It can provide the possi bility of offering limited-term contracts to researchers, thus ensuring some staff turn over. It can also result in a greater inter change of staff between collective research organizations and industry. In the UK, it has resulted in the employment of more re searchers håving industrial experience ra ther than those with a purely academic background. 3.4.8 Range of services. Most of the work of collective industrial research organizations has traditionally been concerned with solving the technologi cal problems of industry. The bulk of the literature on the industrial innovation pro cess, however, has emphasized non-techni cal causes for innovative failure. Partly as a result of these innovation studies, and partly based on their own experiences, col lective research organizations have increas ingly off ered a range of non-technical servi ces. The «eeonomic» services include the training of researchers and managers, ad vice concerning general reorganisation and rationalisation, and advice on marketing techniques and market trends. The avail able evidence suggests that the provision of eeonomic services is generally on the in crease in most countries. 3.5 Trends in collective industrial research. While the modes of organisation and fi nancing of collective industrial research vary considerably from country to country, nevertheless there does appear to be a grow ing convergence in aims and practices. Cer tainly, a number of general trends in collec tive industrial research are observable in ternationally. The most significant of these trends can be summarised as f ollows: — increasing strategic use by governments of collective industrial research as an arm of industrial policy; — greater emphasis on the provision of «eeonomic» services, for example, man agement-training, assistance with mar keting, etc.: that is, collective research organisations are increasingly becoming involved in the complete process of inno vation, rather than solely with the R&D part of the process; — increased support from governments for the utilization of collective industrial re search by small firms, both through the provision of financial assistance for con tract research and through the use of information brokers; — a generally increasing awareness within collective research organisations of their potential to assist small firms, with or without government assistance; — a trend towards the performance of more generic research, notably in the field of microelectronics (several of the newly es tablished, or proposed, collective re search organisations in various coun tries have been of the generic type); — the carrying out by collective industrial research organisations of a higher per centage of contract research for single firms or small groups of firms, rather than collective research for whole sectors of industry — this has resulted in a greater new produet orientation of re search, and a generally increased aware ness of the problems and needs of indus try; — the increasing regionalisation of services in a number of countries, especially the services to small firms; — greater involvement by collective indus trial research organisations in several countries of other research organisations (universities, government research insti tutes) in their activities. It appears that, while the history and practice of collective industrial research has varied greatly from country to country (long-established and comprehensive in Ja pan; comprehensive with a strong bias to wards small firms in West Germany; highly f ragmented, with little government support or direction in the United States), attitudes, aims and practices are converging. While this is partly due to the fact that the ad vanced nations face similar eeonomic and industrial problems, it is also a result of governments becoming increasingly invol ved in policies for industrial innovation, and in particular, of a growing awareness on

is also a result of governments becoming increasingly invol ved in policies for industrial innovation, and in particular, of a growing awareness on

side 216

their part of the potential utility of collec tive research as an important active com ponent in these policies. On the basis of this discussion of collec tive research systems in general, the problems that may arise in such systems, and the recent trends that they have exhi bited in other countries, wc can now move to consider the specific case of Norway. Wc shall first look at the R&D needs of firms, and go on to describe how the Norwegian system for the support of industrial R&D, and NTNF in particular, has attempted to meet them. 4. THE R&D NEEDS OF NORWEGIAN FIRMS What exactly are the R&D needs of Nor wegian firms? The first point to be made is that different firms have different needs, and that those needs vary both with time, and with the stage of technological develop ment of the firm and its products. When NTNF was set up, very few firms indeed had any R&D capability, so their needs then may not have been that dissimilar. Now, however, the situation is very different. Therefore, in attempting to assess the tech nological needs of firms, it is perhaps necessary to make the distinction between firms operating in traditional areas of in dustry — many of which are f acing growing competition from the newly industrializing nations — and high-technology firms com peting in advanced markets on the basis of their market-related innovativeness. For high-technology firms, the needs is to create new technology, or to have easy and prompt access to technology newly created else where (normally abroad in the case of Nor way) in order to keep generating new pro ducts and stay abreast of their competitors. In contrast, firms using traditional techno logy are more likely to need only to adapt existing technology in order to achieve in cremental improvements to existing pro ducts and processes. Increasingly, however, even these firms are encountering the need to gain access to «new» skills, notably in the area of micro electronics, for incorporation in both their products and production-processes. Failure to adopt microelectronics had a catastro phic impact on traditional watch-manuf ac turing firms in Switzerland and West Ger many, for example, and other craft-based industries (such as printing) are facing a similarly severe challenge. Wc should note, moreover, that different firms not only have different needs; they also have different abilities to supply the inputs required to meet those needs. Small firms, especially in traditional areas, are generally unlikely to have the finance, skilled manpower or technical support f acil ities to carry out research, development, and perhaps even the implementation of the R&D in a new product or process, entirely on their own. Medium-size firms may be able to carry out the implementation stage, but need help with research and develop ment, and the inputs required for those stages, while large firms may need help just with research. However, size is by no means the sole determining factor; for example, some small technology-intensive firms may be able to carry out R&D on their own, or with only a limited amount of outside help. In order to establish what precisely are the R&D needs of Norwegian industry, and what role, if any, the state should take in meeting them, one would need to look in detail at: (i) the industrial structure of the country, in particular the numbers of large, me dium and small companies, and their distribution between the industrial sectors; (ii) the needs of different types of firms (for new products or processes; for high technology, or traditional «low» technology; (iii) the capability of firms to meet those needs internally, and hence the type of external help required. It is not within the scope of our study to carry out fully the comprehensive review that this would entail. Rather, wc have at tempted to look in some detail at the needs of firms in the mechanical engineering and electronics sectors, though the problems in these two sectors can be regarded as illustra tive of some of the more important features of the economy and the R&D needs of tech nology-based firms. 4.1 The R&D needs of mechanical engineering firms. This sector consists of a large number of small and medium-sized firms, with a few large firms (generally spanning several sec tors). Because of the somewhat diffuse na ture of mechanical engineering activities, it is difficult to be precise about the structure of the industry. For our purposes, it can be noted that, taking the rather wide definition used by MVL, the Federation of Norwegian Engineering Industries, overall employment in the mechanical engineering sector totals

wide definition used by MVL, the Federation of Norwegian Engineering Industries, overall employment in the mechanical engineering sector totals

side 217

around 100,000. The average size of MVL member firms, which account for more than half of the sector's workf orce, is slightly over a hundred employees. Many of the smallest firms are, however, less engaged in manu f acturing than in carrying out service acti vities for other companies. In our study wc interviewed representati ves from 5 small firms, 23 medium-sized, and 14 large firms (including a few in ship building). Many are old firms, using rather traditional types of technology, and, like their competitors in many Western Euro pean nations, they are experiencing severe economic dif ficulties. The reasons are comp lex, and vary with the different sectors of the mechanical engineering industry. Tra ditionally the strongest sectors in Norway have been in shipbuilding and in the pro duction of specialized machinery (for ex ample, agricultural equipment). As is well known, the shipbuilding industry has suf fered first at the hands of the far more effi cient Japanese yards, and now from compe tition with the low labour-cost Third World econqmies, the move into specialized ship construction håving been insuf f icient to su stain existing capacity. These problems have been compounded by the recent world recession. As the shipbuilding industry de clined, so did the range of general mechani cal engineering workshops providing specialized equipment for ships. According to many of the industrialists interviewed, the problem has been that the shipbuilding sector has been extremely slow to move into the offshore business, partly because of the availability of subsidies for traditional ship building activities, but also because they do not possess the technology or skills to pro duce equipment to the necessary tolerances and specifications. Dn Veritas, reported problems in certifying the equipment of many Norwegian producers, some of whom, during our interviews, recognized this fact. Many now realize the need for more skilled labour, improved production technology, modem machine tools and quality assur ance schemes, and in particular access to more basic research in materials techno logy. And some at least are starting to seek outside help, often in an attempt to enter the lucrative offshore market. However, the resources channelled in the past into lon ger-term research in mechanical engineer ing seem to have been insufficient to create the bank of knowledge and expertise that innovating firms now need to draw upon. The problems experienced by other sec tors of the industry are similar in many respects. There have been structural problems (with low labour-cost countries moving into certain areas), problems with the strength of the Norwegian kroner, and a large number of firms appear to be suff ering from a low rate of both product and process innovation. Many of the firms that wc vi sited have realised, or are beginning to real ise, the need for new process technology to reduce the effects of high labour costs, in particular the need for automation, or semi-automation (through the use of micro processors, robots, integrated manufactur ing processes, etc.). For this, what is required is not so much new technology as adaption and application of existing technology. With two major producers of robot automatic handling devices, and drawing on important work at the research institutes on compu ter-aided design and manufacturing (CAD/ CAM), a few advanced firms (for example, Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk) have developed quite sophisticated process technology. However, these are the exception rather than the rule, and until more of the smaller firms begin to apply advanced technology to their production methods, they will achieve neither the efficiency they need to compete in export markets, nor the capacity to pro duce reliable and high-quality hardware. Many of the firms that wc visited also seem to be experiencing great difficulties with product innovation. For example, a number of previously successful agricultu ral engineering companies have been slow to realize that higher farm labour costs in the industrialised countries necessitate the pro duction of more automated equipment. Gra dually they have lost their export markets, and are now threatened in the home market as well. A few have started innovating, in troducing electronics, for example, into their equipment, and are beginning to re cover. Overall, however, many firms are re alising that the future lies in more special ised products with a higher value-added content. Norwegian firms are normally too small to compete on standard products with the large foreign firms which benefit from economies of scale. Instead, they must at tempt to identify market «niches» not covered by such firms where there are small but significant markets — perhaps in other small countries or in less developed coun tries. The manuf acture of such products will often involve batch production. What are required, therefore, are flexible production processes, so once again process technology is probably going to be more important. And because specialisation is generally brought

production processes, so once again process technology is probably going to be more important. And because specialisation is generally brought

side 218

about through modif ication of existing products, the R&D needs are more likely to be for the modification and use of existing technology, rather than for the creation of new technology (which is perhaps best left to the big overseas companies). If these needs are to be met, then the support of R&D in mechanical engineering will have to be given higher priority than in the past. 4.2 The R&D needs of electronics firms. The electronics industry in Norway comprises a relatively small number of large firms (several at least partly foreign owned) which account for a high percentage of total employment, together with a much larger number of small firms. In total, there are approximately 40 firms that might be regar ded as constituting the electronics sector, al though there are also a number of large electrical engineering firms which have, be cause of recent advances in technology, moved closer to the electronics industry in certain areas (for example, f ibre-optics tech nology). Taking the general electronics and electrical engineering sectors together, the overall employment is approximately 30,000, this being divided almost equally between the two sectors, and the total number of firms is around 60, with large firms (i.e. firms with over 500 employees) constituting around 75% of the workforce. In our study, wc interviewed industrial representatives from 9 large firms, 9 me dium-sized firms, and 8 small firms. Their interests range from the telecommuni cations business, the construction of compu ter hardware, medical electronics, and the manufacture of CAD/CAM terminals, to ac tivities more in the area of electrical engin eering. Out of the 26 firms interviewed, 7 could be regarded as coming in this latter area of electrical engineering. Because of the relatively small number of firms and their very varied interests, it is dif f icult to pick out signif icant trends in the electronics and electrical engineering sec tors as a whole. One can, however, identify a number of areas that have proved relatively successful over recent years. These include: civilian and military telecommunications, and internal communications equipment; minicomputers; automated design equip ment for the mechanical and electrical en gineering industries; navigation and ship borne equipment; and, in the electrical en gineering sector, the manufacture of electri cal cable. Equally, there are a few areas where Norwegian industry has apparently been much less successful, notably in consu mer electronics, but also in integrated-cir cuit manufacture. Because Norway does not have such a long-established tradition and heavy invol vement in. the electrical sector as it does in mechanical engineering, the pressures for structural rationalisation as a result of Ja panese and Third World competition are perhaps less severe. Nevertheless, many of the firms visited have realised that, in the intensif ying international competition in all areas of electronics, innovation is the key to success. They are therefore actively involved in adopting new technologies, generally from abroad. And unlike in the mechanical engineering industry, many of the more suc cessful firms are small enterprises. For most of these firms, their R&D requirements centre on the need to keep abreast of their competitors in a sector that is characterised by fierce competition and rapidly advancing technology. What they most require, there fore, is, first, highly skilled manpower, and, secondly, mechanisms for ensuring good and promt access to «state-of-the-art» tech nology from overseas. However, as far as attempting to create «new» technology is concerned, the barriers to entry are prob ably too great for most Norwegian firms to overcome (a point to which wc shall return in our analysis of the ef forts by SI and AME in the field of micro-electronics). Finally, it is worth noting that some of the smaller firms visited seem to have realised the importance of putting electronics into other industrial products. Given the problems of the mechanical engineering in dustry, and the limited range of alternatives for the future, the active collaboration of mechanical and electronics firms in new product development may prove an ex tremely important avenue for success. As yet, however, all too f ew firms seem aware of the benef its that may arise from the selec tive introduction of electronics technology (and it does not necessarily have to be the most recent and advanced technology) in other industrial sectors. Here, there is per haps a role for institutes to carry out dem onstration projects that would help to con vince some of the currently sceptical firms of the potential benefits. All of this may require a significantly higher level of re sources than has been made available in the past. 5. THE SUPPLY OF R&D, AND THE ROLE OF NTNF So far, wc have tried to specify the R&D needs of firms. The next question is how do

in the past. 5. THE SUPPLY OF R&D, AND THE ROLE OF NTNF So far, wc have tried to specify the R&D needs of firms. The next question is how do

side 219

NTNF and the Government in general try to meet them? Any answer involves first look ing briefly at the the history and evolution of NTNF, its main aims, the type of assis tance it now provides to finns, and its relationship to other mechanisms for the support of industrial R&D. 5.1 NTNF — a brief history 1 . When NTNF was set up in 1946, R&D activity in industry and government labora tories was in general rather low. There was also little infrastructural support from the government for industrial R&D activities. The first three steps tåken by NTNF were therefore (i) to give funds to support research at existing research establishments; (ii) to initiate a fellowship scheme to send people overseas for training, a scheme still in operation today; and (iii) to establish committees of industrialists and researchers to look at different areas of industry and their research needs. In many cases, these committees sugges ted setting up new collective R&D institutes to serve particular industrial and govern ment sectors, one of the main arguments used to justify the establishment of collec tive research institutes being the success of such establishments in the United States and Germany. In addition, NTNF decided to create a main Central Institute (SI) serving the needs of a much wider industrial and government constituency. By the end of the 19505, there were approximately 10 new in stitutes. As each important new need arose, a new institute was set up to attempt to meet it. In other words, at the time NTNF represented an extremely flexible system for the support of industrial R&D. During the 19605, the growth in the num ber of institutes continued, and in addition, after the Research Survey by NTNF in 1964, certain new mechanisms for the support of industrial R&D were instigated. These in cluded the Development Fund (or «Risk Bank») providing loans of «risk capital» to f irms seeking to innovate, and the commen cement of NTNF grants to industry for R&D projects. (By this time, many of the larger firms had strengthened their R&D capabilities, and NTNF provided funds to catalyse further growth in industrial R&D activity.) However, as the support system 1 Much of the information in this section is tåken from the OECD report, Policies for the Stimulation of Industrial Innovation, Country Reports, Vol ll— 2, 1978. centred around NTNF became larger and more complex, the need for more formal strategic planning arose. It was for this rea son that the system of Long Range Plan ning was eventually introduced. The 1970 s have in turn witnessed a num ber of changes in the system. During this decade, it proved.increasingly difficult for NTNF to obtain annual increases in its budget similar to those obtained in earlier years, and only one more institute was founded. Instead, various new general mechanisms and special initiatives (specif ic to a sector or area of technology) were devel oped, including the Innovation Plan (ad ministered jointly by NTNF and the Indus trial Fund), the Ship Plan, and the micro processors initiative. In 1981 (at the time this study was carried out), NTNF compr ised 15 NTNF institutes, 4 affiliated institu tes, 18 Advisory Committees, 2 Ad Hoc Com mittees, 7 Project Committees, and 2 Project Offices (The Space Division, and Norsar), and as Figure 1 in Section 2 above shows, these are merely part of a wider system of state support for industrial R&D. 5.2 The aims of NTNF and of its institutes. The overall objective of NTNF is to pro mote R&D, both in the private sector of industry and the public sector. However, the emphasis of its activities has changed over time. For the first twenty years of its exis tence, NTNFs main aim was to build up industrial and applied research potential, while from the mid-1960's the aim has been more towards increasing the competitive po wer and growth of industry through rein forc i n g the R&D capability of firms which already possess a scientific and tech nical capacity (cf. OECD, ibi d  p. 109). Finally, when the Long-Range Planning system was brought into operation at the start of the 19705, there was a further shift in emphasis. The R&D capability of Norway was to be strengthened not only for the pur pose of aehieving increased prosperity through continued economic growth, but also for «increased human well-being and improvement of the environment», and for «insuring satsif actory settlement and indus trial localization from a geographical point of view» (J.B. Quinn and R. Major, «Norway: small country plans civil science and tech nology», Science 183, p. 179, 1974). Dur ing the 19705, these two additional concerns with the environment and regional develop ment came to absorb an increasing fraction of NTNFs resources, the proportion devoted to the original aim of stimulating economic

regional develop ment came to absorb an increasing fraction of NTNFs resources, the proportion devoted to the original aim of stimulating economic

side 220

growth dropping from about 90% in 1968 to just over 50% in 1978. More recently, how ever, this trend has started to be reversed, on the argument that increased prosperity is first required in order to pay the costs of meeting the second and third goals. The objectives of the NTNF Institutes are also three-fold: (i) to develop long-term research and technological know-how; (ii) to encourage the adaption and us of this know-how and research through contract work carried out for industry and government; (iii) to ensure the widespread use of specialized know-how and technical equipment (OECD, ib i d . , p. 113). Thus, to a certain extent, these three aims correspond to the three stages of «research», «development», and «implementation» in the overall R&D process. In later sections, wc look in turn at how well the institutes per f orm each of these tasks. 5.3 The flo wof funds. 5.3.1 NTNF. It should be noted that a significant amount of this money is in turn recycled back to institutes, since the recipients of these grants are en couraged to use at least part of it in sponsor ing research at institutes. 5.3.2 Mechanical engineering. Håving looked briefly at the funds re ceived by NTNF and how they have been distributed, wc turn next to the two commit tees with which wc have been concerned. Other firms that have received heavy support include Kongsberg Våpenfa brikk, Kværner Brug, Hordaland Mek. Verksted, the TESA companies and SIAG. (Wc also include in Appendix 9 a list of firms that have received support from the Innova tion Plan through the VF Committee.) Amongst the institutes, SINTEF has bene fitted most from VF support, receiving about half (43,5 million kroner) of all VF project funds over the period 1977 to 1981. A number of comments can be made about the VF Committee. First, the average size of its project grants is rather small — in 1981, the average value is 270,000 kroner (compared with approximately 1 million kroner for the TE Committee in that year), which corresponds only to about one man year of effort per project. As a result, both institutes and firms have complained about what they see as a destructive fragmen tation of research efforts. Several people made the point that the VF Committee structure, with all its associated sub-com mittees, is rather large and cumbersome for the relatively small amount of money it has to distribute, and that, because so many dif ferent interest groups are represented, all wanting support, there is a tendency to grant a small amount of money to everyone — «to give everyone a piece of the cake», as some put it. In the view of these critics, one can never expect very startling results from the ensuing small projects. Secondly, it seems that there have been some problems of overlap with other com mittees, particularly the Shipping Commit tee, the Continental Shelf Committee, and the Metallurgy Committee, the reason being rante (million kroner) 35.3 40.4 50.3 59.7 73.1 rF % of total project rante 13% 15% 15% 16% 14% 12% 12% 11% 11% 10% TF project grante to inlustry (mill. kroner) 4c 4.1 3.8 4.8 5.8 5.9 6.6 6.5 7.2 Total NTNF project grante to industry (million kroner) 14.2 15.0 16.1 17.1 21.0 28.0 34.2 34.2 37.6 6,7 VF % of total project grante toindustry * * 25% 22% 23% 21% 17% 19% 17% 15% % of VF funds given to industry * * 55% 41% 47% 51% 45% 46% 39% 39% * Figures not available.

In industry, the main recipients have been AME, Electrisk Bureau (EB), Sim rad, and Norsk Kabelfabrik. Of the institu tes, ELAB and SI have each received very considerable support amounting to just over a quarter of all the TE funds allocated over the period 1977 to 1981, as can be seen from Appendix 10. Four main comments should be made nere. First, the present secretary of the TE Committee, appreciating the need to con centrate research resources, has made con siderable eff orts to increase the average size of project grants in order to avoid the problems of «f ragmentation» mentioned ear lier. Between 1978 and 1981, the average va lue has increased from 400,000 kroner to over one million kroner. In part, this has been made possible by the replacement of the previous rather large and cumbersome system of committees and sub-committees, by a dramatically slimmed-down organi zation. The procedure now is that a d ho c groups are convened to examine questions of more strategic importance (for example, policy in micro-electronics) and are then dis banded on completing their task. It has thus been made easier to curtail long-running and unsuccessful projects that previously would have been supported by an intercon nected network of industrial and institute interest groups. Secondly, there have been considerable problems of overlap, since both the Automa tion and Data-Handling Committee and the Space Division also support electronics R&D. However, there are currently moves within NTNF to remedy this situation by reorganisation and amalgamation of the groups concerned. Thirdly, both the percentage of NTNF project grants distributed by the TE Com mittee, and the percentage of TE funds allo cated to industry, have declined signifi cantly over recent years. In 1972, the Com mittee was responsible for 15% of NTNF project grants, and just over a third of this (35%) went to industry, i.e. a total of about 5% of NTNF project grants were allocated to firms through the TE Committee. By 1979, this figure had been approximately halved. However, some of this drop was comside 223

were allocated to firms through the TE Committee. By 1979, this figure had been approximately halved. However, some of this drop was comside 223

pensated for by increased grants to industry for electronics projects made by the Auto mation and Data-Handling Committee, and by the Space Division. Lastly, Appendix 12, Table 2, shows that TE's support for industry is not so heavily concentrated on large firms as is the case with VF. 55% of project grants between 1977 and 1981 were awarded to large firms of more than 500 employees (compared with 70% for VF), and only 38% of Innovation Plan grants. 5.3.4 The institutes. NTNF institutes receive four types of funding: (a) general funds from NTNF; (b) NTNF grants for specific projects; (c) funds for research done under contract for other government bodies and for firms; (d) funds earned from contracts with customers abroad (including international bodies) (cf. OECD, ibi d  p. 113). It should be noted that the percentage of institute funds obtained in the form of gen eral NTNF support has decreased over time, particularly over the last decade, dropping from 30% to 8%, while the percentage ear ned through sponsored research has in creased to about 55%. This might be partly interpreted as reflecting the increased ability and willingness of industry and pub lic agencies to support longer-term research at the institutes. However, even if such a trend has occurred (and many of the institu tes would probably doubt that is has), it has almost certainly not been sufficiently large to compensate for the considerable drop in the percentage of institute income in the form of general grants. As a result, there has inevitably been some swing in emphasis away from longer-term research towards shorter-term development work. And since general funds have to be used by institutes to cover the costs of educating staff, infor mation activities, and co-operating with other research institutions, little now re mains for discretionary use to support pro mising new areas of research that are at too early a stage to form the basis of a project application to NTNF. Consequently, al though institutes are supposedly autono mous, with their own Boards, in practice they nowadays have very little autonomy indeed. Of the four institutes included in this study, only SI is an NTNF institute. How ever, the sources of finance at SINTEF are not markedly different, with the same four types of income. It has been argued (particu larly by NTNF institutes) that SINTEF re ceives a fifth and very important source of funds in the form of indirect subsidies from the Technological University (NTH). It is true that SINTEF does receive the benefit of f ree buildings, and that NTH staff are often used in SINTEF projects, but in return SIN TEF staff contribute to NTH by providing extensive teaching services. It is SINTEF and NTH policy to try to keep the exchange of services between them roughly in bal ance. However, the most important point to note is not whether one organisation does or does not subsidise the other (over which there is much scope for argument), but that b o t h benefit substantially from their close relationship — if the two existed indepen dently, they would both be worse off. This is of considerable relevance to NTNF institu tes, an issue to which wc shall return later in this report. The financial situation at Rogalands forskning is, however, somewhat different from both SI and SINTEF, in that it recei ves its general funds in the form of grants from the Rogaland and Stavanger Councils rather than from NTNF. However, it too earns the bulk of its funds through NTNF project grants and sponsored research con tracts with industry and public agencies. To sum up, these first sections of the re port have described the range of R&D needs of firms, and the mechanisms through which NTNF currently attempts to meet those needs. In the following sections, wc shall look in turn at the various types of support offered by the institutes (longer term research, development work, imple mentation, and various other services to in dustry), and try to assess their effectiveness and appropriateness to industrial needs. This will be f ollowed by an evaluation of the overall system for the support of industrial R&D. Finally, on the basis of the results from the earlier sections, wc identify areas where there appear to be certain problems at present, areas on which wc suggest the Industriforskningsutalget might profitably focus its attention. 6. ASSESSMENT OF SI'S RESEARCH EFFORTS The Central Institute for Industrial Re search (SI) was set up in 1950. Because a major part of Norwegian industry was con centrated in the Olso area, it was felt necess ary to have a single centralised institute covering a wide range of applied research and able to meet the needs of several of the

it was felt necess ary to have a single centralised institute covering a wide range of applied research and able to meet the needs of several of the

side 224

more important sectors of the Norwegian economy. During its 30 years of existence, SI has grown in size, so that it currently em ploys about 340 staff and has an annual budget of approximately 70 million kroner. Its development has not been without problems, however, particularly during the first half of the 19705, when the Insitute passed through a period of financial crisis. At the time, projects appear to have been costing more than planned and some were not being completed at all. The researchers themselves seem not to have been well geared to meeting the demands of their user community, and were poor at remaining within both budgets and time schedules, f ailings which at the time the central man agement of the Institute were unable to con trol. When the first Director of SI retired after some 25 years of service, there were therefore certain problems to be overcome. Since then, far greater emphasis has been placed on the financial aspects of project management, a point to which wc return in Section 11 when discussing the strengths and weaknesses of the various institutes. SI has three main sources of income: (i) NTNF general funds; (ii) NTNF project grants; (iii) sponsored research. The relevant figures are shown in Table 7 below. It can be seen that over the ten-year period, the percentage of Sl's income de rived from the first of these sources has hal ved from 28% to 15%. The income from sponsored research first declined from 53 % in 1970 to 44% in 1973 when the institute experienced certain financial difficulties, and has since increased to 58%. However, of that 58%, only 32% comes from Norwegian industry, with the remaining 26% from pub lic agencies, other institutes, and abroad. Moreover, of the 32% from Norwegian in dustry, perhaps a third comes from firms receiving support from NTNF or the Inno vation Plan, and there fore represents government money being recycled through industry to the Institute. Therefore, the per centage of SI funds that corresponds to Nor wegian firms investing their own money in the Institute is probably less than 25%. Table 7 Sources of Income at SI for 1970 — 79.
