Wc con centrated our attention on the last two of these, interviewing the Section Heads and about 25 researchers. In these interviews, wc obtained detailed information on nearly 30 projects. Of these, eight could be classified as «research» projects— that is, they began as long-term research work funded initially by NTNF, with industry generally contri buting at a later stage as the work progres sed to the «development» phase. The remain ing 20 were «industrial R&D» projects — i.e. with far less research content, and generally funded by a public agency or by a firm (sometimes with an NTNF grant) right from the start. The assessment of these industrial R&D projects is left to a later section where development projects at all three institutes are considered together. Wc shall concent rate here only on research projects. (1) AUTOKON. This project involved the development of a system for automated ship design, or, more generally, for the numerical design and con struction of large steel structures. The reside 225

of a system for automated ship design, or, more generally, for the numerical design and con struction of large steel structures. The reside 225

search work began in about 1960. Financed initially by NTNF, the Aker Group gradu ally took over more and more responsibility for the funding, although NTNF continued to provide support for small parts of the work. Total R&D costs for the AUTOKON system have been in the region of 50 million kroner, most of which has been provided by industry, although NTNF was heavily invol ved in the early 19605, and it therefore rep resented a large project. At its peak, it em ployed about 15 people at SI, while others were engaged in testing the system at Aker Shipyards. In 1968, Aker set up Shipping Research Services (SRS) to take on marketing and såles of the system. Since then, SI and SRS have worked jointly on further development of the system with the latter taking a stea dily increasing responsibility for the work. There can be little doubt that this was an extremely successful research project. Not only were its results fully implemented in industry, but it was also a significant com mercial success. AUTOKON gave Norway an international lead in certain fields, and the system was sold to over 200 shipyards around the world. The latest version is still being marketed. It has also been used in the design of aircraft and submarines. Comments. (i) One of the main reasons for the suc cess of this project was the long-term nature of the funding, which made possible con tinuity, particularly in the basic research, even though parts of it took longer than expected. (ii) A second and perhaps even more im portant reason for the success was the ex tremely close contact between researchers (at SI) and users (initially the Aker Group, and later the AUTOKON Users Club). This contact existed right from a very early stage, and gave rise to an iterative process in which first Aker explained what they wan ted, then SI interpreted this and made cer tain developments; Aker tried it out, and then made more precise specifications of what they required. (iii) There was a very clear distinction be tween the roles of SI, the Aker Group, and SRS. SI represented the researchers, Aker the users (as shipbuilders), while SRS pro vided the marketing. This is probably the main reason why relations between the three groups have overall remained ex tremely good. (iv) As the work progressed from the stage of research to development and implemen tation, there was a gradual transfer of tech nology and of responsibility for the project from SI to SRS. (v) Another reason for the success of AUTOKON was that the technology invol ved was unique, and could therefore be pioneered internationally. Hence, it was not too difficult to create a significant market. In cases where this uniqueness is læking (for example, the ELDAK project— see be low), perhaps a more effective course for a country of Norway's size might be to import existing systems from overseas and use them, rather than carrying out the R&D required to develop a new system. Experi ence with using them might in some cases then result in the identification of a new problem, where a research programme could eventually lead to a unique and hence ex ploitable innovation. (v) Several researchers at SI felt that a pro ject like AUTOKON would not be possible today. As one of them observed: «It would have been completely impossible to start a project like AUTOKON after 1973. It had lots of basic research parts in it, while now it's all quick and dirty methods giving half-good results.» (2) ELDAK. This was a project where the ultimate goal was to produce an integrated computer aided design and manufacturing (CAD/ CAM) system for electronics. However, its more limited objectives included drawing at tention to the growing importance of CAD/ CAM within electronics, bringing institutes and firms together in this work, and eva luating the concept of an integrated CAD/ CAM system. It ran from 1972 to 1977, and was (at least formally) a collaborative pro ject between SI and ELAB. It was funded by the TE Commitee, its total cost being about 3.5 million kroner. The needs of industry were meant to be represented through the three firms on the steering committee for the project. If AUTOKON was the most successful re search project at SI, ELDAK was surely one of the least successful. When it was termin ated in 1977, there was no operating CAD/ CAM system to show for the efforts, and, according to the firms concerned, there was little benefit to industry. Even the resear chers concerned recognised the failure of the project. «Industry came to SI and ELAB in 1977, and said they no longer believed in the EL DAK concept. They wanted another con cept, and everyone agreed to bury the proside 226

and ELAB in 1977, and said they no longer believed in the EL DAK concept. They wanted another con cept, and everyone agreed to bury the proside 226

ject. The main project leaders had already quit the project and started new projects. No-one wanted to carry on.» However, on the positive side, the project did succeed in bringing CAD/CAM, and the work on it at institutes, to the attention of f irms, and it did contribute experienced re searchers to later CAD/CAM initiatives in both institutes and industry. Commen ts. (i) One of the main reasons for the f ailure of the project appears to have been poor project management. In particular, there was no single project leader, and the degree of cooperation between SI and ELAB was, to say the least, limited. Each institute worked on separate aspects of the task almost inde pendently, changing direction whenever they wished without consultation, and therefore failed to connect up the various parts of the system, in the latter stages of the project. (ii) Doubts were expressed to us about whether the researchers concerned were competent enough to take on the task, with some interviewees feeling that the project was too ambitious or at least too premature. The ELAB staff , it was claimed, had a rather limited experience of CAD/CAM, while SI researchers failed to complete their part of the task. (They did produce the CASS pack age, which was sold to a few firms, but this was not intended at the start of the project.) (iii) Another key reason for the f ailure of the project was the lack of interest and in volvement from industry. At the time, in dustry was generally unf amiliar with CAD/ CAM and with its possible applications. (In addition, one of the firms on the steering committee was close to bankruptcy, and therefore busy with more urgent matters.) The lack of industrial interest meant, first, that there was an absence of feedback on industrial needs into the project. This led to a vicious circle in which industry saw the research work as being too «academic». Sec ondly, it had the result that industry put very little effort (apart from some general advice) into the project, and the funds there fore proved inadequate. (3) EPOKE. When ELDAK was stopped, EPOKE star ted. Its aim was to produce an integrated CAD/CAM system for digital circuits. It has run from 1977 to date, and so far the TE Committee has spent around 7.5 million kroner on the programme. Again, it is a collaborative effort between SI and ELAB, but in this case two f irms (initially three) are more closely involved and are meant to con tribute a sum of money to match that put in by NTNF. However, in the course of inter views at the institutes and with the finns concerned, it became clear that one of the firms appears to have been putting in only some 60% of the amount they should form ally be spending (the remaining 40% con sists of expenses they would undergo any way without EPOKE), while the other firm has been putting in very little money indeed (apart from some testing) — instead they apportion some of their own internal CAD activities to count as their contribution to EPOKE. Some lessons have obviously been absor bed from the earlier ELDAK project. EPOKE has a stronger steering committee on which industry is well represented to en sure that full account is tåken of industrial needs in all the work carried out, and there is a single project manager. From the insti tutes point of view, the research has been reasonably successful, but the benefits to industry are far less certain. One researcher involved was quite open in conceding this. «A large amount of money has been spent on the project, and all the firms have got out of it is a few experienced people. They could have bought the same computer tools from overseas companies for just a fraction of the cost. In addition, there was not proper con tact between the researchers at ELAB and SI, and between us and the final users. When industry comes to put it into produc tion, there will be a problem because by then the researchers will have started to work on something else, and when the users have problems, they won't be able to get any help from us. Institutes are not properly geared to the phase of transf erring research results to firms, and helping them to implement and actually use them.» In industry, the view is even more scepti cal. The aim is that one particular company should take over the system and market it, but as one person closely involved in the project said: «Lots of money has been spent on EPOKE, and little has come out of it (apart from ICASS). (Finn) have the marketing rights, but I'm not sure if there will ever be a product to take over and go out and seil.» C omments. (i) The project got off to a bad start with the bankruptcy of one of the three indus trial partners. This both reduced the total industrial funding available and removed from the project useful expertise from the electronics industry.

trial partners. This both reduced the total industrial funding available and removed from the project useful expertise from the electronics industry.

side 227

(ii) Nevertheless, despite the presence of two finns on the steering committee, there has again been a lack of industrial interest in the project. (Indeed, one of the two firms had previously bought a rival overseas CAD/CAM system and, when the possibil ities of replacing this with a more custom ised EPOKE system began to recede, gradu ally dropped its interest.) The resulting poor contact between researchers and potential users means that there has been insuff icient feedback to the researchers on user-needs, and relatively little transfer of expertise to the users. (iii) Project management, and in particu lar the co-ordination of the two separate institutes with each other and with the work going on in industry, has again proved diffi cult. The first phase of this research involved semiconductor, and in particular transistor, research. It began when Stavik, who had been working in a North American firm on transistor technology, returned to Norway. At the time, there was little R&D on transis tors taking place in Norway, so a research group was set up at SI, which NTNF sup ported heavily. This group drew upon staff from FFI, which also moved into transistor technology in the late 19505. The aim was to produce the technology needed for Norwe gian firms to manufacture electronic com ponents. With this aim, AME was set up in 1965, backed by the Aker Group. However, there were problems in transferring tech nology to AME until Stavik himself moved to the finn. AME began to produce pnp pla nar transistors. At the time, most transistors were of the npn type, so the AME product was relatively advanced and the finn was able to charge a high price. This was obvi ously an ideal product for a company with a relatively small output. The same is true for the pressure sensors developed a little later by SI and also produced by AME. Neverthe less, because of its small size in world terms, AME was continually beset by financial dif ficulties, and at the end of the 1960 s the Aker Group withdrew its backing. Eventu ally G.A. Ring was persuaded to take over responsibility for the financial support of AME. At the end of this first phase, the benefits to industry of the components work were unclear. A Norwegian producer of electronic components had been set up, but the finn had not been a great commercial success, although some of the work at SI in the latter part of the 1960 s did prove rather more beneficial to AME. In particular, the thin film hybrid circuits developed by SI were very advanced, and were used (some years later) by AME in making the high frequency radio sets which led to some recovery in the finn's economic fortunes in the mid-70s. The most recent phase of Sl's micro electronics work has involved monolithic in tegrated circuits and thick-film techniques. From 1969 to date, NTNF has invested some 25 million kroner in this work at SI. The main objective is to assist industry in start ing to use modem micro-electronics, es pecially custom-designed circuits, which could involve production or application of micro-circuits or both. Originally, the main emphasis of the programme was directed towards technology, that is to produc ing micro-electronics circuits in Norwegian industry (at AME). The aim was to design and develop the technology at SI (up to the prototype stage) and to transfer the produc tion capability to AME for the manufacture of the circuits. In some cases, SI has also engaged itself in certain aspects of produc tion, and has been criticised for this by in dustry. Currently, SI receives about 4.5 mil lion kroner for the purchase of equipment. However, according to most of the resear chers, their eff orts are still sub-critical — i.e. below the threshold, or «noise» level, re quired to build up a viable capability for the design and production of micro-electronic circuits. Besides supporting SI, the TE Com mittee has also invested heavily in R&D work at AME. A total of 30 million kroner has so far been spent, much of it on work aimed at the production of micro-electronic components. Vet these represent the least successful of AME's commercial activities, constituting only around 12% of the finn's annual turnover. Moreover, most Norwe gian firms do not appear to have a very favourable impression of AME's products, and have instead turned to overseas manu facturers for micro-electronic components. Recently, relations between AME and SI have begun to become more dif ficult. AME, believing that it has now built up its own R&D capability, is therefore not keen to see NTNF money spent at SI on work that AME at least sees as duplicating their own efforts on the design and production of integrated circuits, money which they feel could be better used to speed up their own develop ment work. Reinforced by the limited success of com mercial production of integrated circuits at AME, the emphasis of the work at SI has,

own develop ment work. Reinforced by the limited success of com mercial production of integrated circuits at AME, the emphasis of the work at SI has,

side 228

over the last two or three years, switched to the design aspects of micro-electronics and the Institute now sees itself as a centre for the custom-design of integrated circuits. Underlying this change is the belief that it is perhaps more appropriate to emphasise the importance of custom-designed inte grated circuits for Norwegian industry, whereby a finn's in-house micro-electronic production capability is perhaps less important than the design (and hence the specific function) of the micro-electro nic circuits. It is therefore important that a firm is involved in the design phase of micro-electronics, production being left to AME or foreign integrated-circuit produ cers. Hence, SI has been developing know how on the design side, in order to teach industry and help them develop a capability for designing and using custom-designed in tegrated circuits. So far, six firms have ex pressed interest in developing their own cus tom-designed integrated circuits together with SI, and the Institute has made a num ber of prototypes. As far as the benefit to industry of Sl's work on the design side is concerned, it is probably too early to east a def inite judgement; one important criticism expressed by some concerns the danger that SI is attempting to assist too many firms — some of which are below viable size for this work — with the result that efforts may again prove sub-critical. C omments. (i) The efforts of SI and AME aimed at the production of integrated circuits have al most certainly been sub-critical. Scale of re sources is obviously a crucial factor in this type of advanced technology. One senior electronics researcher estimated that an in vestment of 10 million kroner a year was needed just to keep equipment up to date in this rapidly developing field. This requires a market of several tens of millions of kroner, and he suggested that AME's likely market was on order of magnitude too small.An in vestment of the size needed could only come from a multi-national company, but for one reason or another no such company ever committed itself to developing and putting into production prototypes built by AME. (ii) At a broader level, the problems of SI and AME in relation to micro-electronics seem to reflect the lack of a clear perspective on the part of the TE Committe a f ew years ago as to where efforts should be concen trated in this field. Whilst the Committee has recognised the importance of concen tration, there appear to have been no gen eral policy directives as to the attention and emphasis which should be devoted to the different (yet inter-related) aspects of micro-electronics technology: design, devel opment, production and application. As the distinctions between researcher, producer, and user have become rather blurred, the setting of priorities — in terms of what SI or AME should and should not do — has be come increasingly difficult, whilst there has been a growing belief that no small country such as Norway can do everything to an equal degree. The situation has not been improved by certain disputes over what should be the division of labour within the area of micro-electronics R&D. For ex ample, SI and SINTEF have sometimes found it difficult to agree who should do what. Similarly, many electronics firms feel resentful about SI involving itself in activ ities, such as micro-electronics pilot produc tion, which, they believe, should be left to industry where firms must react to market forces. Relations have therefore suffered, and firms which might have benefited from SI or even NTNF help have turned away. (iii) As regards the acquisition of new knowledge, the experiences of SI in micro electronics have indicated that the transfer of technology takes place most effectively when people actually move from one insti tution to another. Technology was certainly transferred by Stavik when he returned from North America to SI, and again when he moved to AME. AME has also benefited from its recruitment of former SI-employees (and various micro-processor based firms have in turn grown up around ex AME staff). Without this physical transfer of people, AME would not exist today. Some have expressed the belief that more should be done also in the way of sending SI staff to work at North American universities and electronics firms. As one SI researcher ex pressed it: «You have to fight to get support to do this. SI does not do nearly enough to en courage this sort of thing. I think it is det rimental just to stay here for ever and ever.» (v) In contrast, concentration of re sources on supporting the actual perfor mance of R&D and operation of production activities in micro-electronics has been clear and prolonged. The TE Committee has con centrated a large fraction of its total re sources here on SI and AME, which has left little support for other electronics activities in institutes and particularly in firms. Some

its total re sources here on SI and AME, which has left little support for other electronics activities in institutes and particularly in firms. Some

side 229

electronics firms were particularly critical of this, one putting its views as follows: «Until very recently, SI and AME have had nearly all the money available for micro-electronics. And this has essentially been wasted, with SI and AME supporting each other on ill-considered ventures into high technology areas that they cannot handle. It meant that a few years ago when SINTEF wanted to go into micro-electronics in a big way, their route was blocked be cause SI claimed that this was their sphere of influence.» A number of the more advanced electro nics firms have also stressed what is perhaps the most negative result of the policy of concentration at SI — the lack of highly skilled researchers trained in micro-electro nics technology. Most of Norway's output of industrial scientists and engineers arises from NTH, many of these gaining practical experience at SINTEF. And since SINTEF has not received support from NTNF for micro-electronics design until relatively re cently, the effect on manpower flows into industry has been serious. (v) The very long-term nature of the f unding at SI (this work has been supported for 20 years) also seems to have created cer tain problems. One researcher admitted, «The project could probably have been run in a more efficient and aggressive man ner. The generous support for SI can easily be a pillow on which it is good to sleep. Some of the group have been here a very long time. This stability in personnel has had some bad effects. Their knowledge has not been updated, and at times they tend to fall asleep a bit.» (5) Electro-optic Sensors. This work began at SI in 1973, developing out of the previous work on components, and has so far received 3.8 million kroner from NTNF. The aim has been to develop electro-optic sensors that can be produced by AME and used in Norwegian produets. Like the earlier sensor work at SI, this has proved rather more beneficial from a com mercial viewpoint than the integrated-cir cuit work. Comments. (i) Much of the transfer of sensor techno logy from SI to AME has been accom plished through SI researchers being re cruited by AME. (ii) Sensors represent a more specialised produet than integrated circuits, which gives AME a better chance of competing commercially in both the Norwegian and export markets. (6) Robotics. Work on robotics as suen began at SI in the early 19705, although the Institute had been working on the application of compu ters to automated handling from the late 1950 s within a long-term basic research pro gramme funded by NTNF. Håving gained significant expertiSe (even in world terms) with hydraulic servo-controls and measure ment systems, as well as with computerised control, SI found it difficult to industrialise their output. As one researcher complained: «Wc had gained a little expertise with ro bot arms. But industry thought wc were just playing about. Wc couldn't f ind a use for the robot arm.» The sectors of Norwegian industry that could conceivalby have benefited from this work were rather underdeveloped, and in any case were suspicious of what they saw as the «academic» approach of research institu tes. But SI persisted in trying to seil their ideas to industry, and in the end established contact with a firm that is now a major producer of automated handling techno logy. As part of an initiative made by TESA (the co-operative association of six firms in Rogaland of which the finn concerned is a member) requesting help with the electro nics for the TESAMAT robot, much of the early SI work in this area was finally imple mented in industry. The technical manager of the finn was clear in his praise for SI (and NTNF): «The SI project to develop a servo-control system based on electronic computers was a very smart project. Certainly no-one thought in terms of robots at the time, and it was only later that Norwegian industry was «ripe» to make use of this basic research. But what would industry have done if far sighted people had not funded this research? The industrial benefits could not have been predicted...l could not gi ve you a better ex ample of why basic technological research is usef ul Not only this: if SI had said, «Wc only want high «blue-sky» projects» then their work would have been a flop. They tried to industrialise their work once significant re sults were produced, and the effect today is not only that wc have meth o d s ; wc have produets and processesas well.» At a later stage, SI moved onto work con cerning microprocessor and real-time carte sian-axis movements, software systems and base programmes for robot control, and ro bot vision. This work was funded largely by NTNF, first by the VF Committee and later by the Automation and Data Handling Committee. However, the period from about 1974 to 1978 was not particularly successful

the VF Committee and later by the Automation and Data Handling Committee. However, the period from about 1974 to 1978 was not particularly successful

side 230

in terms of implementing the results of this work in industry. Nor were relations with SINTEF, which was also engaged in robotics R&D, always very good, Indeed, there were allegations of results being «stolen». Then, in 1978, KORO was set up. This informal committee consists of representa tives of Norway's two robot manufacturers, TESA, RF, SI and SINTEF (who joined a little later). KORO has performed an ex tremely important f unction, first of all coor dinating robotics research activities, and secondly bringing together researchers with robot manufacturers and robot users. As a result, the second of the two robot manufac turers in particular seems to have gained significant benefits from Sl's more recent work. In addition, there has been consider able «spin-off» from the robotics R&D to other industrial projects. Prominent exam ples include the automated tunnel-borer de veloped for a major construction company, and work on control systems for an excava tor manuf acturer. Comments. (i) Until KORO was established, the links between the institutes engaged in robot re search and industry were not as good as they might have been. In long-term research of this nature, these links should be built in right from the start, so that researchers are fully informed about the problems and needs of both producers and users. (ii) For process techology, one of the main problems tends to be bringing together the producer of the process (for example, the robot manufacturer) and the user. In the case of robotics, this task has been perfor med by TESA. Once producer and user are brought together, they are then able to specify their research needs quite precisely when they approach an institute like SI. Our interviews with industry suggest that the precise specification of research needs is one of the key factors in determining whe ther a sponsored project at an institute is successful or not. (iii) Again there seem to have been problems between SI and SINTEF. The re lations between research institutes in gen eral are poor. (FFI appears to have closer links with SI and ELAB than they do with each other.) In this case, the poor contact led to needless competition, duplication and even conflict between SI and SINTEF. Eventually KORO managed to resolve some of the difficulties, but the situation should perhaps have been recognised sooner by NTNF. (7) and (8) GPM Internordic Project, and SPICS. These two research projects have only been in existence two or three years, and it is therefore too early to assess the likely benefit to Norwegian industry. S ummary . Of the six long-running research projects that wc examined in detail at SI, — ELDAK — was unsuccessful; — EPOKE — may or may not be capable of being implemented in industry, but by all accounts has been rather expensive for what is likely to be achieved; — micro-electronics — has resulted in some transfer of technology to AME, but has not been a great commercial success, particu larly given the level of resources consumed; — sensors — has involved transfer of tech nology to AME, and with rather more com mercial success; — robotics — has led to significant results that have benefited manufacturers of robo tic and automatic handling devices, and various other firms through «spin-off», pro jects, particularly in automated process technology; — AUTOKON — has yielded a system that has been marketed with considerable suc cess, both in Norway and abroad. Wc leave a further discussion of Sl's strengths and weakness to Section 11, when certain comparisons are made between all the institutes. 7. ASSESSMENT OF SINTEF'S RESEARCH EFFORTS SINTEF was founded in 1950. Soon after the decision to set up the new Central Insti tute for Industrial Research in Oslo, the Technical University (NTH) decided to es tablish their own contract research organi zation at Trondheim, many of the staff feel ing that, in choosing the site for SI, insuffi cient attention had been given to the bene fits of potential links with NTH. Through out its history, there has been extremely close collaboration between SINTEF and NTH, with exchange of personnel, shared use of facilities, and, perhaps most import ant, substantial recruitment by SINTEF of NTH graduates. SINTEF currently has a staff of around 950, and this is still growing. It has a some what complex organizational structure con sisting of Affiliated Institutes (such as the Electronics Research Laboratory, ELAB) as well as SINTEF Departments (see Appendix

structure con sisting of Affiliated Institutes (such as the Electronics Research Laboratory, ELAB) as well as SINTEF Departments (see Appendix

side 231

13). Wc focussed specifically on ELAB and Department 17, the Production Engineering Laboratory. Two other Departments, De partments 16 (Materials Technology) and 18 (Machine Design) also obtain substantial funding from VF, but since part of their activities fall outside the mechanical engi neering sector (and since ELAB and Depart ment 17 are both large and required our full attention during the week of interviewing), these were excluded from the study. Like SI, SINTEF had a single Director during its first twenty years of existence. However, unlike SI, the transition from the first Director to the second does not appear to have been marked by any great difficul ties, nor does SINTEF seem to have faced the same degree of economic difficulty as SI. The smooth transition between one Director and the next was possible partly because the person taking over was previously Rector of NTH and therefore fully familiar with SIN TEF when he started. But of far greater importance is the fact that SINTEF has al ways been a distributed system, as opposed to the centralized hierarchical organi zational structure of SI. The structure of SINTEF is based on a number of largely independent centres, each responsible for their own scientific and financial activities, with only a f airly low degree of coordination and strategic planning carried out by a small central administration. The smooth running of the Institute is therefore less dependent on the Director. Like SI, SINTEF has three main sources of finance: (i) NTNF general funds; (ii) NTNF project grants; (iii) sponsored research. However, this third category is best broken down into sponsored research for in dustry and for the public sector. The rele vant figures are given in Table 8. These show that SINTEF currently earns roughly similar amounts from NTNF projects, public sector projects, and industry, while its sup port from NTNF general funds (5%) is only about one-third the corresponding figure for SI (15%). As with SI, one problem faced by SINTEF is that much of its money from NTNF comes in the form of small project grants, but SIN TEF does seem to be reasonably successful in grouping these projects together, thereby giving some coherence and continuity to its research efforts. For example, Department 17 recently applied for 13 grants which could quite easily be combined to form 6 larger programmes. ELAB is organised into 12 main research groups. Since wc were less interested in ac oustics work, wc concentrated our attention on 9 of these, and on the 6 groups within Department 17. In each case, wc generally interviewed the group leader and one other member of the group, making a total of about 30 interviews in all. The same ques tions were put to them as had been address ed to SI researchers. From these interviews, wc obtained detailed information on about 50 projects. Shorter-Term Longer- Research and Term Development Total Research Projects paid Projects for at least partly by f irms As with SI, wc shall consider the research projects here, and leave an assessment of sponsored industrial research projects to a later section. 7.1 ELAB (1) Material and Component Technology. This project ran between 1963 and 1979, and TE spent some 6 million kroner sup porting the work. It consisted essentially of fundamental research, involving stu dies of thin films, thick films, metals, insula tors and semiconductors. The researchers succeeded in establishing design rules for making various devices (for example, sur face acoustic wave devices), but their work for a long time failed to excite much indus trial interest at least in Norway. In the early 19705, attempts were made to involve AME in the production of certain of these devices, but these never proved very successful. Ac cording to some, the main reason was that AME was at that time heavily engaged in implementing technology developed by SI. The research carried out by ELAB in this area was undoubtedly of high quality. As will be seen later in the discussion of publi cations and citations, their work seems to have had a significant impact on the ad vance of scientific knowledge, and even elec tronics firms, who were generally critical of ELAB's contribution to industry, agreed that ELAB contained some very high calibre researchers. However, much of their early research was carried out largely in isolation from industry, and therefore bore little re lation to the needs of firms. One local finn was undoubtedly helped to apply thick-film technology to their existing products, but most benefits came at a later stage with a pilot production line and, more recently, Norway's first separate thick-film circuits production facility. In addition, some firms have lately begun to take over some of the surface acoustic-wave technology. There have also been some indirect benefits, both in the form of later spin-off projects, and in the form of trained manpower to industry (discussed later). C omments. (i) Several of the electronics firms inter viewed felt that, in view of the large invest ment in this project, the returns had been somewhat disappointing. They argued that, if this work had been supported by NAVF, it would probably be considered a successful project; however, it was carried out with NTNF support, and its contribution towards NTNF's overall objective (of promoting R&D that will benefit Norwegian industry or public agencies) was, they claimed, rather small. They theref ore felt that NTNF, before it begins to support long-term research of this nature, should do more to ensure that it is in an area related to the needs of industry. (ii) Research, particularly long-term re search, needs regular evaluation and good project management. Without this, resear chers are likely to go off in pursuit of ideas that seem «interesting», even if they bear little relation to industrial requirements. That at least is the view of many firms. (iii) The close relationship between SI and AME seems to have created difficulties for electronics researchers at SINTEF whén they attempted to develop some industrial interest in their work. (iv) In the case of one local firm that has benefited from the thick-film technology, one of the most important factors behind the successful transfer of technology and know-how was the recruitment by the finn of the former project leader at ELAB. He is now the finn's Head of Development. (2) Sensors. ELAB's work in sensors began in the early 19705, when it was felt that this would be an appropriate field in which to the use the laboratory's existing competence. (At the time, there was much discussion of finding small market «niches» where Norwegian in dustry could be competitive, and sensors ap peared to be one such field.) ELAB had de veloped certain thin-film technology (see project 1 above), and was looking for possible applications. Since integrated circuits were out of the question (because this activity was already going on at SI), they chose sen sors. An NTNF grant was subsequently ob tained for thin-film work, and some pres sure sensors were developed. ELAB then tried to persuade AME to produce these, but after two years of collaborative work the ELAB

work, and some pres sure sensors were developed. ELAB then tried to persuade AME to produce these, but after two years of collaborative work the ELAB

side 233

project was terminated, apparently because of lack of capacity at AME. Another development concerning work for Dn Veritas aimed at creating a sensor for monitoring ships' diesel engines. After sev eral years working with very advanced tech nology, ELAB succeeded in developing the temperature and wear sensors required. Al though a local electronics firm was interes ted in producing these, AME demanded the production rights, apparently on the grounds that NTNF had decided to concent rate its efforts on helping AME and there fore the benefits of all NTNF-supported work should go to them. Then, after the production rights had been handed over, AME decided not to go ahead with manuf ac turing the sensors. Eventually, after the ef forts to find a Norwegian producer had proved in vain, Veritas turn to a Swedish finn that was interested in producing them, with the result that the benefits from this work have gone outside Norway. More recently, ELAB has turned to ion selective sensors. This time they have suc ceeded in involving AME in production, and AME are now marketing them. lon-selective sensors are a new development, and, al though the market is relatively small, there is currently little international competition. Comments. (i) Again, the close relationship between SI and AME has not made it easy for ELAB to interest industry in implementing the tech nology they develop. (ii) lon-selective sensors seem to represent a good product «niche» in which a finn like AME can complete. (3) Electrical Stimulation of the Nervous System. Work on this topic has been carried out over the last six years. It has been supported partly by NTNF, but mainly by internal ELAB funds. The aim is to take some of the new technologies developed in electronics and transfer them to the field of biomedical equipment, much of which is still based on relatively old, even primitive, technology. This is a relatively small project (the main reason being the difficulty in obtaining funds discussed below), but it has led to sig nificant medical benefits, through introduc ing new techniques thought not to be avail able in hospitals elsewhere in the world. Comments. (i) The transfer of technology from one area of research (in this case, electronics) to another can lead to significant advances and substantial benefits. Moreover, since state-of-the-art electronics is not essential, the transfer and implementation can be a relatively cheap process. (ii) This project illustrates very well the problem of research falling between two possible sources of funds. Applications to NTNF have been turned down on the grounds that this is «medicine», not applied research, and those to NAVF have been re jected on the basis that this is «technology» not science. This example points to the need for better cooperation between the Re search Councils. In addition, it suggests that existing mechanisms for the support of R&D may be slow to recognize the emerg ence of a new «embryo» field of technology. Vet it is precisely at this stage that support is most needed if an international lead is to be established and capitalized upon. (iii) This project also draws attention to some of the problems of prioritisation and concentration of research at Norwegian in stitutes. Though not discussed in the section on SI, the biomedical technology group at SI has had NTNF support for a number of projects. One of these, supported by a TE grant of 840,000 kroner, in vol ved the devel opment of a wheelchair. This was essentially a product development involving fairly un sophisticated technology, and the finn con cerned has decided not to implement the wheelchair handed over by SI, partly be cause of severe technical and design problems. So while SINTEF have not been able to obtain funding for a more basic pro ject, with potential long-term benefits, SI have spent a large amount of money on a short-term product development that a finn might well have been expected to support, had the commercial prospects been better. The loss, at least as far as biomedical engineering in Norway is concerned, is that the failures at SI have recently led to the termination of much of the work in this field (in part because of the sub-critical ef fort), while at SINTEF lack of support has severely hampered their efforts. Had it not been for the SINTEF/SI rivalry, there might have been closer co-operation and a more profitable division of labour. (4) Electro-optics. Work on electro-optics began in 1972. It has been supported first by NTNF, and more recently by the Telecommunications Agency (PPT) and industry. NTNF has so far invested about 6 million kroner (includ ing 1 million kroner for 1981). In 1980, the

Telecommunications Agency (PPT) and industry. NTNF has so far invested about 6 million kroner (includ ing 1 million kroner for 1981). In 1980, the

side 234

work received support of 1 million kroner from NTNF, 0.5 million kroner from PTT, and 0.35 million kroner from industry. The work has had three aims: (a) materials technology — to develop the process of making fibres; (b) measurement — building up equipment for characterising fibres and evaluating properties; (c) applications of fibre-optics. Realising from their earlier work the im portance of interesting industry at an early stage in the project, ELAB visited some of the major cable-manufacturing firms. The manufacture of electric cables involves f airly traditional technology, and initially the firms were not very enthusiastic, parti cularly about the first of the three aims described above. It therefore took a few years for ELAB to demonstrate to the firms the possibilities, and to convince them. Now, two firms are keen to develop expertise and keep abreast of the technology, even if they are not yet seiling any products based on the new technology. Moreover, a third finn (a subsidiary of a multinational company) has also given some support, partly to ensure that its competitors do not steal a march on it. The PTT has played an increasing role in co-ordinating the electro-optics research, di viding up the various activities between ELAB and industry, and in setting goals (for example, the development of a test-system). Comments. (i) The important role of PTT in bringing ELAB and industry closer together should be noted, as should the use by PTT of the mechanism of «procurement» for the stimu lation of R&D, a mechanism of ten neglected in discussions of government R&D policy. (There have, however, apparently been problems of lack of initiative and poor inter nal co-operation at PTT over the last year as a result of individuals associated with this project changing jobs and internal reorgani zation. These have had adverse effects on the co-operation between PTT, ELAB, and industry so essential for this projecfs suc cess.) (ii) One problem associated with a project of this nature is deciding who should benefit from the results of collective research. Often the general NTNF policy seems to be to create technology «for all», although there are exceptions to this like AME. However, of feiing new technology to all the firms may mean that n o n e will be prepared to take it up. Individual companies are understand ably reluctant to back a project such as this one on electro-optics it they think that the results of their investment in ELAB will be made freely available to their competitors who may then implement the new techno logy without «paying the entrance fee». The PFI practice (see Appendix 1) of choosing the firm most likely to benefit from new technology and then working alone with them might be judged «unfair» by rival f irms, but may well lead to a greater level of overall benefit to the nation. (iii) The initial doubts of cable-manufactur ing firms concerning the first aim of the programme — the development of techno logy for the production of fibres — have to some extent been reinforced. Two firms were rather critical of ELAB's intention to enter a high-technology field where, given the level of resources available, at best a duplication of existing work was all that could be achieved. What these two firms most wanted was the development of basic expertise on fibre-optics that could be tap ped when they imported already developed technology. As far as these firms were con cerned, ELAB's desire to enter the field of new production technology was not what industry required. The development of basic expertise was sufficient. However, it should be noted that the two firms which were cri tical are associated with multinational cor porations, and their needs and views may not therefore be typical of Norwegian elec trical firms. In addition, there is perhaps a certain inconsistency in the firms expecting ELAB to be able to develop basic expertise in optic fibres without any involvement in their production. (iv) Probably a more important failure in this project has been the inability to attract risk capital from independent Norwegian companies. The technology developed at ELAB was very advanced, and it came at a sufficiently early stage to warrant an ap proach to certain firms, which might then have been able to develop a significant local market based on various unique appli cations of electro-optics in electro-mechani cal industries. So while the level of techno logy in this project was very high, the strate gic thinking perhaps was not. (5) ELDAK. This project has been dealt with in the previous section on SI. (6) EPOKE. This has also been covered earlier.

(7) Fault-Tolerant Computing. This work began at ELAB as an internally financed project in 1976. Since 1977, the TE Committee has supported it to the tune of 1.4 million kroner. The main aim is to gain knowledge and experience in the area of fault-tolerant computing, and to transfer this to industry. Two companies are repre sented on the projecfs steering committee, ensuring that industrial needs are fed into the research process. So far ELAB has transferred a little knowledge to these and other firms interested in the results, but no more substantial benefits have yet emerged from the work. Comments. (i) The steering committee ensures that the needs of firms are tåken into account by the researchers, which is crucial in a project of this nature; but unless ELAB soon begins to produce results of more interest to firms, their commitment to the project is likely to decline as it has done in other projects. (ii) Outside ELAB, doubts were expressed to us about whether the researchers involved would be able to make any signif icant im pact in this field. It was stressed that, when Norwegian research institutes decide to pur sue technologies which are already being developed overseas by far more generously funded groups, then competitiveness is only possible if the project is carried out by ex tremely able researchers at the foref ront of their field internationally. (8) Integrated-Circuit Design. This work only began at ELAB in 1979, and so far it has received total NTNF sup port of 1.5 million kroner. In 1981, the re searchers were awarded twice the sum they requested, an unusual occurence but one in line with TE's current emphasis on the de sign of integrated-circuits. The aim of the project is to establish a centre for custom designed integrated circuits. So far, ELAB has designed circuits for one finn, and is starting to attract interest from others. It is, however, far too soon to assess the success of this project. The question might neverthe less be asked as to why the previous ELAB work on materials and component technol ogy was not terminated earlier so that re sources could be transferred sooner into the obviously important field of integrated circuit design. (9) Simulation of Digital Transmission. Between 1972 and 1976, NTNF provided support of 0.6 million kroner for this project. In 1976, PTT became interested, and has since spent about 1.5 million kroner on the work Industrial firms, however, initially showed a certain lack of interest, but, partly through the efforts of PTT, they have now become sufficiently enthusiastic to start in vesting in it (contributing just over 0.5 mil lion kroner in 1980). C o mmen ts . (i) Like the electro-optics work, this project shows a gradual evolution through several stages — the research was first funded by NTNF, then a public agency (PTT) took over, and now industry is beginning to con tribute to the development work and to gain some of the benefits of the earlier research. (ii) The role of PTT as a co-ordinating agent, using procurement as a tool to stimulate industrial R&D and convincing firms of the need to invest, should again be noted. (10) Microwave Circuits and Antennae Systems. Begun in 1973, this project has so far re ceived approximately 5 million kroner from the TE Committee. Initially, the aim was to produce microwave circuitry, developing the basic techniques required, but more re cently work on microwave antennae and technology has been added. The project has already led to the development of an auto matic (CAD) system for the design and test ing of microwave components. One firm in particular has benefited a great deal, instal ling a system developed by ELAB, while other firms have also started to gain some benefit. Comments. This project has been carried out by what is generally regarded as one of the most highly proficient research teams at ELAB. However, perhaps a more important reason for the successful transfer of technology to the main finn concerned in this work was the recruitment of the former group leader at ELAB to work for the company. In ad dition, there have been other exchanges of personell between institute and finn for a few days at a time. Again, this emphasises that the best mechanism for the transfer of technology and its implementation in new products and processes is through the move ment of people. Summary . the Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk CNC product.
Based around the Kongsberg computer, this
product was one of the first CNC control
systems in the world when it appeared in
1969. Since then, it has pro ved highly suc
cessful (indeed it is regarded by some as the
«Rolls Royce» of the market) and has been
sold all over the world. Department 17 has
continued to work on machine tool CNC
developments, enabling Kongsberg to con
stantly improve their product-line.
(2) Part-Programming Centre.
This is the software system to produce and
check programmes for different machine
tool systems. Again, research work in the
Department led to a prototype and eventu
ally a product (the PC 200) that Kongsberg
have been able to seil in the second half of
the 19705. The work carried out at SINTEF
was f unded by NTNF, while Kongsberg were
given approximately 4 million kroner from
the Innovation Plan to implement the sys
tem.
(3) Direct Numerical Control (DNC) for Integrated Manufacturing.
This programme was f unded by NTNF be
tween 1974 and 1977. It in vol ved coupling
together the first two developments descri
bed above, and again resulted in a product
for Kongsberg.
C o mmen t .
(i) At present, only one Norwegian mech
anical engineering firm is sufficiently tech

for Kongsberg.
C o mmen t .
(i) At present, only one Norwegian mech
anical engineering firm is sufficiently tech
nically advanced to benefit from the bulk of
Department 17's work on numerically con
trolled machine tools. The Departmenfs re
lationship with Kongsberg is closer to the
FFI pattern of interaction with industry
(through close collaboration with selected
individual firms). Because there are no Nor
wegian competitors, there have not been the
same problems as Sl's close involvement
with AME has led to in the electronics sec
tor. This måkes it much simpler to transfer
technology from institute to industry, and
opens the way to the extremely close coop
eration that has characterized the relation
ship between the Department and Kongs
berg over the last 15 years. One researcher
described the situation as follows:
«Wc are really Kongsberg's R&D depart
ment»,
while at Kongsberg the view was that,
«Wc would not be alive but for SINTEF and
Bjorke. He has been very important for the

Over the years, there has been a suc
cession of new systems based on the ideas of
Professor Bjorke and his colleagues, many
of them successfully implemented and pro
duced by Kongsberg, or incorporated in the
subsequent improvements to the products.
The pattern has been one of continuous ev
olution: first, technology creation (or com
petence building); then technology transfer
(or competence use); then technology cre
ation in a new area, and so on.
(4) Robot CNC.
Begun in 1977 on the basis of internal
f unding, this work has to date received sup
port of about 1 million kroner from NTNF.
The aim is to develop a general control sys
tem for handling devices on production
lines. The Department decided not to adopt
the already existing SI system for CNC but
to develop their own, a decision criticized by
KORO on the grounds that scarce resources

side 237

should not be used to duplicate research ef fort. Since the two Norwegian robot manu facturers already make their own control systems, they have shown little interest in SINTEF's work so far. As a result, the re searchers do not know exactly what firms want and what sort of product is required. C omment. (i) Unless firm industrial contact and in terest is established soon, it is doubtf ul whe ther this programme is likely to yield major industrial benefits. At present, it seems ra ther less successf ul than the work in nume rical control for machine-tools. (5) Dedicated Production Control Systems. In 1973, it was realised at Department 17 that production control using microcompu ters would become increasingly important in industry. Two software systems were de veloped and built, based on the Kongsberg mini-computer. These have subsequently been sold to a number of medium-sized and small firms. The programme was completed in 1979, håving first been supported inter nally, then by NTNF, and finally by indus try. Again, this seems to have been a suc cessful project, and this time it is medium sized, rather than very large, companies that have benefited. C o mmen ts . (i) Success in implementing this work has depended heavily on SINTEF personnel working for short periods of time in the companies concerned. This movement of re searchers into industry has played a large part in transf erring the technology to firms with a minimum of problems. (6) Manufacturing Cell. A total of 10 million kroner has so far been spent on this programme, just over half coming from NTNF. The goal is to divide up f actories into manufacturing «cells». Profes sor Bjorke recognised that what most Nor wegian firms required was not complete automation (which would be resisted by the workforce, and, if implented, lead to higher unemployment) but a work «amplifier». In this, workers operating the cell for a single shift would stock it up so that it was able to work automatically around the clock for the next two shifts. The cell-concept thereby links together and attempts to solve a num ber of problems f acing Norwegian industry. First, there is the legal restriction against night shifts which can severely limit the productive use of expensive capital equip ment. Secondly, there is the question of the motivation of the workforce. The manufac turing cell is interactive — it leaves human beings much more in control (something Bjorke sees as crucial, håving himself worked on the shop-floor). It also permits decentralisation of management. Workers can plan their own work, rotating jobs, for example, if they so choose, and hopefully this will result in enhanced motivation. Thirdly, there is the economic factor — it helps reduce the eff ect of high labour costs on Norwegian products by introducing a higher overall level of automation into pro duction. Fourthly, the system is modular in nature, and firms can install different ele ments as and when investment can be affor ded. Another feature of the system is that it can be custom-designed, thus offering potential benefits to firms of markedly dif ferent sizes (especially medium-sized en terprises), as well as capable of being imple mented across a range of different indus trial sectors (it can, most importantly, be used for small as well as large batch produc tion). The manufacturing cell is about to be in dustrialised by Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk, who hope to produce the system (the cost of some 45 million kroner is likely to be met indirectly by the US Air Force as part of the F lOO parts deal). The first stage here will be to develop a pilot project at Kongsberg where the equipment is used and tested in house. In addition, Department 17 is de veloping further aspects (such as quality supervision, and equipment supervision) to the cell concept with the aim of arriving at an integrated manufacturing system. C omments. (i) The project began with an unusually clear view by the researchers of the future needs of industry for: (a) semi-automation, but not complete automation, in order to increase effi ciency while at the same time being suit able for use with small batch production; (b) decentralisation; (c) day-shift work only; (d) reduction of the effects of high labour costs. (ii) On the basis of this, a strategic plan was developed in which theoretical develop ment of the cell concept would be followed by implementation of the first phase at Kongsberg. After operation and testing of the prototype system on its own facilities, Kongsberg would produce and market a range of different modules.

After operation and testing of the prototype system on its own facilities, Kongsberg would produce and market a range of different modules.

side 238

(iii) This is one of the few R&D projects in institutes where prior economic calculations have been made of the likely costs and pay back for firms implementing the system. Ac cording to Professor Bjorke, these suggest that it could be profitably adopted by most companies manufacturing complex mech anical components that use numerically controlléd machines and batch production; with the minimum cost of a system being around 500,000 kroner, several hundred Norwegian companies could apparently benefit, with a payback-period of between 12 and 18 months. If these calculations are ac curate, the manufacturing cell could have a tremendous impact on the economy, as well as håving considerable export possibilities. (i v) While Department 17 has by all ac counts produced a commercially viable sys tem, and Kongsberg are willing to under take development to the market stage, it was extremely difficult to find the necessary funds for industrialisation. According to Kongsberg, the costs of development amount to around 45 million kroner (with 10 million kroner going to SINTEF), and at present there are no mechanisms to support prototype development by firms. Without the happy circumstances of the Fl 00 deal, the system might not have been developed further. (v) The main problem with this project will be non-technical in nature — convinc ing firms that, if they take the risk, they will benefit. Mechanical engineering firms tend to be rather conservative, and are not easy to convince. Moreover, researchers are often not very adept at marketing themselves (al though Department 17 appears to be rather better than most). Perhaps what is needed is some sort of R&D «broker». Alternatively, perhaps for purchasing this sort of innova tion, what is required is a government backed «insurance scheme», under which firms would be expected to find their own money to implement the new system, but were guaranteed that, if it proved unsuc cessful, their costs would be recompensed. Such a system already exists for inno v a t i n g firms under the Industrial Fund, and perhaps this could be extended to pro vide guarantees to firms adopting radically new technology produced by Norwegian manufacturers. This might then encourage firms to adopt a less conservative attitude. And if the manufacturing cell system does prove as profitable as the calculations sug gest, such an insurance scheme would not prove very expensive to operate. (7) Process Technology. Work in this area began in 1976, and to date NTNF has given 2.2 million kroner in support. The overall aims are to increase knowledge of machining light alloys and es pecially aluminimum; to develop suitable machine-tools; to produce new cutting data; and to circulate this information to interes ted sectors of Norwegian industry. This pro gramme of research links in with the Government strategy to add value to alu minium before it is exported, and theref ore to develop expertise on machine tools for aluminium. As with the previous project, a market survey was carried out, and this sug gested the existence of a signif icant «hole» in the market. Department 17 hope to transfer the technology to a machine-tool factory that has been badly affected in recent years by foreign competition, but which the re searchers believe would be able to compete successfully in this specialised market. C o mm en ts . (i) Again, the project began with a clear view of the needs of Norwegian industry, and in particular the need to add value to primary products before export. (ii) Based on this, a well-defined strategy was drawn up. (iii) A market survey has been used to es timate market needs and the likely success of the new product. S ummary . Out of the 7 main research projects that wc assessed at Department 17, — Robot CNC — has experienced problems because of the lack of industrial interest and the consequent shortage of infor mation on user needs; — Process Technology — is proceeding suc cessfully so far, and is likely to be imple mented in the near future; — Manufacturing Cell — is starting to be implemented, and could have a very con siderable impact; — CNC, Part-Programming Centre, DNC, and Dedicated Production Control Sys tem — have all been implemented, and firms are benefiting. 8. THE ASSESSMENT OF ROGALANDS FORSKNINGS RESEARCH EFFORTS RF was established in 1975 for three main reasons: (a) the need for the Regional College to have a research capability; (b) to meet the R&D needs of local industry;

in 1975 for three main reasons: (a) the need for the Regional College to have a research capability; (b) to meet the R&D needs of local industry;

side 239

(c) because of the feeling that Rogaland had previously been somewhat neglected in the national distribution of R&D resources. From the start RF has had very close coll aboration with the Regional College, with the same exchange of staff, shared use of f acilities, and recruitment of staff that cha racterise SINTEF's relationship with NTH. As did NTH with SINTEF, the Regional Col lege has expended a good deal of resources in nurturing Rogalandsforskning into a position of near financial independence. From the beginning, the underlying philosophy at RF has been to build on, and take maximum advantage of, its proximity to Rogaland firms. SI and SINTEF in parti cular are both rather distant for good com munication to be maintained between them and Rogaland firms. RF, with its much better contacts with local firms, has the potential to keep abreast of current indus trial needs and problems, providing the «radar detection service», as one RF resear cher put it, that the more distant institutes cannot supply. In addition, it can share both equipment and expertise with local firms. A second element of RFs philosophy is to build on areas of local industrial strength — in particular, petroleum technology and ro botics — and on the tradition of mutual co-operation between firms. Thirdly, it was recognised that RF did not in general pos sess the resources to compete with SI and SINTEF on basic research. Instead, RF had to concentrate on applied research and pro duct development geared closely to meeting the more pressing needs of industry. Some RF researchers wryly describe their mission as that of «bare-foot technicians», approach ing firms directly and offering to seil them skills. Implicit in this is the recognition that, in order to resolve the great majority of in dustrial problems, one does not have to have f irst-rate expertise or knowledge of the most recent and most sophisticated technological advances. As a result, while in some areas RF actually carries out its own research, in others it instead serves as a «middleman» between industry and the big centralised in stitutes. RF's long-term objectives can hence be divided into two. First, it will continue to develop as a national or even an internatio nal centre for petroleum technology. The Petroleum Technology Department is al ready the biggest and perhaps the leading Norwegian centre (at least for certain areas), håving found it relatively easy to obtain funds from Stavanger-based oil companies (which are «encouraged» by the Government to invest in Norway in order to improve their chances of being awarded further North Sea sites). Currently, this Depart ment plans to approximately treble in size over the next fi ve years to employ about 100 people. It hopes to buy its own oil rig so that it can develop automation techniques and improve rig safety. In addition, Government agreement has now been given for the intro duction of an MSc course on Petroleum Technology in co-operation with the Regio nal College (which perhaps sees this as a way of gaining «back-door» entry to the uni versity status up till now denied it — it is worth noting in this connection that the site of the college and RF is still referred to as «The University Site»). Besides petroleum technology, there are hopes that the indus trial automation group at RF will also grow to form a national centre. RF's second long-term goal is to streng then its position as a regional centre serving local industry. There are a number of ways in which RF aims to achieve this. First, it plans to establish a Product Development Laboratory, where small and medium-sized f irms can send their staff to work tempora rily, using RF equipment and drawing on the expertise of the Institute's researchers. Such a laboratory is felt by RF to be parti cularly useful in the field of micro-electro nics, for example, where firms may wish to introduce microprocessors into their pro ducts or processes, but lack the resources to do it on their own. Eventually, it is hoped that the laboratory will become a Regional Innovation Centre. However, the critical problem is obtaining general f unds to set up the necessary infrastructure, since state support for R&D is almost entirely pro ject-oriented. RF aims to begin by obtaining funds for a five-year programme, and then to build up from there. It has re cently been given a small sum for establish ing a grinding laboratory, and sees this as representing the start of a new and less pro ject-oriented system of funding. A second element in the plans for RFs development as a regional centre is for the Institute to serve almost as a regional office of NTNF, helping local firms apply for grants, and arranging for longer-term re search projects to be carried out at RF or in NTNF institutes. To a certain extent, RF has already begun to assume this role, al though not in any formal or systematic manner. Thirdly, RF seeks to achieve much closer co-operation between all the local agencies providing help to firms — the State

formal or systematic manner. Thirdly, RF seeks to achieve much closer co-operation between all the local agencies providing help to firms — the State

side 240

Technology Institute, the local council plan ners, the industrial associations, the newly formed INKO, and RF itself. Ideally, RF would like all these agencies to be housed in one building at RF, forming what has been termed a «Technical Mercantile Centre». Fourthly, RF plans to expand its provision of training for the local industrial work force, organising courses on computing, for example. Lastly, RF would like to establish «swap» arrangements with firms, whereby people from industry come to work at RF for a few months, and RF staff are seconded to work in firms. RF currently has a staff of about 75 employees, but is still growing ra pidly. It is divided into three Departments — Social Science, Petroleum Technology, and Industrial Automation and Computer Science. Its budget in 1980 was 14.2 million kroner, 0.7 million of this coming from the Rogaland County and the Stavanger Coun cils, 1.5 million from NTNF (in the form of project grants), 2.0 million from other government departments, 9.7 million from industry, and the remaining 0.3 million from local authorities. Like SINTEF, it has a very low level of general funds, the money from NTNF being tied to specific projects. In our interviews, wc concentrated on the Industrial Automation and Computer Science Departments, and from the 10 re searchers wc obtained information on 16 projects. Apart from some of the work car ried out by the Petroleum Technology De partment, most of the R&D activities at RF involve «development» rather than «re search» and are funded by industry (jointly with NTNF or by the firms alone). One could perhaps describe the industrial automation work as the start of a longer-term project, although it is more a family of related pro jects that began in 1977. The first phase of the work aimed to develop an integrated robot-machine system. One part of this in volved using an existing Trallfa robot for ploughshare-grinding at an agricultural equipment manufacturer, while the other was to develop a seam-tracking system for welding. This work cost about 2 million kroner, 0.8 million coming from NTNF and the rest from industry. Subsequently there have been several related projects, for ex ample on the deburring of metal castings, and on welding for an excavator manufac turer. Comments. (i) RF is still very much at the stage of building up expertise, and the local firms interviewed felt that it is therefore not yet able to offer much help in the way of skills and expertise. (The ploughshare-grinding work, although completed, has not yet been implemented by the finn concerned, and it is therefore too early to judge its success.) A number of f irms, particularly those that are members of the TESA co-operative, seem to have made a deliberate decision to «give RF a chance» through sponsoring work there that could perhaps be done elsewhere, as well as donating equipment and machinery. (ii) The decision by RF to concentrate on industrial automation was tåken on the ba sis of a strategic view of the long-term needs of Rogaland developed in co-operation with local finns. The effect of North Sea oil has been to raise wages in the region, and hence to increase the need for automation of the production process. It is perhaps not with out signif icance that the two Norwegian ro bot manufacturers are in this region, since they too have been responding to the same pressures. (iii) RF has realised that it cannot hope to compete with SI and SINTEF in terms of the range and level of expertise it offers. Instead, the Institute has to take full advan tage of its geographical proximity to local firms. This it appears to be doing at present, with most staff håving good contact with firms and an awareness of their current problems and needs. However, there have been cases where RF has attempted to dup licate the ef forts of SINTEF, without håving the necessary expertise or capacity, and KORO and local firms have on occasions been critical of this. 9. WHO USES THE INSTITUTES, AND FOR WHAT? Håving in earlier sections examined some of the longer-term research carried out at the institutes, the next question to be con sidered is «Who uses the institutes, and for what?» This is considered here, while the next section focusses solely on those firms that have used specific institutes for carry ing out sponsored R&D, and asks how suc cessful their contacts have been. 9.1 The use of institutes in general. The main use of institutes by firms is for carrying out sponsored research projects, of ten aided by NTNF grants. However, in ad dition to these, there are various other uses including: (1) the use of central facilities at the institu tes (for example, instruments that the firm cannot afford to purchase);

other uses including: (1) the use of central facilities at the institu tes (for example, instruments that the firm cannot afford to purchase);

side 241

(2) testing, certification, or standardisation of products; (3) provision of non-technical services (for example, help with management or mar ket-forecasting); (4) small contracts given to institutes by f irms to carry out f airly routine pieces of work where the main aim, as far as the firm is concerned, is to develop or main tain links with the institute as a poten tial source of new technology; (5) small contracts where the main purpose is to attempt to recruit trained staf f from the institute. The sponsored research projects can also be broken down into a number of categories. In what follows, projects were first of all classified according to whether they invol ved the development of (A) a new product or (B) a new process. These two main catego ries were then broken down into f our subca tegories: (1) the industrialisation of a product/pro cess developed at the institute (perhaps in the course of one of the long-term research programmes described in previ ous sections); (2) the institute has been given prime re sponsibility for the development of an entire product/process by the finn; (3) the institute is developing part of a product/process for a finn; (4) the institute is carrying out background research for product/process develop ment. In the case of process development, a f if th sub-category was included — the develop ment of software for production planning and control. On the basis of these categories, wc then examined the type of use made of institutes by the seventy firms that wc visited. It should be emphasised that this sample of firms was not wholly representative of the overall electrical and mechanical engineer ing sectors of Norwegian industry; it is al most certainly biassed towards those firms that d o use the institutes. The main reason for this is that wc were keen to interview a large number of the main users of institutes, and theref ore had insuff icient time to estab lish contact with as many firms not using institutes as would have been needed to give a fully representative sample. As a result, the figures presented below on the percent age use by firms of institutes are almost certainly an over -estimate of the use made by institutes of Norwegian industry as a whole. Nevertheless, they do illustrate cer tain trends which, wc believe, are characte ristic of Norwegian industry in general. So what use have firms made of institu tes? Table 10, below, shows the percentage of firms visited that have made a particular use of institutes. It can be seen that, for both mechanical engineering and electrical firms, just over a half (57% and 58% respec tively) have sponsored process development projects at the institutes, while the figures for «other uses» are also f airly similar (60% and 69%). The big difference between the two industrial sectors concerns product de velopment projects; only a quarter (26%) of the mechanical engineering firms visited have used the institutes for such work, com pared with three-quarters (77%) of the elec trical firms. Indeed, for the latter, the main use of institutes has been for the develop ment of part of a product (category A 3), while for mechanical engineering the main uses are testing and certification (C 2 — 48%) and software for production planning and control (B 5 — 45%). Overall, electrical firms seem to have used the institutes ra ther more than the mechanical engineering firms — only 8% of firms reported håving had no contact, while for the latter the fig ure was 19%. However, both these figures, and particularly the second, almost cer tainly underestimate the overall percentage of firms in the country as a whole not using institutes, the reason being the unrepresen tative nature of our sample discussed ear lier. Evidence for this comes from the fact that small firms (which are rather under represented in our sample) make much less use of institutes than do their larger coun terparts, as wc shall see whwn wc now con sider the t y p e s of firms using the institu tes most heavily.
