suggests that size of finn has a dominant effect — none of the small firms have used institutes for process development work, while all but one (93%) of the large firms have used the institutes for this. The size of a finn also seems to affect the likelihood that it will use institutes for product devel opment projects — only 3 out of the 20 firms (i. e. 15%) with less than 200 employees have used institutes for this function, compared with 8 out of the 22 firms (36%) above this size. Even for «other uses», finn size is still a signif icant f actor, with only half the smaller firms (of less than 200 employees) employing the institutes for these, compared with two thirds of the larger firms. This is despite the f act that one might have expected smaller firms to have a greater need for such services from institutes, since they are gen erally less likely to be able to afford these services on their own. (They are, for ex ample, more likely to be unable to afford to buy certain items of equipment, and there f ore to require the temporary use of central f acilities at an institute.) One possible expla nation for this is that the costs of such ser vices, although small compared with the costs of sponsored projects, are still too great for many small firms to meet. If so, this suggests the need for pref erential treatment to be given to smaller firms so that their use of institutes is subsidised to a certain extent. That smaller firms require special help is a theme that runs through most of the assess ment that f ollows, and in the final section, it is one of the areas that wc suggest is worthy of further discussion by the Commission. From Table 12, one can see that the R&D intensity of a finn also seems to affect the likelihood that it will use institutes. 43% of the high R&D intensity firms have spon sored product-development work, for ex ample, compared with 17% of the low R&D intensity firms. One probable reason for this is that the former are more likely to employ researchers who are able to keep informed of the research activities of institutes, to see the possibilities for collaborative projects, to specify to institutes exactly what the firm requires in such a project, and gener ally to talk to institute researchers on their own level. Firms without staff capable of doing all this are obviously at a severe dis advantage. However, it should be noted that the ef f ect of the R&D intensity of the finn on its use of institutes does not appear to be as great as that of its size. Indeed, the reason why certain of the figures for institute use by «low» R&D intensity firms are higher than those for «medium» R&D intensity firms, is probably that many of the former are amongst the largest firms, and that for them the effect of size dominates over that of R&D intensity. Turning next to electronics and electrical engineering firms, wc see from Table 13 that finn size is again important. A rather higher percentage of large firms with over 200 em ployees have used institutes than smaller firms. And because of the nature of the sam ple of firms visited, the figures for institute usage by small firms are almost certainly more of an over-estimate for Norwegian industry as a whole than those for larger firms. Therefore, as with mechanical engin eering, wc must conclude that the institutes seem to be signif icantly better at helping the larger firms.

So far wc have considered the use of insti tues in general by firms. The next stage is to examine the use of individual institutes, and the nature of the services that those institu tes offer. Tables 15 and 16 show the use by mechanical engineering and electrical firms of SI, SINTEF, and «other institutes» (pri marily Ch. Michelsen Institute and Roga landsforskning). The first of these suggests that, for all but one of the R&D functions, mechanical engineering firms make rather more use of SINTEF than they do of SI. The same appears to be the true of electronics and electrical engineering firms (see Table 16), particularly for product development and process development work. The reason for this is that SI has, in its longer-term research, concentrated its attention on helping a relatively small number of electro nics firms (and one in particular). This con centration has on occasions been resented by firms not included in this select group, and they have therefore been less willing to sponsor projects at the institute. However, wc shall leave f urther discussion of product and process development projects to the fol lowing section, and instead concentrate here on the «other uses» (categories Cl to C 5) to which institutes are put. Both SI and SINTEF offer a wide range of central facilities (category Cl), and SI also operates an instrument loan service that is well used by industry and public agencies. Similarly, both offer facilities for testing, certification and standardisation (category C 2). However, Tables 11 and 13 above show that these facilities are used mainly by large firms, even though one might have expected small firms to have at least an equivalent need for such services. As for the provision of non-technical services (category C 3), none of the institutes currently supply such ser vices on any significant scale. Some firms award contracts to institutes primarily for the purpose of developing and maintaining links with the institutes as potential sources of new technology (cate gory C 4). Such new technology may come either from the institute's own long-term research efforts, or from the institute moni toring and diffusing overseas technology. There is a certain amount of surveying of the literature on develop ments in overseas technology, but it is far from clear that this represents a very effec tive way of transferring technology. A far better mechanism, at least according to the researchers interviewed, involves the send ing overseas of institute staff for short periods. This has proved extremely success ful at FFI (see Appendix 1), where it is per f ormed on a relatively large scale and invol ves most research staff at one stage or another in their careers. It is far less com mon in other institutes. Of the 16 resear chers interviewed at ELAB, 5 had spent a period in an overseas university or finn (the 5 håving worked total of 8 1/2 years over seas), while at SI only 4 (out of 24) had done so (for a total of a mere 3 years). More could perhaps be done to encourage such periods of secondment for institute staff; this would surely strengthen the institutes' ability to monitor and diffuse the results of overseas research work to users in Norway, and thereby improve this particular service to firms. A fif th use made of institutes by firms is as a source of trained manpower (category C 5). As is apparent from the earlier discus sion of the nature of the innovation process, one of the essential inputs is skilled man power. SI, with a staff-turnover of about 9% per annum over the last decade, has pro vided a flow of trained manpower for indus try (about two-thirds of those leaving have joined industry), and several of the institu te^ former staff have been actively involved in setting up new firms. (High turnover of staff, particularly in some groups, has, how ever, led to problems because of the lack of experience of the remaining staff.) SINTEF has had an annual turnover of about 13% over the last decade, of which just under half have gone to work in industry, so it too has provided industry with a supply of skilled manpower. Many NTH students re gard a subsequent period of 2 or 3 years research at SINTEF as the final part of ) Some of this monitoring is carried out centrally at NSI, but very few of the researchers or firms that wc spoke to found the services offered by NSI at all useful. The methods this institute uses do not appear to represent a very eff icient mechanism for transferring the results of research work carried out overseas back to potential users in Norway. Purther research needs to be carried out on this problem. their technological training, so that there is less of a problem in recruitment at SINTEF than at SI. However, few former SINTEF staff seem to have set up their own f irms, at least in the Trondheim area. Why this has not happened is not clear. Perhaps SINTEF provides too satisfactory an environment for its more enterprising staff! RF, because it has been growing rapidly, has had little staff turnover so far, although one former employee has set up his own firm, which appears to have a promising future. Besides these various uses of institutes described here, there are in addition various other outputs from the institutes that do not fall into the above categories. One such function is the organization of training courses for industrial personnel. Several SINTEF staff are regularly engaged in teaching EEU courses (lasting 1 to 2 weeks) for people from industry, for example giving instruction on quality control. SI has orga nized seminars (for example, on custom designed integrated circuits) to which firms have been invited, but tends to provide in dustrial training courses only on a rather irregular basis. And RF places considerable emphasis on this task of training or retrain ing, organizing couses (on industrial auto mation, for example) in conjunction with the Regional College, as well as holding sem inars and shorter courses (e.g. on micropro cessors). A second output is consultancy work and special help for small firms. Both SI and SINTEF carry out a large amount of con sultancy-type projects for firms, but it has unfortunately proved difficult in the avail able time to obtain systematic data on this. (SI, for example, carries out about 3,000 small projects a year, but many of these take the form of use of technical support facil ities, dealt with above.) In addition, all three institutes are starting to provide various types of special help for small firms, for ex ample, an advice service on microprocessors. However, it has not always proved easy for institutes to obtain the interest of small firms. SI sent out 900 leaflets advertising its microprocessor advice service, and received a mere 25 replies, only half of which were from firms. Department 17 at SINTEF cir culates (through MVL) information on pro cess technology, but many of the smaller firms that wc spoke to stated that they found the reports of little use, generally be cause they could not understand them. to transfer knowledge or technol ogy. Department 17 seem to have realised this. In their scheme for introducing quality-control circles into finns, and in the technical consultancy service on numeri cally-controlled machines (a scheme oper ated in conjunction with STI), a consider able amount of time is spent actually visit ing small firms and discussing their problems. Another initiative tåken by SIN TEF has been to set up a branch in Narvik which works in co-operation with STI and the local Engineering High School. This of fers help to firms in the North of the coun try, and, although it took some time to deve lop links, again visits to industrial firms (most of them small) are starting to prove f ruitful, bringing in contracts for SINTEF. It cannot be emphasised enough that small firms (unless they have some previous personal contact) do not generally approach institutes or NTNF, nor do they make much use of written information circulated to them. Institutes and NTNF, if they wish to help, must visit them; in other words, an a c t i v e approach is essential. In the past, most institutes have not done this, and, as a result, their links with small firms have been rather weak. To us, as outsiders, it also seems rather puzzling that more has not been done to co-ordinate the help for small firms offered by institutes with that pro vided by STI. If there were closer co-ordi nation, institutes could benefit from the strong links that exist between STI and large numbers of small firms, while STI could benefit from the technical expertise of institute staff . The existence of such mutual benefits is readily apparent from the experi ence of the SINTEF branch office in Narvik — initially, it had difficulty in establishing systematic contact with small firms, but it has been considerably more successf ul since its links with the local branch of STI were strengthened. One further output from the institutes is worth mentioning. This concerns their con tributions to scientific knowledge, as eviden ced by publications and citations. For re search work (as opposed to development and implementation), one of the objectives is to increase our understanding of the material world. Researchers, unless they are con strained by conditions of secrecy, therefore tend to write up their research and publish it in journals where it can be read by a wider audience, and bring them recognition from the scientific community. Other resear chers, if they find the work interesting and useful, may then cite the published articles concerned in references in their own publi cations. Thus, the number of articles pub lished in research journals, and the number of times those articles are cited by other researchers, are two indicators of the con tributions to the advance of knowledge made by groups of researchers. Wc therefore looked at the number of research articles produced by SI, SINTEF and FFI between 1975 and 1979 (the researchers at RF only began to produce written articles in 1979) in the fields of electronics and mechanical en gineeringg, and at the number of times these articles were cited in 1979 in journals covered by the Science Citation In dex. SI, on the other hand, has produced significantly fe wer international publications, and these have received a relatively small number of citations, suggesting that their impact on the advance of knowledge has not been as great. (These results are thus consistent with the comments of electronics finns dis cussed in Section 11, about the calibre of the staff at the institutes.) Finally, it can be seen that Department 17 produced far fewer re search publications, but this is almost cer tainly because there is less emphasis in mechanical engineering on publishing scientific papers (particularly in the inter national journals covered by the Science Citation Index)asa means of trans ferring knowledge. Moreover, the papers that are written in this f ield make less use of ref erences to previous work, and this, toge ther with the poor coverage by the Science Citation I n d e x of Scandina vian journals, probably explains why these articles do not seem to have been cited in 1979. Håving described the various types of out put from institutes and given some indi cation of their use by industry, wc can now move on to consider how successful the ser vices of f ered by institutes are in meeting the needs of firms. In this, wc concentrate on sponsored research projects since these con stitute the main source of contact between institutes and firms. 10. ASSESSMENT OF SPONSORED INDUSTRIAL R&D PROJECTS CARRIED OUT BY THE INSTITUTES In attempting to assess the sponsored in dustrial research projects (i.e. those paid for by firms) carried out by the institutes, wc adopted two approaches. First, wc asked a significant proportion of the researchers at each of the institutes about the main pro jects with which they had been involved over the last 5 to 10 years, questioning them on how successful they felt these projects to have been, and what factors had influenced success and failure. Secondly, wc visited the firms concerned to obtain their evaluations of the work performed for them by each of the institutes. Finally, wc examined whe ther these two approaches yielded consis tent results. 10.1 Views of researchers. Researchers at each institute were ques tioned extensively about the details of pro jects that they had helped to carry out. Then, on the basis of this information, they were asked for their judgements as to how successful these had proved, in particular whether (i) the project had been completed with little or no benefit to industry; (ii) the project results have not (yet) been implemented, but there has been some benefit to industry (in the form of in creased knowledge, for example); (iii) the project results have been imple mented by industry (in a new product or process); (iv) it is too soon to tell. After excluding projects coming under ca tegory (iv), wc then calculated the percent age of the remainder falling into categories (i), (ii) and (iii). The results are shown in Table 18 below. These figures suggest that the record of Department 17 at SINTEF in carrying out sponsored research projects has been better than average (in 85% of the cases, the re sults seem to have been implemented by in dustry), while SI has a rather higher than average percentage (29%) of projects that have not led to benefits to industry. As for RF, most of the projects (10 out of 16) exam ined were at too early a stage for them to be assessed, and not too much significance should therefore be attached to the figures concerning the small number of completed projects. These figures are obviously open to cer tain objections, and should therefore be treated as suggestive rather than conclu sive. In particular, the sample size is not very big, the projects compared are of differ ent types (a point to which wc return below), and the researchers may obviously be bias sed in their assessments — and perhaps biassed to a differing extent at the various institutes. These three objections were to a large extent overcome in the industrial as sessment part of the work where the sample size is much bigger, and is indeed suffi ciently large to break down the different types of project into a number of categories. In addition, there seemed to be no a priori reason why the 70 firms interviewed should be biassed in any systematic way in favour of one institute rather than another. (The fact that many firms were, as wc shall see below, rather critical of SI cannot be ascrib ed to their geographical distance from the institute, since some 40% of the companies interviewed were in the Oslo region.)

If these tables are compared with the pre vious table summarising the views of insti tute researchers, it can be seen that the assessments of researchers and finns on the success of projects are f airly consistent. Ac cording to the firms, 61% of the projects sponsored at SI have led to results that have been implemented, while at SI a figure of 59 % was obtained. For SINTEF, the corre sponding figures are 76% and 72% — again relativély consistent given the sample size involved, and significantly higher than at SI. In the case of RF, in view of the small sample size and the fact that most projects are still at a comparatively early stage, not too much significance should again be at tached to the percentage figures on the im plementation of project results; but in 75% of the cases the firms expressed satisf action with the progress made by the institute so far, a figure similar to that for SINTEF (76 %), and substantially better than that for SI (50%). In the light of this consistency between the views of researchers and firms, the fol lowing conclusions can perhaps be drawn. For projects sponsored at SINTEF, in ap proximately one-quarter of cases the results were not implemented, the firms involved reporting «unsatisfactory» or «mixed» views on the work done by the institute. For SI, the figures appear to be rather higher. In about 40% of the projects, the results have failed to be implemented, and in about 50% of the cases the finn reported «unsatisfac tory» or «mixed» views. This suggests that SI has been significantly less successful than SINTEF in satisfactorily carrying out spon sored research projects for industry. Finally, in 25% of the cases, concerning RF, firms had «mixed» views (no firms had «unsatisfac tory» views), while the figures on the imple mentation of project results are (as wc saw above) probably too small to be very signifi cant. Overall, it seems that so far RF has been reasonably successful in the work that it has done, or is doing, for firms. Håving looked at these aggregate figures on the success of sponsored research pro jects, it is useful as a next step to break these projects down into the various categories used in the previous section. Wc can then ascertain the main uses made of institutes, and the respective success rates for these different types of project. (It should be noted that the boundaries to these various cate gories are not always very distinct, and that in a small number of cases projects had to be allocated into more than one category.) The types of project carried out by the various institutes are shown in Table 21. It can be seen that the main use of SI has involved the industrialisation of products developed at the institute (type Al), followed by A 3, the development of part of a product for a finn. At SINTEF and RF, far fewer projects have been of type Al, the main uses håving involved the development of part of a product (A 3) or process (B 3) for a finn. This concentration an Al-type projects at Si is perhaps accounted for by a small number of spin-off companies from Si (for example, AME, Norwegian Electronics, ICAN), which retain extremely strong links with the Insti tute. Staff in both the Institute and these firms work closely together on NTNF pro grammes, and in turn the finn involved is rewarded with a project to industrialise the results, when and if this stage is reached. Many of the firms that are «excluded» from this close network of past and present SI employees are, however, less certain about the benefits of such institute-industry col laboration. Table 21 also shows the percentage of each type of project judged by firms to have been carried out satisfactorily. For projects of type Al at SI, the figure is 77%, but the A 3 projects seem to have been considerably less successful, with only 33% judged «satis factory» by firms. (It should be noted, how ever, that since the Al projects were by and large carried out with a small number of firms håving strong personal links with SI, the views of those interviewed in these firms may have been somewhat less candid than those obtained for the other types of project, largely at other firms.) At SINTEF, the cor responding figures for the main types of project (A 3 and B 3) are 92% and 75% respec tively, and for RF 100% and 40% (but these are for very small sample sizes, and may not therefore be that significant). At SINTEF, process de velopment projects have also proved less sa tisfactory than product development pro jects, but for both, the levels of satisfaction (50% and 71% respectively) were signifi cantly higher than at SI (where the corre sponding figures are 9% and 50%). It seems clear that with one or two notable excep tions, most electronics and electrical engin eering firms do not appear to have been very satisfied with projects carried out by SI, par ticularly in recent years. Turning now to mechanical engineering firms, it can be seen from Table 23 that for all three institutes a majority of the projects have involved process development, and in particular the development of part of a pro cess for a finn (category B 3). This is in line with the suggestion in section 4 that Norwe gian mechanical engineering firms gener ally have a greater need for process develop ment rather than product development. In the case of SINTEF, approximately four fifths of the projects (21 out of 26) have in volved the development of processes rather than products, and, according to the firms, these have mostly (86%) been completed sa tisfactorily. At SI, in contrast, the ratio of product to process development projects is much more equal (7 to 9) suggesting that SI has been somewhat less successful in meet ing the demand from mechancial engineer ing firms for process development work; but, as with SINTEF, these projects have gener ally been satisf actorily carried out, the over all percentage satisfaction rate (75%) being double that for electronics companies (37%). This indicates that SI has been far more successful in projects sponsored by mech anical engineering firms than in those for electrical and electronics firms, perhaps be cause the latter are in general more techno logically advanced and therefore more ex acting in the demands they place on institu tes. Håving seen that different institutes and different types of projects have varying suc cess rates, the next question to consider is, «What factors account for these differen ces?» One possible factor has already been mentioned — whether the project involves product or process development. But there are others, including whether the project is initiated by the f inn or the institute, the size of the firm involved, and the R&D intensity of the finn. 1 The effect of each of these fac tors can be seen in Table 24. *) Vet another is distance of the finn from the institute. For SI, projects involving product deve lopment have been råtner more successful than those involving process development (55% compared with 40%). In addition, size of f inn also seems to have been a signif icant factor — only 38% of projects for smaller firms with less than 200 employees have been satisfactory, compared with 57 % of those for larger firms (over 200 employees). In the case of SINTEF, the only one of the f our factors considered here that appears to have a significant effect is whether the pro ject was initiated by the f inn rather than the institute, the respective levels of satis faction being 80% and 64% respectively. Finally, for RF, all four factors seem to have had some impact; product development projects, projects initiated by the firms, pro jects for smaller firms, and projects for high R&D intensity firms, all seem to have been significantly more successful than projects of the opposite type. The relevant figures for the electronics and electrical engineering sector are shown in Table 25. For SI, these show a relatively low satisfaction rate for process development projects in particular, and also for projects initiated by firms and projects for firms with a low R&D intensity. (The eff ects of these factors can perhaps be seen more clearly in Table 26.) The converse of this is that SI has been more successful with product development work, with projects that it, rather than firms, has initiated, and with work for high R&D intensity firms. The explanation for this seems to lic in the fact that SI has concentrated its electronics research eff orts on the development of cer tain micro-electronics products, using the competence birilt up in the long-term re search programme described in Section 6. This work was obviously initiated by the institute, and the technology developed is suitable for transfer only to the higher R&D intensity firms. Because of the concen tration on this type of work, projects in other areas of electronics initiated by firms, particularly low R&D intensity ones, have received proportionately less attention, and have theref ore tended to be less satisfactory as far as the firms are concerned. THE INSTITUTES — STRENGTHS AND WEAKNESSES It is obviously of interest to ascertain the reasons why firms have had more successful dealings with some institutes than with others. In an attempt to identify the possible reasons, wc again adopted the two-fold ap proach of asking both firms and institute researchers for their views. In this section, wc consider each of these in turn, and from them attempt to arrive at conclusions about the relative strengths and weaknesses of the institutes studied. 11.1 The views of firms. During the industrial interviews, firms were requested to identify the main problems encountered in dealing with those institutes at which they had sponsored re search projects. On the basis of this, they were then asked to point to areas in which those institutes might be able to improve and thereby provide a better service to in dustry. The areas mentioned have been grouped in a number of categories, and the results are shown in Table 30 below. It is important to note that these figures ref er to the problems that the firms themselves brought up for discussion. If wc had instead asked directed questions on each possible type of problem, wc would undoubtedly have found a much higher percentage of firms citing these as areas in need of improve ment. In other words, the figures under estimate, perhaps quite appreciably, the percentage of firms encountering each of these problems. If wc first consider the responses of the electrical and electronics firms, it can be seen that for SI by far the most commonly cited problem concerns the calibre of the staff ; in over a third of cases, finns feel that this needed to be improved. Also frequently mentioned were the need for better project management, for better contacts with in dustry, and the adoption of a less academic approach. These three problems are appar ently shared with ELAB at SINTEF, al though the slightly lower percentage figures for the latter suggest that the problems are not quite as severe as at SI. However, ELAB could, in the view of firms, certainly do more to improve its links with industry, several firms (17%) mentioning that it should tem porarily transfer staff to ensure the success ful implementation of project results in in dustry, and (14%) that it should employ staff with more industrial experience. If ELAB did this, there might then be less of a ten dency to adopt what the firms see as too academic an approach to industrial R&D. As for mechanical engineering firms, the main problems encountered at SI con cerned, first, the administration of projects, and failures to keep to budgets (25%) and time schedules (19%); and secondly, the need for better links with industry through the temporary transfer of staff to industrialise the results of projects (19%), employing staff with more industrial experience (13%), and adopting a less academic approach (13%.) Similar views were expressed on SINTEF

Fi nally, for Rogalandsforskning, half the firms mentioned that the Institute is still in the phase of building up its expertise, and that, until this process is completed, its ability to help the more advanced firms in particular will remain limited. How much justification is there to the complaints of firms about the calibre of re searchers, and their lack of industrial ex perience? In the course of our interviews with the researchers, wc obtained some in formation of relevance to this question, and this is summarised in Table 31. It can be seen that ELAB researchers have had very little industrial experience indeed. Only four of those interviewed have actually worked in industry, and then only for about a year each. However, the ELAB researchers do have a high percentage of PhDs. Depart ment 17 in contrast has few PhDs, but con siderably more industrial experience (over half of those wc spoke to have worked for 4 or more years in industry), and much more frequent contact with industry. The situ ation at SI is that few of the researchers interviewed have PhDs, and, although 3 staff have had 9 or more years industrial experience, for the remaining 21 the average is just under 0.5 years. Besides this relative lack of industrial experience for most SI researchers, there is also a fairly low fre quency of contact with industry. Finally, at RF there were no PhD holders among those researchers interviewed in the Industrial Automation and Computer Science Depart ments (although two other researchers in terviewed did have PhDs), but the staff have had a relatively large amount of industrial experience, and are in very f requent contact with industry at present. It would therefore appear that the problems identified by industry are not en tirely without foundation. In particular, the smaller percentage of PhD holders at SI compared with SINTEF, and the relatively small output from SI of publications men tioned in Section 9, would seem to be consis tent with electronics firms' views on the re spective quality of the researchers at the two institutes. Similarly, the complaints about the lack of industrial experience at SI and at ELAB would seem to be largely justi fied. 11.2 The views of institute researchers. Table 31: Qualifications, Industrial Experience, and Frequency of Contact with Industry of Researchers Interviewed bed as negative in attitude), while at SI the reverse is true, with perhaps only a quarter being generally positive, and the remainder being rather negative (and the attitudes of a minority can only be described as extremely critical). SINTEF is obviously not without its problems, one of the most frequently men tioned (by just over half of those interview ed) being its inability to help small firms. This is certainly consistent with the picture that emerged earlier in our discussion of the use of institutes by firms of different sizes. Another problem centres on the balance be tween longer-term research and short-term development work, with approximately half the researchers believing that financial pressures on SINTEF have driven it too much towards the latter. While most firms interviewed did not share this view, with many complaining that the work of institu tes was too academic, a small number of the technologically more advanced firms did agree with the researchers, arguing that in the long run industry would benef it more if there were greater emphasis on long-term research programmes in order to build up competence at both SINTEF and SI. A third problem mentioned at SINTEF is the relatively poor links between certain of the research groups, and particularly be tween different departments. However, the converse of this is that the departments do have considerable autonomy, and several re searchers in fact pointed to this decentra lised structure as one of SINTEF's strengths (and indeed one of its advantages over SI). The decentralised SINTEF structure is one that permits a great deal of flexibility, with the more successf ul departments and affili ated institutes growing as the demand for their services increases, and the less success ful remaining static or declining size, in a continous process of evolution. Such an evo lutionary system is apparently more readily capable of switching resources so as to meet the challenge of new technological demands swif tly and ef f ectively, than is the more cen tralised and hierarchical system found at SI. In view of this, the wisdom of the current moves to reduce the decentralisation at SINTEF and to «divisionalise» the depart ments must be seriously called into ques tion. Indeed, the need for the continous in ternal evolution made possible by decentral isation will become all the more essential once SINTEF as a whole ceases to expand, as it surely must do in the near f uture. Fourthly, just over a third of researchers ref erred to the problem of salaries, arguing that the level of these was such that SIN TEF was finding it increasingly difficult to recruit and to keep good researchers, and almost impossible to attract researchers with industrial experience (these would have to accept a drop in salary of 20% or more if they lef t industry for employment in an institute). The effect of North Sea oil has apparently been to increase the salary dif ferential between industrial and institute based R&D, and this process is likely to con tinue. In addition, several firms have real ised that the best way to recruit staff from NTH and SINTEF (many of whom are re luctant to leave the area) is to move to, or set up a local branch in, Trondheim. If this happens on a large scale, this will further add to the salary problems. One final problem raised by ELAB resear chers concerns their relationship with NTH. When ELAB was set up and its staff were relatively inexperienced, a system was insti gated whereby NTH professors were made the formal supervisors of ELAB projects. Given the current level of expertise among ELAB staff, this arrangement is now per haps redundant and has led to some resent ment in cases where institute staff feel the NTH professor knows less about the project concerned than they do. problem, as with most of the others men tioned above, it was apparent that the need for change has already been widely recog nised within SINTEF, and that steps were already being tåken to remedy the situation. Overall, the impression gained from SIN TEF researchers was that their problems were far from insuperable, and that the or ganization would prove sufficiently flexible to cope with these difficulties. At SI, in contrast, researchers were gener ally far less optimistic about the ability of the institute to meet the challenges it faces. Indeed, several of the problems brought up relate to the way SI is managed. In particu lar, over half complained strongly about the pressures imposed on them to obtain a fixed percentage (60%) of their funds from outside NTNF. Since the financial difficulties in the first half of the 19705, the central manage ment at SI has placed great stress on this percentage, seeing it as a measure of the ability of research groups to seil their servi ces to industry, and hence as an indicator of their overall research performance. A group seiling a high percentage of its services to industry or public agencies is judged to be performing successfully and vice versa. While the use of this performance indicator may have had a positive eff ect initially, put ting pressure on researchers to complete their work and ensure that the results were of use to outsiders, now researchers are in creasingly being forced to take on short term consultancy-type projects in order to keep the industrial percentage up. As a re sult, there is very great emphasis on obtain ing sponsored research contracts, but very little on how well they are carried out. Many researchers felt that the reliance on this performance indicator has had, over recent years, a deleterious effect on the overall re search capability of the institute in that far too much routine consultancy work is now carried out. The percentage of funds earned from contract research is certainly o n e in dicator of the performance of a research institute (although it is probably only rele vant to the stage of transferring technology from the institute to industry, rather than to earlier stages in the R&D process), but there are other indicators, not least of which being the quality of the research, the con tent of research reports, and the success rate in implementing research results in indus try.

of which being the quality of the research, the con tent of research reports, and the success rate in implementing research results in indus try.
Trying to manage an institution using a single indicator of research performance is somewhat akin to attempting to run a nation's economy by looking solely at the supply of money (the experiment currently being undertaken in the UK!), or piloting an aircraf t using the speedometer (and neglect ing the altimeter, compass, wind-speed indi cator, etc.). Attempts to administer complex systems using but one indicator of perform ance are unlikely to be successf ul in the long run, and, according to its staff , certainly do not seem to have been in the case of SI. Related to this is a second problem, the management structure at SI. Whereas at SINTEF there is a considerable degree of decentralisation among the constituent de partments, the heads of department exercis ing strong control and direction over their groups (Department 17 has a particularly well articulated strategic plan), at SI one of the weaknesses identified by researchers is at the level of the section management. In the interviews, it was suggested that section management does not exercise much direc tion, nor does it provide a very efficient link between researchers and the central man agement, with the result that the former feels that the latter are not sufficiently aware of their work and their problems. One symptom of this weakness is perhaps the prolif eration of paperwork, with researchers håving to fill in f orms to account for every hour of their time. (In contrast, at SINTEF, department heads seem to be sufficiently in touch with researchers not to require this on the same scale.) And because the admin istration involved in setting up a new pro ject is substantial, one consequence is that in many cases it has become uneconomical for SI to take on projects below a certain size (one man-year or less), thereby diminishing Sl's ability to help small firms. (High costs is one of industry's main criticisms of SI.) However, the criticisms voiced by resear chers of the management at SI may merely be symptoms of a deeper malaise that has its roots in the institute's difficulty first of all in recruiting top-class researchers, and sec ondly in providing them with an intellectu ally stimulating environment similar to that found at SINTEF (by virtue of its relation ship with NTH) and which ensures that re searchers are constantly rejuvenated by their exposure to new ideas and new people. It is clear that perhaps the major differ ence between SINTEF and SI is that the former is closely integrated with NTH, while SI has only weak links with the University of Oslo.

major differ ence between SINTEF and SI is that the former is closely integrated with NTH, while SI has only weak links with the University of Oslo.
This gives SINTEF several advanta ges, one being a ready supply of new re cruits, bringing with them a constant stream of fresh ideas. Secondly, the substan tial involvement of SINTEF staff in teach ing and supervising NTH students provides

side 265

them with a measure of intellectual stimu lation that is again conducive to the gener ation of new ideas. Thirdly, NTH staff rep resent a reservoir of skilled manpower that can be drawn on when required, enabling SINTEF to undertake projects that would otherwise be impossible. Lastly, both SIN TEF and NTH gain certain financial ben efits from the shared uselof equipment and facilities. Overall then, it is the constant inflow of new people and new ideas, the two essential ingredients for successf ul research, at least in the long term, that are the great strength of SINTEF. SI, because it is largely denied these benefits, is evidently at a severe disadvantage. Moreover, this disadvantage can only grow with time, as the problems become mutually re-inforcing — the less stimulating research environment at SI måkes it less attractive to potential recruits, the best of whom may therefore choose em ployment elsewhere, thereby denying SI one of the main inputs needed to restore its positions. (In this context, it is worth noting that FFI obtains its supply of recruits through national service, while the sending of its staff to universities and high-technol ogy firms overseas provides it with a source of new ideas and with a way of providing intellectual stimulation for its staff. See Ap pendix 1.) There is one final problem at SI that is worth mentioning. Since it was set up, SI has always been consiered as the Central Institute, attempting to cater for the tech nological needs of a whole range of Norwe gian industrial sectors. As the costs of R&D have escalated, so this role has become in creasingly inconsistent with the level of re sources available to the Institute. According to some, resources have therefore been spread too thinly. It was argued that far more specialialisation and concentration of efforts are required to overcome this, even if it means abandoning Sl's claim to be the Central Institute for Norway. Since both researchers and firms suggest that there are considerable differences be tween SI and SINTEF, it is worth listing the relative strengths (many of these are readily apparent, and have not therefore been dis cussed in detail here) and weaknesses iden tified in the interviews. These are summa rised in Tables 32 and 33 below. Finally, let us consider Rogalandsforskn ing. Given that it is only over the last two years that RF has become involved on any significant scale in technological research and development work (and even now its Automation and Computing Science Groups are still f airly small), it has managed to make some significant achievements. Of these, perhaps the most important is the way in which it has begun to develop a new and potentially very successful method of working with industry. It has recognised the need to capitalise fully on its geographical proximity to local firms, with the result that most of its researchers work in very close and direct contact with the firms sponsoring projects. This has three main benefits: it ensures that short-term projects are com pleted relatively promptly since researchers are less likely to become sidetracked in pur suit of something that is «interesting» but not particularly relevant — as may happen when the contact with industry is weak; it means that RF researchers, through their discussions with firms, are better able to keep in touch with the new problems and needs of firms as they arise; and it results in RF being less academic-oriented and more industry-oriented than SI and SINTEF. RF has also tåken advantage of the strong social links within Rogaland.Many RF re searchersre locally born, and they know people in firms and how industry is orga nized. RF's relatively small size also gives it some advantages over SI and SINTEF, notably in its ability to react quickly to initi atives, particularly from smaller firms, and in its willingness to carry out small projects lasting a few man-months which SI and to a lesser extent SINTEF cannot handle (be cause they are not interested, or because their bureaucracy måkes small projects re latively expensive). Finally, it has enabled TESA firms in particular to strengthen their technological efforts, through helping to educate their workforce, and through taking responsibility for some of the deal ings with NTNF. However, RF also faces a number of problems, one of the most serious being its comparatively poor links with other parts, even local parts, of the Norwegian research and development system. For example, RF does not have very much contact with the Stavanger branch of the State Technology Institute. This has good links with a large number of firms, especially small firms, and RF could undoubtedly benefit from those links. The justification generally given for the poor links between STI and RF (and the NTNF system in general) is that STI of f ers a lower level and more practical form of help. But even if it were true that the two organizations were providing help in two different areas (and in fact there is a very large «grey» area of overlap, where coside 266

Besides STI, RF also has relatively weak links with the national research insti tutes. For example, few researchers at RF know much about the work being carried out at other institutes. To a certain extent, RF suffers from not being an NTNF insti tute — it is still on the f ringes of an NTNF system that, to some outsiders, has the ap pearance of being a rather exclusive «club» for the centralised institutes and the large, often state-owned, finns. The situation has been somewhat improved in the case of ro botics by the establishment of KORO, the mf ormal committee set up (on the initiative of the TESA co-operative) to co-ordinate work on robotics (and avoid duplication) at RF, SI, SINTEF, and the two robot manu facturers (see Section 6). But RF is still not very well represented in the NTNF commit tee structure, and theref ore f eels that it suf fers when decisions are being made on the distribution of funds. A second major problem at RF centres on the shortage of qualified staff, this being a serious limiting factor in the number and type of projects the institute can take on, and the speed with which they can react to new initiatives. One group already has en ough work to keep it fully occupied over the coming year, while in certain areas of tech nology, RF lacks the «critical mass» of re searchers needed to make a worthwhile con tribution. There are difficulties in recruit ing new staff partly because so few are trained in Norway, and partly because of the low salaries offered in relation to industry in the Stavanger area. stayed, but this may become a more serious problem in the near f uture. A third dif ficulty f acing RF, and one men tioned by most of the researchers, concerns the financial structure of the institute. Here, the problem is not so much the overall budget (which is likely to continue increas ing fairly rapidly over the coming years as the institute maintains its growth), but the level of core funding that can be used for longer-term research, and to equip laborato ries. There is little doubt that short-term research keeps people on their toes as they struggle to meet externally imposed dead lines; but perhaps each researcher should be f ree to spend a certain percentage of his or her time on longer-term research to build competence and enable the institute to pro vide a better service to industry in the fu ture. So far, little consideration seems to have been given at RF to this question — to how big a percentage (10%, 30% or 50%) should be spent on longer-term research, and to how the financial support permitting such a distribution of effort should be ob tained. Instead, researchers give the im pression of (and complain quite strongly about) rushing from one industrially spon sored project to another without any clearly thought out strategy as to how RF should be trying to develop in the longer run. Lastly, RF's extreme youth raises certain problems. Because the first technological project only began in 1977, and there were only two in 1978, much of the equipment has to be bought or built from scratch in each

first technological project only began in 1977, and there were only two in 1978, much of the equipment has to be bought or built from scratch in each

side 268

new project. And because RF has only be gun to help firms on a signif icant scale over the last year or so, the benef its it has had for industry thus far are rather limited. It has established good contacts with some firms, but it is still not very well known amongst others. As the number of RF researchers increases, so greater consideration must be given as to how to contact these latter firms and to inform them of the facilities RF has to offer. Merely organizing seminars and waiting for firms to turn up may not be sufficient. Associated with RF's compara tive youthfulness is its rapid growth over the last two years, which has also presented various difficulties. Some groups of resear chers are no longer in good contact with each other because the mf ormal channels of communication relied upon when the insti tute was still small are no longer effective. There is currently a shortage of office space, and there have been various administrative problems as the organization of RF has been slow to adjust to the institute's growth. These problems are likely to become more acute in the future as some groups within RF grow faster than others. In particular, the Petroleum Technology Department plans to treble in size over the next five years, and for the other sections there is a possibility that they may become merely service groups to Petroleum Technology (for example, carrying out computing for them, rather than working on their own external projects). To sum up, wc would tentatively conclude that so far RF has proved a qualified suc cess, although it is really two or three years too soon to judge its success reliably. This raises the question of whether an institute similar to RF would be appropriate for other regions in Norway. To answer this, wc need to identify the reasons for RF's success. Wc would argue that one of the most important f actors contributing to the successful devel opment of RF, at least as far as its work on automation is concerned, has been the TESA co-operative and its member firms. TESA supported the plans for RF partly for negative reasons — their experiences with SI and SINTEF had been mixed because these institutes were too far away and ap parently not very interested in the problems of smaller firms — and partly for positive reasons, in particular the feeling that Roga land industry needed to have an institute on its doorstep, and one that concentrated on the areas of most interest to local industry (especially industrial automation). When RF was set up, it was one of TESA's mem bers who saw the need to give RF a chance to get started, even though little could be expected from RF to begin with. One of the researchers at RF summarised the situation as follows: «(The firm) wanted us to do the work be cause of local patriotism. They, along with other local industrialists, thought it would build up and strengthen local industry if they could set up a local institute with strengths in industrial automation. The work could have been done in another insti tute. But firms saw the benefit of håving a local institute where they could just jump in the car, drive across, and kick you when things are not going right». There can be little doubt that RF has benefited greatly from the spirit of mutual co-operation already existing between local firms. RF has been able to build u p from this co-operation. If TESA had not existed, and RF had been imposed on the region and had tried to build downwards, then its task would have been considerably harder. So without TESA and the long history of co-operation over technological develop ment in Rogaland, it seems clear that the achievements of RF in the field of automa tion at least would have been much more limited. An institute like RF, situated in another part of Norway, would probably therefore have a far harder task in the ab sence of such a positive environment. (It would also not have large oil companies on its doorstep keen to invest locally in order to demonstrate their gratitude for being al lowed to benefit from the country's oil wealth.) Those who advocate the setting up of more regional institutes should therefore look very carefully at the willingness and ability of local industry to first support such an institute while it is still in its infancy, and later to take full advantage of the facil ities it offers when it reaches maturity. Without this, it may well be judged that the extra strains imposed by new regional insti tutes on an already stretched national R&D budget outweigh the resultant regional benefits. As for the particular case of Rogalands forskning, it is true that the institute may not yet have made very significant demands for support from NTNF. However, its con tinual growth and ambition to carry out larger projects will in the future undoub tedly result in pressure on traditional fund ing patterns of institutes (which are based to a large extent around the activities of SI, SINTEF, and CMI). Clearly, if local inter ests are willing to support financially the

(which are based to a large extent around the activities of SI, SINTEF, and CMI). Clearly, if local inter ests are willing to support financially the

side 269

f urther development of a regional research unit, then in terms of national R&D policy no-one can take issue with such «bottom-up» developments. But if the longer-term aim is to become a general technological univer sity through the back-door (after a decision has already been tåken at a national level not to support such a development), then the whole question of the future of RF is one that should be discussed seriously in the near future by Norwegian policy-makers (particularly in view of the criticisms voiced by OECD in their review of Norwegian science policy that there were already too many research institutes). Already a centre of excellence is being set up for petroleum technology, and the hopes of people at RF seem to be that this will act as a spring board for expansion into other areas of re lated technology, until the basis of a full scale technological university is created. In view of this, there are several important questions conceming national research pol icy that should be asked: does Norway need another large central research institute? Should it be made clear to RF that it will not be allowed to become anything more than a regional research institute (apart from in petroleum technology)? If so, how should it relate to the existing central research insti tutes? What position should NTNF take vis-a-vis applications for resources from RF, and from the small number of regional insti tutes that are hoping to emulate the growth of RF? In the short time available for carrying out this project, it has not been possible to provide definite answers to questions such as these. However, it is clear that some of the firms which have worked closely with RF do hold strong views on these issues and do f oresee certain changes. The views of this prominent Rogaland industrialist are not untypical: «To build up RF like SI would cost too much, and it should not be done. It would be a mistake. Already RF are beginning to es tablish their own projects without any plat form in industry, and this is dangerous. Up till now they have avoided projects such as these. Wc have told them our opinion, and that their future should lic in being a small, relatively specialised institute.» In view of these fears, it is obvious that urgent attention needs to be given to ques tions of the type raised in the preceding paragraph in order to produce a clear and explicit national policy towards regional re search institutes and RF in particular. 12 THE SUPPORT OF INDUSTRI AL R&D — AN OVERALL ASSESSMENT In previous sections, wc have focussed on the sponsored research projects carried out by institutes, the views of firms on the suc cess of those projects, and the strengths and weaknesses of individual institutes. But how well is the Norwegian collective research system as a whole working? In particular, is NTNF currently meeting the research needs of industry? And are the institutes, es pecially the central institutes (SI, SINTEF, and CMI), providing the support required by firms? These are two of the more general questions put to firms after wc had discus sed with them details of specific projects or contacts with institutes. The views of firms are obviously particularly pertinent, since they, along with public agencies, represent the principal «users» of the NTNF system and of the services provided by institutes. And since their views were obtained under conditions of confidentiality (all quotations from interviews used in this report are anonymous), they can presumably be tåken to reflect reasonably accurately their true feelings. Thus, in many cases, their views were probably expressed far more critically than would have been the case in public statements, where there might be a f ear that criticism would in some way jeopardise the firnVs future chances of obtaining NTNF support. 12.1 The overall view of firms. What are the views of firms? Their repon ses fall mainly into four categories: (1) those who believe that the collective research system, as currently constituted, is working well, and is in no need of any change; (2) those who believe the system is working reasonably satisf actorily, but could defi nitely be improved; (3) those who believe the system is not work ing very well, and is in need of major changes; and (4) those who find the current system com pletely unsatisfactory, and believe that it should be scrapped and replaced by a completely different system. In addition, there are some mechanical engineering firms who either chose to ex press no views on the system, or, perhaps more signif icantly, have no knowledge of its working at all. The responses of electrical and mechanical engineering firms are shown in Tables 34 and 35.

The mechanical en gineering firms are, if anything, more criti cal. First, previ ous access to NTNF resources is clearly a key factor. Appendix 12 shows that firms with over 200 employees have received 83% of the grants to industry made by the VF Committee and 67% of those from the TE Committee. In other words, NTNF support for industry has been heavily concentrated on the larger companies. f irms are more critical of such a system. And because they believe they have little chance of obtaining funds, many of those that are f ully aware of the NTNF system and what it can offer, are unwilling to invest the appre ciable resources required in writing a pro ject proposal. Secondly, in the mechanical engineering sector in particular, smaller firms tend not to have technically trained staff with the ability to establish and maintain contact with NTNF and the institutes. They are therefore less able to draw up proposals for projects that contain a strong research ele ment, often a crucial f actor in determining whether NTNF support is received. A num ber of firms that had applied reported great difficulties, even in just attempting to specify their needs and resource require ments in a manner acceptable to NTNF. One might have expected that such firms would have received some help in applying to NTNF from STI, with which many of them deal in relation to non-technical mat ters (see Tables 11 and 12 in Section 9). That this has not happened is probably the direct result of a strongly ingrained mutual dis trust that seems to exist between STI and NTNF. The former apparently believes that NTNF serves only large firms and the insti tutes (which STI views as ill-equipped to meet the needs of small firms). And NTNF seems to regard STI as an organisation of low-level management consultants dealing primarily with firms whoese needs are es sentially non-technical. A third factor is the single application date each year for NTNF project proposals. This is almost certainly more of a problem for small rather than large firms, since the latter generally have longer time-horizons, and are therefore better able to f orecast and specify their future R&D needs. Lastly, among those small firms that are engaged in R&D work, there is a f ear that, if they submit their projects to NTNF com mittees on which their larger competitors are often represented, their ideas will be «stolen» or support for them will be blocked. Similarly, the NTNF requirement that the results of work it helps to support should be made freely available, is often more of a problem for small firms (which are likely to have a large number of competitors) than for large companies enjoying a position of monopoly or oligopoly. All this it not to imply that large firms are totally satisfied with the system. Certainly, a few large companies have benefited con siderably from NTNF resources, and large firms in general tend to be far better repre sented on the NTNF committee structure. In addition, they normally prossess the ex pertise and administrative back-up to deal eff ectively with NTNF, thus improving their chances of receiving funds. Nevertheless, many of them feel that they are not getting the support that is needed, and several pointed rather critically at the distribution of resources by NTNF committees. For ex ample, if one excludes Dn Veritas, only 21 million kroner was allocated to industrial firms by the VF Committee over the 5-year period between 1977 and 1981, compared with 43 million kroner to SINTEF alone. With a mere 4 million kroner a year avail able for industrial projects in this sector, most firms felt that the impact of NTNF could never be more than marginal. While larger firms regard it as absolutely essential to increase NTNF industrial fund ing by an order of magnitude or more (many arguing that this should be done by reduc ing the very substantial subsidies currently given to declining industries like ship building), few would like to see the larger sums of money distributed in the form of NTNF project grants. Instead, they expres sed a pref erence for a system closer to that currently used to administer the Industrial Fund and in particular the Innovation Plan funds. This has at least three advantages as far as firms are concerned. There is no re quirement that the results of the work be made freely available. The lead-time be tween applying for funds and receiving a grant is generally much shorter. And thirdly, and most importantly for mechani cal engineering firms, the average size of grants is considerably larger (651,000 kroner compared with 366,000 kroner for the period 1977 to 1981). 12.3 The effects of firm R&D intensity. It was clear from the industrial interviews that, although finn size is a crucial variable in determining views on the collective re search system, it is by no means the sole determinant. In particular, R&D intensity of the finn also seems to be important. How ever, the effects of R&D intensity are some what more complicated than those of size, as Tables 38 and 39 make clear. In the case of the electrical and electro nics sector, firms with a high R&D intensity are in general more critical of the institutes and particularly NTNF.
