would be less critical of the collective re search system, for the reasons outlined above in the discussion of the advantages of large size. Part of the explanation for this discrepancy probably lies in the fact that the very advanced electronics firms, many of them relatively small, are generally «ahead» of the institutes in terms of techno logical competence. One such firm put it as follows: «The institutes are supposed to be at the top of their technological field. But if you look at the technically successful companies in Norway, these are all much better than the institutes and much more advanced.» This and other similarly placed firms are therefore rather critical that the system cannot offer them more help. But perhaps the main explanation is that the size effect discussed earlier is far greater than any R&D intensity effect. And since most of the large electrical firms (generally in the elec trical engineering sector) have a low R&D intensity (and vice versa), this explains why the low R&D intensity firms appear to be more satisfied. For the mechanical engineering sector, the picture is even more confused. The high R&D intensity firms are less critical of the NTNF system, but more critical of the insti tutes, than their low R&D intensity coun terparts. The reasons for this are far from obvious. Perhaps they are less critical of NTNF because they possess the staff cap able of f ormulating strong research propos als, hence ensuring that they receive appre ciable f inancial support from NTNF. On the other hand, their own R&D capability may be so advanced that the institutes are able to offer them little help. All that one can say with any certainty is that in this sector the ef f ects of finn R&D intensity are consider ably smaller than those of finn size. Overall, however, the main conclusion of this section is not so much that different firms have different views, but that the great majority believe the collective re search system needs to be changed and im proved. It is to a discussion of the changes that they and institutes would like to see that wc turn in the final section. 13. CONCLUSIONS AND SUGGESTED AREAS FOR DISCUSSION One of the main reasons why the Science Policy Research Unit was invited to carry out an assessment of Norway's system for the state support of industrial research was the belief that outsiders would perhaps be in a better position to identif y areas within the system in need of change. In our inter views with rasearchers and f irms, wc there f ore made a point of stressing that the inter viewees should be as frank and honest as possible — if they believed that there were problem areas, they were asked to bring these up and discuss them fully. Bef ore examining their responses, it must first be emphasised that our focussing on certain problem should not be interpreted as implying that Norway's collective research system, and NTNF in particular, is poor. It is not. In international terms, it seems to work relatively well, particularly in view of the relatively small amount of resources available. There is probably closer contact between research institutes and firms than in many other countries. NTNF, in the post-war years particularly, seems to have played a significant role in developing the R&D capability of Norwegian industry; and there are many examples of highly success ful industrial projects that began as longer term research in institutes, progressed to the stage of development, and were transf er red to industry, which then gained consider able commercial benefits. Prominent ex amples, as wc have seen, include the AUTO KON system, and numerically-controlled machine-tools. However, just as the collective research system needed re-orienting in the mid-1960s after the first 18 years of NTNF's existence, so some parts of the system are probably in need of change today. There are perhaps two main reasons for this. First, over the last decade the world economy has changed rapidly and dramatically, bringing with it the need for changes in the structure of the Norwegian economy. Norway can either wait until those changes are forced on it (through firms going bankrupt — but past experience has shown that government sup port for ailing companies is an extremely expensive way of tackling this wider problem, as Norway has found with its 300 million kroner a year subsidy for the ship building industry); or it can attempt to anti cipate those changes and take preventative action in advance to ensure that the chan ges are as painless as possible. Whether the present system for the support of R&D is sufficiently flexible and fast-reacting to do this is one of the questions that wc have addressed. A second change since the 1960 s has been the greatly increased R&D cap ability of at least some Norwegian firms, many of which are currently amongst the

change since the 1960 s has been the greatly increased R&D cap ability of at least some Norwegian firms, many of which are currently amongst the

side 275

principal recipients of NTNF support. A sys tem originally devised to help finns with little or no internal R&D capability may not be completely appropriate for helping firms that now possess this capability to varying degrees. Before going through the various issues that wc believe merit consideration by the Industriforskningsutvalget, it is worth stat ing briefly how these were identified and views on them obtained. The process began with a survey of the literature on collective research, the results of which have been dis cussed in Section 3. This suggested some of the possible problems that should be con sidered. Then, in the first set of interviews with senior officials and institute directors in December 1980, individuals were asked to identify the main strengths and weaknesses of the Norwegian collective research system, and were questioned about areas identified in the literature review. Wc were thus able to draw up a list of issues on which focus, and a systematic set of questions was subse quently put to researchers and firms in the course of the interviews over the next two months. At the end of each interview, re searchers were asked to summarise their views on the issues previously discussed by completing an attitude survey. In this, they were presented with a set of statements, for each of which they circled a number de pending on the extent to which they agreed or disagreed with the statement. The results are presented in Appendix 14. It can be seen from statement 1, for example, that 68% of the researchers interviewed believe that the NTNF system is in need of change. Wc have attempted to synthesize the main issues emerging from the two sets of industrial and institute interviews under twelve headings, although in many cases an issue will relate to several of these headings, so there is much cross-referencing between the various sub-sections. The twelve head ings can in turn be grouped together in f our categories (although again with a certain amount of overlap between them). These re late to: (1) the relationship of collective research to Norwegian industrial strategy on the one hand, and to other mechanisms for the support of R&D and innovation on the other; (2) NTNF; (3) the research institutes; and (4) industry. Wc shall consider each of these in turn, but at the same time attempt to show that the linkages between these various components of the collective research sys tem are extremely important. It must be emphasised once more that what f ollows is not so much a set of recom mendations, as the identification of areas that might profitably be examined by the Commission, together with some suggested changes that might be worth considering. In certain cases, some of these changes have already been discussed in Norway (for ex ample, changes to the NTNF committee structure), and in a few cases may even have begun to be implemented. Because wc are outsiders, and because of the very limited time available for carrying out this work, wc have obviously not been able keep fully abreast of such events. If some of the chan ges wc suggest have already begun to take place, then at least our discussion of them may give them f resh impetus, and help them overcome the opposition they are likely to encounter. 13.1 The relationship of collective research to industrial strategy, and to other mechanisms for the support of R&D and innovation. 13.1.1 The need for a national industrial strategy. Problem — Any assessment of the mechanisms for the support of industrial R&D must be situated in the broader con text of national industrial policy. An R&D policy can only be eff ective if it is fully inte grated into the national industrial strategy, while an industrial strategy, if it is to be successf ul in the long term, must surely con tain as one of its integral parts a clearly f ormulated R&D policy. The role of technol ogical innovation in promoting industrial competitiveness has been widely recognised (see section 3.1). The importance of an expli cit industrial strategy for the support of R&D policy, on the other hand, has perhaps been somewhat under-estimated in Norway 1 — judging from the comments made by in dustrialists during our fieldwork. A signifi cant number of interviewees believe that the government has devoted insufficient at tention to f ormulating a strategic industrial policy, in which promising industrial sectors and firms would be given preferential sup port. One institute director put it bluntly: ') There is certainly less emphasis than in Japan, for example, where the Ministry of International Trade and Industry first of all draws up its industrial strategy, and then builds an R&D policy into it.

example, where the Ministry of International Trade and Industry first of all draws up its industrial strategy, and then builds an R&D policy into it.

side 276

«Wc have no strategic industrial policy»; while the following statements typify the views of many firms: «There is no overall strategic view on the direction of the Norwegian economy.» «Håving no industrial policy is the main problem. In our field (telecommunications), all our main competitor countries, and es pecially Japan, have clear industrial pol icies. In Japan, there is heavy government support, for example through government purchasing policy. France is the same. The French Government has spent large sums of money on restructuring the telecommuni cations industry. But in Norway, the government does not use subsidised prices or help with R&D when buying from Nor wegian industry. Nobody can expect us to compete under these conditions, especially when labour costs here are amongst the highest in the world. So the lack of a cohe rent industrial policy is the main problem in Norway.» As evidence to support such views, many firms pointed to the example of large subsi dies provided for firms in difficulties, parti cularly in the ship-building and textiles sec tors. A subsidy to such companies may give some temporary financial respite, but often the eff ect is to make the situation worse for other, previously healthy companies in the same sector, or to prevent early rationalis ation in an industrial sector in structural decline, as the statement by this firm måkes clear: «One of our main competitors is a finn that went bankrupt, but which the Govern ment took over. It is now back in the market with lower prices. Everyone knew that it went bankrupt because of over-capacity in the market. Vet the Government helped it to restart, so there is still over-capacity in the market, and all the other firms, includ ing us, are now suffering as a result.» Even some of the recipients of such government subsidies recognised the long term dangers of such a course. For example, a number of mechanical engineering firms interviewed in this study made it clear they realised that their long-term f uture was out side the ship-building industry, and that, although they wished to diversify and had considered doing so, the subsidies for ship building made it financially attractive in the short term not to change direction. One finn put it as follows: «Wc foresaw the need to change early from ship-building to off-shore engineering....But in the five years 1975 to 1980, it has been easy to make money in ship-building — in fact, easier than in off shore engineering. This is because of the higher subsidies. These have been too high to permit re-organization into different areas of technology.» The perceived absence of an industrial strategy and R&D policy may account for some of the difficulties experienced in long term planning by NTNF. Only 20% of the institute researchers whom wc interviewed believe that Norway's f uture R&D needs are built into current research programmes. The much-heard criticism that NTNF is spreading its R&D f unds too thinly over too many projects (80% of researchers feel that funds should be concentrated in larger grants — see statement 30 in Appendix 14) and industrial areas highlights the f act that, in order to concentrate resources, strategic choices must first be made. Although it could be argued that NTNF should not shy away from its responsibility for making such policy choices for the allocation of its funds, the absence of clear directives from the Ministry of Industry does not seem to be making its task any easier. Possible changes — Greater re cognition needs to be given to the role that R&D policy can play in improving indus trial performance, and to the fact that selec tive use of R&D resources, (in the form of grants, subsidies, or procurement contracts could therefore be used to promote either certain key industrial sectors or individual dynamic firms in otherwise less important sectors. Whilst the recent Ministry of Indus try White Paper on Industrial Policy (St. Meld. nr. 54) appears to indicate a shift away from the use of government subsidies for declining firms in financial difficulty as a major instrument in industrial policy, it seems less clear when it comes to indicating which industrial sectors and firms are to become the growth-points of the Norwegian economy. A positive formulation of Norway's long term strategic industrial needs, and the con struction of a coherent national policy to wards research, development, and innova tion (tasks for which the Ministry of Indus try should presumably have overall respon sibility) are both essential before one can begin to select the R&D projects that are to be backed with public funds. Without them, many researchers and firms feel that the present NTNF Long-Term Planning system is little more than an annual budgeting ar rangement, 1 rather than an instrument for helping to establish policies and priorities. J ) As one institute director said, «The old longterm planning system (at NTNF) is really a budgeting system. Everything is divided into many small areas. These areas are generally equivalent to institutes or to areas of work in institutes. The main problem is that there is little change over time.»

13.1.2 Rationalisation and co-ordination of the mechanisms for the support of research and development. Problem — At present, NTNF, the In dustrial Fund, the Development Fund, the Innovation Plan, the Branch Fund, STI, INKO (and even banks, although wc have not considered this source of finance in our study) are all to a greater or lesser extent involved in the support of R&D. This has led to two types of problem. First, because the system seems in the main to have grown up on an ad hoc basis (whenever a new need arose, a new mechanism was established, often because politically this was the easiest way to gain access to the necessary re sources), the present mechanisms are in some cases no longer appropriate to today's (and tomorrow's) industrial and technologi cal requirements (74% of researchers inter viewed feel that existing mechanisms are no longer appropriate — see statement 12 in Appendix 14). Secondly, because the system is complex, if not confused, it is certainly difficult for firms to use (as many of our industrial respondents noted), and probably not very easy to administer either. (It is worth noting here that 74% of institute re searchers believe that Norwegian firms are not taking full advantage of the facilities and expertise available at government f unded research institutes — see statement 3 in Appendix 14.) Possible changes — What is re quired is a clear reformulation of the goals of Norway's R&D system, a distinction be tween the constituent parts (taking into ac count what should be seen as legitimate areas for state intervention), an allocation of the constituent tasks to the different par ties concerned (NTNF, Industrial Fund, STI, etc.), and a decision on the relative priority to be given to each. This should be made a priority by the Ministry of Industry. Some of those goals would presumably in clude the following: (a) The support of longer term «strategic» research, that is, research likely to benefit industry in 5 to 10 years time. (For research with a longer time-scale, support should be entrusted to NAVF — this may require better co-ordi nation between Research Councils than there is at present.) Of particular interest might be the so-called «generic» technol ogies, that is areas of technology with poten tial applications in several sectors of indus try. The administration of this could per haps be handled by NTNF programme com mittees (see section 13.3.1. below). Currently, it does appear that longer-term research is not being aceorded the priority most believe it to merit, with NTNF funds split into a large number of small projects — often with short-term industrial needs in mmd — so that concentration of research efforts within the institutes is difficult. 76% of in stitute researchers (see statement 11 in Ap pendix 14) feel that more longer-term re search should be carried out at Norwegian research institutes (including 77% at FFI where researchers have little to gain from a re-orientation of NTNF's funding prior ities). This view is shared by many senior industrialists in large finns who believe that such long-term strategic research would ul timately lead to the greatest benefit to in dustry (and in the meantime produce the technologically skilled researchers, used to working in t e a m s , that industry so cruci ally needs at the moment). (b) The support of specific areas of «industrial R&D» — i.e. work with a shorter time scale before com mercial implementation that is mi t i - ated by industry. This might be car ried out by firms, or by firms in conjunction with institutes, but not by institutes alone because of the need for very close contact between researchers and firms in this sort of work. The choice as to whether or not to use an institute for part of the work would rest with the finn. At present, it is clear that many firms are put off from applying for NTNF funds because they believe, rightly or wrongly, that such money will be granted only if they agree to spend half of it at an institute. As one said, «Wc feel afraid of håving help from NTNF. If you get help, you have to use re searchers and an institute which takes half the money.... The result is it involves too much paperwork, and it generally leads to too much basic research. It is unlikely to produce much of practical use. If wc could get money to do the work here, wc would apply funds.» In view of the doubts expressed by firms on the ablity of NTNF committees alone to assess the likely industrial impact of work of this type, the best system for administering this might be a combination of NTNF com mittees (suitably reorganized — see 13.2.1. below) and the Industrial Fund, i.e. a system similar to the present arrangement for oper ating the Innovation Plan. However, as many industrialists stressed, such help can not be eff ective with the level of funds cur rently allocated to support R&D in indus try. Compared to the high direct subsidies

for ailing firms (many industrialists would say «too high»), the positive support for creating new technologically advanced in dustry seems extremely lo w. In 1981, only approximately 40 million kroner was avail able from NTNF in the form of industrial projects (with 12% of this going to Dn Veri tas, which is perhaps more akin to an insti tute than a firm). For the mechanical engin eering sector coming under the VF Commit tee (and excluding Dn Veritas), less than 3.5 million kroner has been allocated to firms. The problems fac ing the companies are huge compared with the help they get from the NTNF system.» Given what many feel to be a pressing need to stimulate R&D (in process automa tion, new products, improved quality and reliability), a very considerable increase would seem necessary. Without this, such firms may not be in a position to exploit all the emerging opportunities associated with oil-field development. Similar arguments apply to the electronics industry, which must have strong inf rastructural support if it is to develop into the high value-added industrial sector needed by Norway to main tain its international industrial standing. (c) Technical help for small firms (non-technical help is discussed in section 13.4.3 below). Whereas measure (b) is most likely to benefit companies with some internal R&D capability, this measure is directed at firms (generally small) with no such capability. Such firms are normally unable to make effective use of NTNF and the institutes at present (see section 13.4.2), and need special help. This could be pro vided by STI itself, or by STI acting as a «broker» or «middleman» between small firms on the one hand, and NTNF and the institutes, on the other. It would, however, require better co-ordination between NTNF and STI than exists at present. (Some of those interviewed feel that this would be best achieved by establishing a Board within the Ministry of Industry to oversee and co ordinate the activities of NTNF and STI.) In addition, NTNF might provide general f unds to institutes to cover the costs of giv ing certain forms of special help to small firms (for example, subsidised short-term consultancy, although care would be needed to ensure that the interests of private con sultancy firms were not over-ridden.Fur ther, it would seem that the technological capability of STI would need to be improved and the organization ré-oriented from its current concern primarily with matters of economy and factory re-organization, to give greater emphasis to technological con siderations. (d) Monitoring and diffusing the results of overseas tech nology. This is probably best done de centrally (rather than through a central clearing house like NSI), either by each in stitute accessing the technology it needs by scanning the literature, or by encouraging institute staff to work for a temporary period overseas at a leading finn or research institute (see section 13.2.3). The advantages of person-embodied dif f usion are far greater than those from library-based methods, al though there is clearly a need for both. (e) Providing a «sign-posfe ing» service to firms — that is, a guide to the various types of help available to industry for the support of R&D. 82% of researchers believe that smaller firms are often unaware of the facilities available for the support of R&D (see statement 19 in Appendix 14), and many firms are all too aware of this problem. «Small firms just don't know where to ap ply for money. Wc don't really know what to do. Wc have been lucky and are beginning to learn, but wc still don't really know where to get money for R&D.» «The very big firms always know how to apply for money. But wc don't know much about how to go about it, how to word appli cations, which institutes giye what sort of help. So wc need information on what is available, and where you can ask for help of a certain kind. If you don't happen to know the right people to talk to, you cannot find anywhere to go.» However, this second finn's assertion that at least big firms know how to apply for support is evidently not always true, as this statement by a finn employing several thou sand staff måkes clear: «I do not actually know what government support is available. Some companies spend a lot of time finding out. I would rather spend the time on productive work.» Perhaps NTNF could commission some one to write a manual for firms, explaining how to get in touch with NTNF, how to
