complete NTNF applications, what other f orms of support are available, and how to deal with institutes so that they provide the help required (by writing clear specifi cations, insisting on fixed price contracts, and so on). Illustrative case-studies of suc cessful and unsuccessful dealings between f irms and NTNF or institutes could be inclu ded. It should be written by someone in in dustry with substantial experience of deal ing with the system. However, perhaps more important is that NTNF should adopt a more a eti ve ap proach. Many industrialists strongly made the point that, rather than «sitting back» in Oslo and waiting for industry to approach them, NTNF should devote far greater ef forts to visiting firms to learn of their problems, help formulate project proposals, and check on the progress of existing pro jects. To do this might involve the need to recruit staff with more industrial experi ence into NTNF, and it would certainly re quire far greater co-operation with STI than currently exists. 13.1.3 The relationship of collective research to other measures for the support of industrial innovation. Problem — Collective research is merely one among several possible mechan isms by which governments can attempt to stimulate industrial innovation. One of the most important of these is an innovation conscious procurement policy. However, as the following comments by firms make clear, this is a tool to which the Norwegian Government seldom has recourse at present: «Too often the Norwegian Government goes abroad for its purchases instead of helping Norwegian industry develop new produets. The procurement agencies are af raid of taking responsibility for equipment specif ications and performance, and instead prefer to buy «off the shelf» foreign equip ment. The Government is only interested in buying Norwegian equpment if it is clearly better and cheaper. Otherwise they buy ab road.» «The Government should be more careful in its purchasing. For example, the Post Of fice is buying Philips computers. They could have given a development contract to Nor wegian industry, in the same way as FFI did with the laser range-finder. As it is, the technology will belong to Philips in Eind hoven. The Government should learn from the military.» Possible changes — At present the Ministry of Industry måkes only very limited use of procurement as a tool for stimulating research, development, and innovation. Experience overseas as well as in Norway (see the discussion of Norsk Data in Appendix 1) suggests that procurement can be a most ef f ective method of encourag ing innovation. For example, evidence from the development of the US semiconductor industry suggests that, while most of the important early iriventions and innovations arose as the result of private initiatives, government (military) procurement played a key role in accelerating the widespread dif f usion and adoption of semiconductor de vices. If the Ministery of Industry were therefore to considerably increase its use of this mechanism, the potential benef its could be very great. Besides procurement, there are a variety of other measures at the disposal of govern ments. Government subsidies, for example, perhaps in the form of tax incentives, can be used to stimulate demand and thereby en courage the investment needed to get inno vations «over the threshold» from R&D to commercial implementation. The French Government, for example, in its attempt to encourage industrial innovation in telema tics, has subsidised the cost of receivers. The Norwegian Government could perhaps draw on the experiences of others with these vari ous tools for stimulating innovation, and start to use them on a rather larger scale than it does at present. Provided they were properly integrated with each other, they might then permit a much stronger and more eff ective innovation policy than exists at present, and one which might greatly en hance the overall national industrial strategy. 13.2 NTNF. In this section wc examine possible chan ges to the organization of NTNF, and the need for NTNF to concentrate its resources and to devote greater attention to the moni toring, assessment and quality control of re search work. 13.2.1 The re-organization of NTNF. Problems — In the interviews with both industrialists and institute staff, a number of problems associated with the cur rent organization of NTNF were identified. First, there appear to be diff iculties related to NTNF's attempt to fulfill two roles at the same time — funding research, and operat ing institutes. Indeed, such are the problems associated with this that, of the researchers who have definite views on this question, just over two-thirds believe that NTNF

such are the problems associated with this that, of the researchers who have definite views on this question, just over two-thirds believe that NTNF

side 280

should be split into two separate parts ra ther than continuing to try to combine the two roles (see statement 13 in Appendix 14). One aspect of this problem is that, within NTNF committees, there are generally two sets of interest groups competing for the same resources — institutes and finns. From discussions with those who have been members of committees, it appears that one result is a rather complicated inf ormal sys tem of cross-alliances and bargains, as insti tutes and firms manoeuvre, attempting to «solicit» partners who will strengthen their case for funding. From the figures discussed in section 5.3, it is apparent that the bulk of project grants are allocated to institutes, with only approximately one quarter going to firms (and some of that is recirculated back to institutes through sponsored re search projects). The firms at least interpret this as the result of NTNF feeling a sense of responsibility towards its institutes, or at least being more receptive to lobbying from institutes rather than industry. The follow ing view is fairly typical: «There is constant conflict between the research institutes trying to make sure their f inancial resources are as adequate as poss ible, and the firms. If a finn puts in a pro posal, the institutes say, «Wc will do all this, and you will do only that». Because they have better contacts with the people giving out the money, it often seems that the com mittees steer most of the money in the direc tion of the institutes rather than the firms.» However, perhaps a more important fac tor is that institutes are generally more skilled than firms in writing strong propos als. This was the comment at one finn: «I worked at an institute. With my back ground, I know I could write an application, and get money for it, regardless of the content of the work I pro p o s e d . There is more emphasis in the as sessment on the style and the technical pro f iciency of the application, than the content of the proposed work.» Consequently, an application from a finn, even though the proposed work is very pro mising, may be turned down because the proposal in poorly written. (This is a parti cular problem for smaller firms, which are less experienced than large companies in including a research element in their pro posals, and making what are essentially de velopment projects appear as «research and development» work.) This may partly ex plain why 63% of the researchers intervie wed disagree with the statement that most good R&D projects are funded (see state ment 4 in Appendix 14), while only 29% agree with it. The large firms in particular recognise that most project grants are awarded to in stitutes, and they theref ore attempt to link their applications with those made by insti tutes. In some cases, they appear to do this even in the case of projects for which, were it not for the possibility of state support, they would have little interest, or where the institute concerned may not contain the best qualified people to carry out the re search. In turn, each institute recognises that, in order to compete successfully for f unds with other institutes, it has to show that its projects are «industrially relevant». From the firms' point of view, the aim is to steer institutes closer to their own areas of interest, or even to persuade them that cer tain research is of such priority that the institute should apply for funds itself. If they are successful in this latter goal, they are able to get the research done without håving to commit 50% of the resources themselves. However, firms that are unable to find suitable institute partners instead have to apply for grants in their own nåme. Because they then have to contribute 50% of the costs, and because of the time and resources required to prepare and submit a project proposal, they may decide that the eff ort is not worthwhile. The problems associated with the existing system were well summarised by the follow ing two industrialists: «The danger of the present (NTNF) system is that institutes go to a company and ask the finn to become involved and to do a project. They suggest to them that the Government will pay half the project price, and that they can therefore get a subsidy. Too often the finn will jump at the offer, bewitched by the idea of a subsidy, and not ask if the product is good or bad for the company. They think gullibly that they are getting a good deal. Later on, the finn will recognise that it has been cheated in being dragged into the project by a good salesman from the research institute.» «Research institutes deliberately involve competitors on suggested projects, so sup port from industry is received because no finn can afford to be left out. Institutes of ten seem more interested in getting money than in really helping industry.» A second problem centres on the NTNF committee structure. There are few who dis agree with the statement that the number of committees should be reduced (for resear chers, just 13% disagree — see statement 15 in Appendix 14). The committee structure

that the number of committees should be reduced (for resear chers, just 13% disagree — see statement 15 in Appendix 14). The committee structure

side 281

grew up around the previous NTNF Direc tor, and while he may have been able to handle 20 lines of commucation from the committees (and 15 from the institutes), it must be doubted whether this is the most efficient, organizational structure. More over, the committees themselves may no longer be appropriate to today's technologi cal problems (see statement 26 in Appendix 14) — in some cases, they overlap and there is duplication of effort, while in other cases researchers fall between two or more stools, and are unable to obtain support from any of the committees (a problem already re cognised by NTNF and discussed in NTNF's Arbeidsformer, 18 Fe bruary, 1981). Thirdly, there is the question of NTNF committee membership, Because Norway is a small country, there are often few «neut ral» experts to judge project applications. Again this can give rise to potential conflicts of interest. A committee may be f aced with the task of judging an application from the organization of one of its members. Alterna tively, a proposal submitted by one finn may be rejected by a committee which contains a representative from its main competitor. As a result, many firms are understandably re ticent about submitting applications for their best projects to NTNF because of a fear that their (often larger) competitors, judging their proposals, will steal the idea; they theref ore prefer to wait until they can find their own resources from elsewhere to fund the R<ScD, thereby losing what is often precious time. One finn described the situ ation like this: «There is a big bureaucracy with NTNF which is very hard to penetrate. Some firms have made an industry of applying for grants and getting on committees. In 1973, when I applied, it became obvious how close NTNF and these firms were. So if one ap plies, your applications are given to these firms for consideration. They can hold things up as long as they like if there's any chance of competition... l cannot accept my competitors judging my application. Once you apply, you have no control over who is peering into your papers.» Many firms obviously deeply resent this domination of committees by certain large firms and by institutes: «The committees tend to have people on them from the institutes and the big compa nies. These are the people who get most of the money. It's not direct discrimination, but it is something like that. The commit tees consist of the establishment — it's a sort of «club». If you are outside, it's difficult to get money. It's not because they wa n t to keep people out, but because they just talk to people who speak the same langu age.» Overall, the industrial interviews led to a clear conclusion — that it is extremely dif fi cult for a firm to obtain an NTNF grant unless it is represented on the relevant com mittee, or at least has a committee member prepared to act as an advocate for its case. This is recognised even by institute resear chers, 46% of whom agree that groups not represented on NTNF committees are rarely awarded grants, compared with only 19% who disagree (statement 25 in Appendix 14). A final problem concerns long-term plan ning. Because projects are only funded a year at a time, planning for more than a year in advance is often rather difficult. This causes difficulties in both institutes and firms (who are unable, for example, to hire consultants on a long-term basis). Possible changes — To overcome these perceived problems, what is required is a separation of the two roles played by NTNF, combined with a re-organization of the committee structure so that there is no longer direct competition for funds between institutes and firms. Some of the changes required might include the following. (a) For administering research in each strategically important new area techno logy (identified as part of the national in dustrial strategy), a programme committee should be set up. The membership of this should be kept as small as possible. It might include one first-rate researcher, one indus trialist, one overseas expert (to avoid the problem of conflicts of interest mentioned above), and perhaps one representative from the relevant industrial R&D committee (see (b) below). The programme committee would begin by inviting «bids» from the in stitutes for carrying out a long-term re search programme in the area. Instead of relying solely on written proposals, the pro gramme committee might also interview the research leaders of the proposed program mes. The chosen institute would then be given long-term funding (perhaps for a period of 3 to 5 years (see section 13.2.2). The programme committee would monitor the progress of the research and the eventual transfer of technology to industry, and would finally be disbanded. (b) The administration of the «industrial R&D» grants could be handled by NTNF committees similar to those currently exist ing. These might give grants to indus try (private or public) to carry out indusside 282

handled by NTNF committees similar to those currently exist ing. These might give grants to indus try (private or public) to carry out indusside 282

trial R&D, either on their own of in con junction with institutes. However, since they would no longer be dealing with appli cations from institutes, the present 20 com mittees could probably be drastically reduc ed in number, new committees being chosen in such a way that they correspond more closely to current technological needs. These committees should n o t be f ixed — as R&D interests alter, so should the commit tees. Another change might be that these committees would be able to give grants of up to 2 or 3 years duration, again subject to satisf actory progress and gradually increasing financial responsi bility by the finn. As with pro gramme committees, the membership should be kept as small as possible, enabling decisions to be tåken quickly, and the use of overseas members might be encouraged to obtain more «neutral» judgements. The com mittees would be expected to devote a signi ficant proportion of their time to «quality control» of existing projects (see section 13.2.3), rather than concentrating most of their eff orts on proposal evaluation. Finally, and perhaps most importantly, the ke y criterion in the selection of industrial R&D projects would probably need to be the likely industrial benefit of the wor k , rather than whether or not the technology is «interesting». 1 This would in volve the committee taking far more ac count of the circumstances of the finn con cerned — in particular, its needs, its ability to meet those needs with or without NTNF help, and its past record (if any) for commer cial success with R&D projects. (c) The third part of NTNF's reorgani zation concerns the administration of insti tutes. Here, the aim should perhaps be for far greater decentralisation, increasing the powers of institute boards, and hence reduc ing NTNF's responsibilities. In f act, perhaps a formal legal separation between NTNF and the institutes might be considered, with each institute f ormally constituted as an in dependent, self-governing organization. The alternative would be an organizational sep aration w i t h i n NTNF, whereby responsi bility for institutes would be clearly separ ated from that for the support of firms, and given to a board which would then plan and co-ordinate activities at the institutes in such areas as capital investment and per ') As one finn put it, «the main problem is that the committees look at what is technologically interesting, rather than what technology is needed to do good business.» sonnel policy. In our view, however, this would provide a rather less satisf actory solu tion than a formal legal separation, since, while perhaps reducing the conflict between institutes and firms, and between certain institutes, it would still leave established in stitutes with a powerf ul leverage over NTNF f unds. It would therefore not encourage the restructuring of institutes that at present many people feel is essential. In contrast, formal separation between NTNF and the institutes would result in far more open competition for research funds, and, if insti tutes were unable to respond to changing needs, they would find that their funds were gradually declining. Formal separation would, of course, mean that institute boards would have to be considerably strengthened in line with their new responsibilities. Each board would be responsible for the planning of the institute's future activity, checking that those plans were generally adhered to (at present, institute researchers claim that they are f ree to change plans from one year to the next without anyone paying much attention), and establishing criteria for selecting which industrial R&D projects the institute should engage in and which it should not. Another important function of the board would be to monitor and evaluate systematically the research performance of the institute, perhaps every 5 years or so. NTNF's responsibility towards institutes would then be reduced to providing general funds merely to cover the costs of (i) giving special help to small firms (see section 13.4.2) — this could be administered by a joint NTNF/STI committee; (ii) personnel development of institute staf f , enabling institutes to send staff abroad (to monitor overseas technology) and on «industrial sabbaticals» (see section 13.3.3) — these costs would be in propor tion to the number of staff at the insti tute, and this would "not therefore require much administration at NTNF. All other costs (for the administration of the institute, sickness, project applications, etc.) would then have to be covered by an appropriate overheads charge to the strate gic research programmes and industrial R&D projects. Institutes that found diffi culty in obtaining sufficient programme grants and contract research would then re alise rather sooner than they do at present that they needed to make alterations. With these changes, NTNF would, as a result, have three main components: (i) various strategic research programme committees, perhaps under an overall technology policy committee;

as a result, have three main components: (i) various strategic research programme committees, perhaps under an overall technology policy committee;

side 283

(ii) a small number of industrial R&D com mittees; (iii) a small section (perhaps a joint commit tee with STI) responsible for the provi sion of special help to small firms. The institutes would be wholly autono mous, legally separated from NTNF. 13.2.2 The concentration of research efforts. Problem — For most research, there is a certain «critical mass» or «noise level»; if the resources are below that level, little pro gress is made, and the resources are largely wasted. This was a point made by many insitute researchers. In a country the size of Norway, resources are obviously limited; but because so many interests are represented on the committees, there is of ten a tendency to give small amounts of support to every one. In other words, as one intitute director put it, «The committees end up trying to mini mise the level of dissatisf action, rather than maximising the eventual level of satisfac tion.» The result is a f ragmentation of research activities, and sometimes duplication of ef fort. At the level of the institute, because their income consists of a large number of small, mostly short-term grants, all tied to specific pieces of work, there is very little autonomy or freedom to plan more than a year ahead. In addition, institute staff have to spend a considerable fraction of their time writing large numbers of project proposals. SI, for example, receives funds from NTNF for 50 different projects, most of them very small (one man-year or less). Consequently, the great majority of researchers (86%) at insti tutes want to see greater concentration of resources on larger and longer-term re search programmes (see statement 30 in Ap pendix 14). The fragmentation also affects firms. Ma jor companies, in order to receive a large total sum of money from NTNF, send in a barrage of grant applications. Like institu tes, they reason that the more they submit, the more they are likely to be funded, as the f ollowing quotation måkes clear: «Wc have no problem in inventing propos als. The more you apply for, the more you get.» The committees then have to spend much time sifting through all these proposals. In deed, in the VF Committee, pressure of work has become so great that money is provi sionally allocated to projects bef o r e the final submission date. Possible changes — For institu tes, one of their main sources of finance should come in the form of the programme grants already mentioned. The long time scale involved with them (3 to 5 years) would give the institutes greater f reedom in plan ning ahead, and more continuity in their work. However, these grants would only be given in strategically important areas, so the institutes would have to accept some reduction in their freedom to choose areas of research. In addition, no institute should have an automatic right to a fixed number of large programmes or to a set percentage of available research funds. Programmes should be allocated on merit, and reflect the past «track record» of the researchers con cerned and the likelihood of future success. This could probably only be achieved with the formal separation of NTNFs two func tions (allocating research funds and admin istering institutes) discussed above. Pro gramme grants, because they would be much larger, would also mean that NTNF had to process fewer proposals each year, leaving it freer to concentrate on quality control (see section 13.2.3). One obvious danger with longer-term pro grammes is that the work of institutes may become divorced from industrial needs. To avoid this, two steps could be tåken, in ad dition, of course, to ensuring strong indus trial representation in strategic planning. First, the programme committee could be expected to make regular site visits to moni tor the progress closely. Secondly, gradu ally increasing industrial invol vement could be built into the funding of the programme. For ex ample, for the first two years, NTNF might pay 100% of the costs; in the third year, the institute might be expected to obtain 10 % of the funds from industry or public agen cies, in the fourth year 25%, in the fifth year 50%, and in the sixth year 100%. If in any year the institute f ailed to obtain the requi site industrial support, then the committee would seriously consider whether the pro ject should continue, or be terminated and the resources switched to some other strate gically important area. Turning next to the firms, those which submit large numbers of grant applications to NTNF are often the firms in the strongest position to meet the costs of their R&D work themselves. Some of these firms are honest in admitting that they treat the grants merely as a subsidy to the finn, and

the costs of their R&D work themselves. Some of these firms are honest in admitting that they treat the grants merely as a subsidy to the finn, and

side 284

that the work it is used to support would have been carried out even if no grant had been awarded (see section 13.4.1). As far as such firms are concerned, the rationali sation they give to this is that, since they pay taxes, they see no reason why they should not attempt to attract back to the finn as much state support as they can. One possible change that might be considered is restricting the number of proposals that NTNF will consider from each finn, perhaps to f our. This would not aff ect smaller firms, which tend to submit only one or two pro posals, and it would force larger companies to perform some «weeding out» of weaker proposals before they send them to NTNF, thereby cutting down the work-load of NTNF committees. (NTNF support for in dustrial research projects carried out by very large companies should probably not be entirely stopped — even if the firms are able to pay for all the work themselves — be cause it is essential that they remain in con tact with the institutes if the latter are to transfer the technology developed in strate gic research programmes to industry.) 13.2.3 The monitoring, assessment, and quality control of research work. Problem — At present, nearly all the emphasis within institutes and NTNF is on writing the project proposal, and virtually none is on project res u 1 1 s . This point was made quite strongly by one institute director: «There must be more emphasis on the re sults of work. Everyone spends time on pro posals, and no-one on quality control. Good work stands out, but poor work does not show.» Institutes often see a written report as representing the end-result of a project ra ther than the implementation of the results in industry, forgetting that firms are very often unable to implement the technology on their own. And even these reports are sometimes poorly written because the re searcher is convinced that NTNF will file it without first reading it. One finn com mented rather scathingly: «It doesn't matter what you put in the reports to NTNF. Only the formal criteria have to be met. It doesn't matter whether the R&D carried out is a success or not.» Possible changes — Both strate gic research programmes and industrial R&D projects should have a clearly speci fied hand-over period during which insti tute and firm work together (see sections 13.2.2. and 13.3.3). The need for such a period when both sides co-operate is clear from the lessons at FFI. The feedback from industry which such an arrangement permits will then provide a measure of quality control on the institute's wbrk before the project is fi nished. Secondly, institute boards should them selves carry out monitoring and evaluation of the research at the institute. This could be done annually, together with a more tho rough review every five years or so, using some of the methods adopted in this study (in particular, systematic interviews with re searchers and firms). Thirdly, in the case of strategic program mes, the NTNF programme committee might be required not only to read the final report, but to interview the people con cerned (researchers and industrialists), and to submit a short assessment of the degree of success of the research to the technology policy committee (proposed earlier in sec tion 13.2.1), or to the NTNF Director. This would pay particular attention to the main reasons for the success or failure of the work, so that the lessons could be incorpor ated in the selection procedure for future programmes. In a similar way, the NTNF industrial R&D committees would be expected to allo cate a substantial fraction of their time to project-evaluation (as opposed to pro p os a 1-evaluation). This would necessitate them visiting institutes and firms (see sec tions 13.1.2 and 13.4.2 on the need for NTNF to adopt a more active approach). While a detailed assessment of all the projects sup ported by a committee might not be possible, every committee could be requested each year to look at a number of the most suc cessful and least successful projects it had f unded with the aim of identifying the prin cipal reasons for success and failure. A short report containing their conclusions could then be presented to the NTNF Director so that again the lessons could be absorbed when proposals are being judged in the fu ture. 13.3 The institutes. This section considers the various func tions of institutes, the need for a constant regeneration of their staff , and their role in the transfer of technology. 13.3.1 The role of collective research and the functions of institutes. Problem — From our interviews with researchers and firms, it appears that at

13.3.1 The role of collective research and the functions of institutes. Problem — From our interviews with researchers and firms, it appears that at

side 285

present there is a certain confusion about the role of collective research in supporting industrial R&D and innovation, and its re lationship to other mechanisms for achiev ing that aim (financial incentives to firms, government procurement, etc. — see section 13.1.3). This confusion is particularly appar ent in discussions as to what are, or should be, the functions of research institutes. It is clear that, for a variety of reasons (particu larly economic pressures and the reduction in the level of general funds from NTNF), some institutes are becoming increasingly involved in non-research activities, includ ing consultancy-type work — this has brought them into rivalry with consultancy firms which resent what they see as «unfair» subsidised competition — and even (as was seen earlier in section 6) certain aspects of production. These shifts in the functions performed by institutes seem to have tåken place w i t h o u t any overall strategic deci sion that such shifts were required or desir able. Certainly, if companies had been asked for their views, many would have been hos tile, as the statements of these firms make apparent: «SI is particularly a culprit. They have a philosophy, «Lefs bring things to a proto type-level — industry doesn't understand us anyway». Vet SI doesn't actually understand what it is to make a product. There is the same tendency at other institutes...Produc ing products is not just a matter of technol ogy. Sometimes institutes have good ideas, but they are not relevant to the needs of Norwegian industry. So the role of institutes should not be to produce prototypes — that must be done in firms.» «The institutes should not be in the busi ness of short-term contract research. What is done now should be handed over to com panies. This might be very painful to long term employees at the institutes, but indus try would welcome these staff into organi zations that have market f orces as boundary conditions.» «My strong view is that the system has fallen between two stools. The institutes are neither profitable organizations account able to the market, and håving to continu ally justify their existence — they don't have to do that because they are half-sub sidised and lead a sheltered life where they are not geared to the compromises needed in industry; nor are they any longer a breeding place for ideas — their technical level is not that high. So they neither serve profitable research nor long-term research. They are amateurs in both.» Possible changes — What appears to be needed is a complete re-assessment of the role of collective research in the light of prevailing demands for industrial R&D on the one hand, and the ability of some f irms (but not others) to supply some of the necessary technological developments themselves on the other. It might then be possible to specify more precisely which f unctions the institutes are clearly required to fulfill include: (1) Longer-term strategic research. As suggested earlier, institutes might put in bids to NTNF programme committees to support work of this nature. As this work passed through the development stage and approached the prototype production stage, the institute would generally not develop a prototype on its own, but would either (a) persuade a firm to build the prototype (with the help of the institute); or (b) some insti tute staff might break away to set up their own company based on the new technology; or (c), if (a) and (b) proved impossible, the work should be shelved. The exception here is with radically new technology, where a finn might not be able to commit the resources needed for building the prototype. In such cases, it may be necessary to continue the prototype deve lopment stage at the institute, while at the same time taking positive steps to build up either a new company or competence in an existing enterprise. (2) Industrial research and development. It was suggested in section 13.2.1 that firms might apply for project grants to fund such work, and that they might then choose to have some of the work performed by an institute. Thus, a second f unction of institu tes would be to carry out sponsored R&D for firms and public agencies. Institutes would be suppliersto industry, not compe t i t o r s for funds. (3) Special help for small firms. The nature of this help and the way in which it might be funded are discussed in section 13.4.2 below. In view of the f act these three sources of funds could be separated within NTNF (each being administered by a separate set of committees), it would be relatively easy, when necessary to alter the balance between the various types of activity at institutes in line with formulated policy. Subsidiary problem — Some NTNF institutes, particularly the very specialised ones, may not be working in strategically important areas, whether for industry or government, and would thereside 286

the very specialised ones, may not be working in strategically important areas, whether for industry or government, and would thereside 286

fore be unable to obtain programme funds. Possible changes — Ideally, such institutes might, over a reasonable period of time, be closed down (or, if working in areas of more basic research, apply to NAVF for funds). According to one very senior NTNF of ficial, this would have already tåken place were it not for the tenure system. In the long run, the Commission ought to consider whether NTNF should continue to subsidise unimportant or poor research just to main tain jobs. Institutes which find themselves in this position could initially perhaps con centrate on: (i) industrial R&D, attempting to expand and cover a wider range of technology; (ii) the provision of help to small firms; (iii) retraining of institute staff (see section 13.3.2 below), perhaps by sending them to NTH, or to overseas universities or advanced technology firms, the aim be ing to give the institute a chance of eventually obtaining programme sup port in a strategically important area of technology. Alternatively, some of them might be temporarily seconded to work on long-term research program mes at other, more strategically placed, institutes (see section 13.3.3). In the twin responsibilities of NTNF were to be separated (as discussed in section 13.2.1), the decision as to whether to close an institute or to re-orientate its research ac tivities, would be the responsibility of its board rather than NTNF. 13.3.2 The regeneration of institute staff. Problem — Successf ul research de pends ultimately on the skills and creativity of the researchers. Research institutes, if they are to remain productive on a long term basis, need to have a continuous inflow of new people and ideas, and a constant development and evolution in the skills of its incumbent staff. Without this, there is an inevitable tendency towards rigidity and stagnation. This seems to have occurred in some Norwegian research institutes. While part of the problem reflects the ageing pro cess aff ecting most of the institutes, and the consequent limitations on recruitment and promotion, this eff ect can be minimised in a number of ways. In particular, SINTEF achieves this regeneration of people and in flow of ideas through its association with NTH, and FFI through military service and through overseas training of its staff. SI has no such ready source, and this may well be the main factor underlying the current problems at the Institute (see section 11). As one institute director put it, «The establishment of any research insti tute idependent of a teaching institution is fatal. NTNF hasn't really appreciated this.» 67% of the researchers interviewed feel that NTNF institutes would benefit from closer links with university science depart ments, while only 15% disagree (see state ment 16 in Appendix 14). Possible changes — Institutes need two main types of recruits, new grad uates, and engineers or researchers with in dustrial experience who therefore possess some understanding of such commercial considerations as cost and reliability. The first of these can best be provided by inte grating the institute with a university or regional college. The problem is that there is at present only one technicial university and, as technology continues to become in creasingly important to the survival of Nor wegian industry, this may well prove insuf f icient. Hence, changes may be required in the educational system. The existing uni versities could place greater emphasis on technological courses. If this were to happen at Oslo University (as is currently planned), then a closer association with SI would seem the most practical arrangement, although for the full benefits to be achieved, SI would almost certainly need to be moved into the same buildingsas the new university technology departments. In addition, more regional colleges with technology depart ments may prove necessary. For the second type of recruit — engine ers and researchers with industrial experi ence — what is required is a more flexible salary structure to ensure that such recruits are not severely f inancially penalised when they move from industry to an institute (see also section 13.3.3 below). Besides ensuring a constant supply of able recruits, an institute must also have some mechanisms for combating the effects of ageing among its incumbent staff. There are a number of ways of attempting to do this. First, the greater interchange of staff with industry (in the final stages of industrial R&D projects, or through industrial sabat ticals) suggested in the next section would ensure that institute researchers were peri odically exposed to new challenges and problems. Secondly, there is the undoubted stimulus from combining research with teaching. It is clear from our study at SIN TEF that the involvement with students for ces researchers to read more widely than

research with teaching. It is clear from our study at SIN TEF that the involvement with students for ces researchers to read more widely than

side 287

they otherwise would, and hence to keep up with the literature on recent research devel opments. At SI, few of the researchers are able to benefit in the same way because of the considerably more limited contact with Oslo University. Lastly, if a research insti tute is closely linked with an educational establishment, and if the institute f inds that some of its older researchers are becoming less productive or less able to attract grants for their work, then such staff can perhaps f ind an alternative outlet for their energies in teaching. If this happens, then the college or university might in exchange be more willing to let some of their younger staff take part in the institute's research pro grammes, thereby providing a further sti mulus to other institute staff. All this obvi ously requires a higher level of co-operation and indeed integration of NTNF institutes and educational establishments than exists at present. 13.3.3 The transfer of technology. Problem — There are two aspects to the problem of technological transfer. First, the Norwegian collective research system does not seem to have been very effective in monitoring and diff using the results of over seas technological work to potential users in Norway. Secondly, Even when institutes carry out an R&D project satisfactorily, the results are often not implemented by indus try in the form of a new product or process. For example, there are often difficulties in moving from the laboratory prototype stage to a production prototype, a process which requires a range of skills that typically nei ther the institute alone nor the finn alone possesses. What might be described as «the first law of technology transfer» is that «The best mechanism for trans f erring technology is through the movement of people». This is one of the clearest lessons from the experiences at FFI in particular. Let us look in more detail at the various stages in the transfer process that are of particular relevance here. The first involves the transfer of technology from overseas to Norway. This is especially important for a country that carries out less than 1 % of the total world R&D. NTNF is formally respon sible for the monitoring and diffusion of overseas technology, but at present this task seems to be relatively neglected. (Certainly the people whom wc interviewed do not feel that NSI is making much impact through its bibliographic techniques.) A second stage concerns the transfer of scientific and technological information b e t w e e n institutes. On the basis of our interviews, it seemt at present that the links between institutes are very poor — most researchers have little idea what their col leagues elsewhere are doing. Only 29% of institute researchers think that there is good co-operation and exchange of infor mation between Norwegian research insti tutes, while over twice as many (61%) dis agree (see Appendix 14, statement 10). The third stage concerns the transfer from institutes to industry. Wc encountered many cases where, although the project was completed by the institute and a report writ ten, the results were not then implemented by the finn concerned. In some cases, parti cularly with smaller companies, this was be cause the firm did not possess people with the necessary expertise to take over the technology, and transform it into a product or process. In others, it was more the f ault of the researchers, who, lacking any experi ence of working in industry, were unable to produce results that were capable of being implemented. This was a particular problem with product-development, with difficulties of ten arising because the product was tech nically too sophisticated. Possible changes — For monitor ing overseas technology, more funds should be provided for financing institute staff to work overseas for temporary periods in uni versities or advanced technology firms. This is done on only a very limited scale in NTNF institutes at present, and should be intro duced at least to the level found in FFI, where this scheme has been operating with considerable success for many years. (At the same time, this would provide a mechanism for promoting abroad those areas of tech nology where Norway is very advanced in world terms, but which it does not fully ex ploit at present.) The exchange of personnel between insti tutes would probably be rather harder to arrange. However, perhaps institutes, when putting in bids for long-term research pro grammes, might be encouraged to recruit staff from other institutes on a temporary basis (i.e. on secondment). In some cases, this would enable them to draw up stronger research teams than would otherwise be the case, as well as ensuring that, when visiting staff returned to their home institutes, they took with them the skills and knowledge they had developed. They might then form the nucleus of new long-term research pro grammes, and this could be particularly im portant for institutes which currently might

might then form the nucleus of new long-term research pro grammes, and this could be particularly im portant for institutes which currently might

side 288

not be in a strong enough position to attract long-term programme grante (see section 13.3.1). For f acilitating the transfer of technology between institutes and industry, a number of mechanisms can be suggested. First, in strategic research programmes, institutes could be expected to recruit, on secondment for one or two years, a number of research staff from industry. At a later stage, when they returned to their f inn, they would be in a far stronger position to take over and im plement the results of the programme. It should be noted in this respect that many firms reported the recruitment of students (from NTH in particular) as one of the best means of gaining access to technology. After håving worked on projects, often in connec tion with SINTEF, such students seem to constitute a vital element in the techno logy-transfer process. The situation is, how ever, rather different at SI and other insti tutes, where formal integration of student training and collective research is much less evident. Perhaps the main way SI could im prove the diffusion of its work into industry is through far greater formal contact with Oslo University (perhaps under the auspices of the new Engineering Faculty currently being mooted at the University). Secondly, for industrial R&D sponsored by firms at institutes, the project should per haps not just end with a written report as it so often does at present. Instead, the insti tute could be expected to produce a report about 80% of the way through the project, and institute staff might then spend the re maining 20% of the time working at the finn, implementing the results, developing prototypes, and starting to put the technol ogy into production. In addition, financial support might be given to encourage firms to send one or more of their staff to the institute for the first 20% or so of the project to help specify what was needed from the institute more precisely. (This would also have the effect of ensuring that firms only used institutes for sponsored work to which they were fully committed — see section 13.4.1.) A third possibility is to encourage long serving institute staff to go on an «industrial sabbatical», perhaps once every 5 or 6 years, where they spent 6 or 12 months working for a finn, either in Norway or overseas. (Better still would be some sort of «swap» arrange ment involving both institute and industrial staff.) Institutes could each year circulate a list of researchers (along with their interests and areas of expertise) who were available for «loan» to industry. In effect, institutes would serve as a «skills library», where firms could «borrow» skills (in the form of resear chers on industrial sabbaticals) for a tempo rary period. Such an arrangement would have the effect of ensuring that most insti tute researchers were used to working in a commercial environment, as well as bring ing them into contact with prevailing indus trial problems, while industry could obvi ously benefit appreciably as well. Lastly, the salary structure for institute researchers could be made more flexible so that institutes are better able to recruit people with industrial experience. (The sala ries should not, however, be so generous that researchers never wish to return to in dustry!) 13.4 Industry. In this final section, wc consider the situ ation of firms — how some of them cur rently appear to be abusing the collective research system, how small firms require special help, and the need of industry in general for non-technical as well as techni cal help in its attempts to innovate. 13.4.1 Abuse of the system by firms. Problem — At present, certain firms are clearly abusing the collective research system. Some promise to put in 50% of the costs of a project to match the NTNF grant, and then fail to do this. Instead, other R&D work by the firm (work that sometimes bears little relation to the project being sup ported) is classified as the finn's contri bution. This is cited by institute researchers as one of the main reasons why collabo rative projects fail. One researcher put it as follows: «In joint projects with industry, wc often f ind that they don't carry out their share of the work. This is the reason why projects often get behind. Firms end up saying that they just don't have the capacity to do the work — that their staff are more concerned with day-to-day production problems.» And firms themselves confirmed that this practise does take place, although most de nied that they themselves were guilty of it! «In our company, wc do put in the 50% that wc are meant to. But I know some companies do not because I have been inside the system. It is always difficult to draw a border between what is the project, and what is not. Wc do use the funds on the project, but other firms I know do not.» It should, however, be emphasised that

what is the project, and what is not. Wc do use the funds on the project, but other firms I know do not.» It should, however, be emphasised that

side 289

this form of abuse is not generally a consci ous premeditated act by firms. All too often, a firm will go into a project with a strong commitment to playing a full part in the work, but unforeseen pressures of day-to day development activity subsequently in crease and manpower resources can no lon ger be spared. As the project continues, es pecially if it is of a longer-term nature, it goes steadily down in the firms R&D prior ities until the finn sees little gain in con tinuing to put resources into the project. The co-operating institute may then pres surise the finn to continue as a «sleeping partner» in order to avoid losing the NTNF grant. A second abuse of the system is by larger firms who apply to NTNF for money to sup port work that they themselves can afford. They regard NTNF grants as a subsidy, and hence a way of increasing their profits: «Wc applied because the board and I wan ted to make as large a profit as possible. This is just a subsidy. To be frank, the money could be better used in other companies.» Two firms in fact referred to NTNF sup port as a «Christmas present»; after håving applied for support, and while waiting to hear the result of the application, they meanwhile carried out much of the work for which they had soiight support. As one said, «You don't know until too late whether you will get the money from NTNF. You have to make a decision whether to go on or not with the work long before the grant is given. So if you then get a grant, it comes as a nice Christmas present. Wc don't even put the grant into out budget.» Possible changes — The first of these problems tends to occur most fre quently when the finn is not very enthus iastic about the project, perhaps håving been persuaded to join the work by an insti tute which needed to have an industrial partner in order to obtain NTNF support. To avoid this, what is needed, perhaps, is a mixture of the «carrot» and the «stick». The «carrot» involves ensuring as far as possible that the finn i s enthusiastic about the pro ject, since it will then almost certainly put in far more than the 50% required. This might be achieved through some of the mechan isms for the exchange of personnel discussed in section 13.3.3. These would also encour age firms to set aside resources specifically for the project right from the start in order to pay for sending one or more of their staff to work at the institute. Firms might be less likely to enter into projects to which they were only half committed if they knew that first they had to make an immediate invest ment of this sort, and secondly they would be required to bear increasing financial re sponsibility for the project, as suggested in section 13.2.1. The «stick», on the other hand, might take the form of a possible visit by the NTNF committee to the firms con cerned. Such visits would preferably occur with a minimum of advance notice. The committee could check on the progress of the project, interviewing the staff involved and asking to see evidence of the efforts made by the finn. (This would not be the sole purpose of the visit — it would also permit NTNF to find out about the problems of the finn, and some help might be given to the finn on the formulation of future project proposals.) NTNF does not need to check eve r y project. Merely the possibility of a thorough review should be enough to deter most firms from failing to put in the resources promised. This should be coupled with improved procedures for en abling firms to extricate themselves from co-operative projects when they find it no longer possible to make the required con tribution. Curtailment of the second type of abuse might be partly achieved by the earlier sug gestion (in section 13.2.2) that NTNF should consider a limited number of project appli cations from any one finn in a year. In addition, NTNF committees probably ought to look more closely at the ability of firms to pay for the R&D internally, in order to es tablish whether they really «need» support. A large finn that applies for a grant corre sponding to 1 % of its annual R&D expendit ure is likely to be less in need of NTNF support than a small company for which a grant of the same size represents 30% of its annual R&D budget. NTNF already has fig ures on the amount spent each year by firms on R&D (it collects these as part of its stat istical activities), so it should not prove too difficult to introduce this extra consider ation into the project selection procredure. 13.4.2 Help for smatter firms. Problem — As was seen in earlier sec tions, some firms are not being particularly well served by the Norwegian collective re search system. The problem is that different firms have very different R&D needs (for new products or new processes; for very adv anced technology or for minor improve ments to existing technology). They there fore require different mechanisms to meet them, not all of which are currently proside 290

minor improve ments to existing technology). They there fore require different mechanisms to meet them, not all of which are currently proside 290

vided by NTNF or by the other channels for the state support of research, development and innovation. At present, NTNF and the institutes are relatively good at helping (i) large firms (with more than 500 employees); (ii) medium-size firms that have formed into co-operatives like TESA; (iii) firms which, irrespective of size, have their own R&D capability; (iv) firms where there is already some personal contact with the institutes or NTNF (like a former institute researcher working for the firm). However, they appear to be far less suc cessful in helping medium-size and small firms where this personal contact does not exist, the reason being that it then takes the finn much more time and effort to find out who is the best person at the institute to approach for help, how to contact NTNF, how to write a satisfactory research pro posal, and on. One finn related its experien ces as follows: «Wc actually applied for money from NTNF five or six years ago. This was a fiasco. They send you a lot of very compli cated f orms, and after you spend a long time trying to find out how to fill them in, and then write an application, they send a bu reaucrat from Oslo. All he seemed to be in terested in was how many «educated people» wc have in the factory. But what use is it asking how many PhD holders wc employ? No small firms employ such people, but wc still have some good engineers. Wc then got the reply that wc are not in good enough shape to do innovation. If that is what they think, they should look at our record!» It is because of experiences like these that many smaller firms have reached the con clusion that, «Wc'rc not elever enough to get NTNF support or to engage the research institutes in carrying out projects for us.» And most institute researchers admit their inability to help, only 8% of those in terviewed believing that their institutes are successful in meeting the needs of smaller firms (see statement 27 in Appendix 14). Possible changes — Since the TESA companies do appear to be able to use NTNF and the institutes with considerable benefit, greater encouragement could be given (perhaps through tax incentives) to medium-size firms to join together in such co-operatives. For these to be successful, it would seem that three key conditions must be satisfied. The member firms must not be direct competitors in terms of produets, but at the same time they should share a general interest in the same process technology 1 (ro bot welding, for example). And, third, they should be situated geographically close to one another. For smaller firms, other mechanisms seem to be needed. One has already been mentioned — that a more technologically active STI (together with INKO) could act as a «broker» between the firms and NTNF or the institutes. There is, is course, the op tion of NTNF opening up regional of f ices, as SINTEF has done in the North of Norway (at Narvik). This would entail setting up a completely new level of organization which would, in many ways, merely duplicate the STI national system. Given the good con tact STI already has with smaller firms, it would seem that a more technologically oriented STI presents a better option than establishing a new set of offices. It should be noted in this respect that the establishment and maintenance of contact with small firms is not easy, and it was only when the SINTEF Narvik office recruited an experi enced local ex-STI employee that the office began to make any real impact upon North ern industry. Secondly, the institutes could be given funds to enable them to offer initially free and then subsidised services to small firms. This money could, for example, be used to provide do-it-yourself product development laboratories, training courses, and free ad vice on formulating projects and writing NTNF proposals. One finn commented, «The resources you need to put into a pro ject before it becomes suitable for a grant are quite large. It can be difficult for a small company to do this because they require those resources for other purposes.» And since small firms have great diffi culty in filling in the present NTNF grant application forms, a much simpler appli cation form may be required in the case of companies with less than about 50 em ployees. For both medium-size and small firms, another change from which they would benefit is greater flexibility in the handling of project applications. There could be s e v - eral application dates each year, ') One such co-operative organisation apparently failed largely because of the diversity of its membership, which included furniture factories, mechanical engineering firms, and plastic manuf acturers, and which theref ore shared f ew coramon technological interests.

furniture factories, mechanical engineering firms, and plastic manuf acturers, and which theref ore shared f ew coramon technological interests.

rather than one. This would be a crucial improvement for many smaller f irms, where research and development work generally has to be carried out quickly if it is to be worth doing at all. This finn's views are typical: «If wc have an idea for a product and want to get NTNF support, wc have to submit it by the end of next June. Wc hear about the grant in November, and start work the fol lowing year. Wc cannot wait such a long time for product development and innova tion. The present NTNF system is only suited to research institutes or big firms where they have longer-term plans. The sys tem should be more flexible.» If, in addition, the number of proposals from each finn were restricted, as suggested in section 13.2.2, this would mean that the processing time for applications could prob ably be significantly reduced, again to the benefit of small firms in particular. Finally, NTNF needs to adopt a more active ap proach, going out to visit firms rather than merely waiting for them to apply. Most smaller firms reported håving had very little contact of this sort with NTNF. As for the possibility of establishing more regional institutes, two factors should be borne in mmd. First, Norway already has a large number of institutes in relation to the size of its population, as the OECD report on Norway remarked in 1970. And as wc saw in section 13.2.2, one of the main needs is for more concentration of research efforts than exists at present. Secondly, it would seem from our discussion of Rogalandsforskning that its achievements so far have depended to a large extent on a number of special factors, including the nearby presence of oil companies, and the prior existence within the region of a tradition of industrial co operation and in particular on the activities of the TESA companies. Since these special factors are unlikely to be present to the same extent in other regions, the case for f urther regional research institutes is by no means clear. Policy decisions on this ques tion need to be tåken at a national level (see the discussion at the end of Section 11 for further details). 13.4.3 The provision of non-technical help. Problem — Almost all the emphasis in NTNF and the institutes is on providing technical help. Vet much previous research policy work suggests that innovations often fail more as a result of non-technical fac tors, such as a lack of management skills, inability to f orecast user needs, or poor mar keting (see Appendix 2). This is backed up by the evidence from our interviews with firms. For many, their main needs were non technical rather than technical, a fact which most researchers seem to realise since most agreed with the statement that there is little point in helping firms technically if they do not possess the management and marketing skills to create an economically successful new product (statement 31 in Ap pendix 14). Possible changes — Neither NTNF nor the institutes are currently geared to providing non-technical help. At present, STI does a great deal in the way of providing non-technical help, but this is at a level generally of use only to smaller firms, and even then it is not linked to the techni cal support provided by NTNF and the insti tutes. The situation would certainly im prove if formal links were established be tween NTNF and STI (see section 13.1.2), but it would still be necessary for institutes to build up their own non-technical support services, since it is not only the small firms which are in need of such help. There are two obvious ways in which this might be achieved. First, if the institute is associated with a university or college, it might start to draw upon the expertise of economists, management scientists, etc., and eventually to recruit some of these onto its staff . (De partment 17, for example, has already begun to do the first of these.) Secondly, the «swap» arrangements with firms discussed above (in section 13.3.3) might be used to obtain the services of people from large firms who have skills (in management, marketing, etc.) that they could pass on to small firms during their stay at an institute. As for NTNF, when its committees eval uate industrial research grant applications, they might be asked to pay greater attention to whether the non-technical inputs re quired for successful innovation have been tåken into account by those seeking sup port. In our assessment of projects, wc f ound f ew cases where any systematic market sur vey had preceded the start of the project, yet our FFI study shows that a clear recognition of user-needs at an early stage in the R&D process is extremely important in ensuring the success of that project. In cases where a firm applying for support is unable to pro vide the non-technical inputs itself , it could be directed by NTNF to a consultancy finn or institute that is able to help, and the NTNF grant might include an element for supporting this.

13.5 Concluding remarks. In this final section, wc have considered the three main components of the Norwe gian collective research system — NTNF, the research institutes, and industry. For each, wc have suggested a number of areas where the Commission might discuss the possibility of change. At the same time, wc have seen how collective research is part of a wider process, and how it cannot be con sidered in isolation from other mechanisms for the support of R&D, from innovation policy measures, and from national indus trial strategy. Indeed, al l these must be set in an international context. Here, two points need to be made. First, our assess ment leads us to conclude that, in relation to those of its principal competitors, Norway's system for the support of industrial R&D is by no means a poor one. Secondly, although solutions to the problems currently faced obviously have to be specific to Norwegian conditions, lessons can nevertheless be learnt from the experiences with collective research systems overseas. Blessed with the unique opportunity presented by its oil wealth, Norway has the chance to streng then its R&D capability so that industry can face the 2 lst century with confidence.

Appendices A.l Forsvarets Forskningsinstitutt (FFI): From Applied Research to Industrial Production 1. Introduction. FFI is a civilian applied research institute directly responsible to the Ministry of De f ence. Its primary aim is to provide an R&D basis for the development, production and use of weapon systems by the Norwegian military forces; a secondary aim, and one stressed by the management of FFI, con cerns the transfer of technology generated at FFI to Norwegian industry in general and to the defence-related industrial sector in particular. The annual budget of FFI is cur rently around 105 million kroner. 1 It has approximately 500 employees and a yearly R&D output totalling around 320 man years. In the appendix, wc attempt to ident ify the main characteristics of the FFI «model» for carrying out R&D, and to draw lessons relevant to research institutes in the civil sector. R&D activities at FFI are organized within five divisions and two groups: — Division for Electronics; — Division for Weapons and Equipment; — Division for Physics; — Division for Underwater Warfare; — Division for Toxicology; — Operational Analysis Group. The field-work carried out during this study was mainly concerned with R&D ac tivities of the Electronics Division of FFI, which represents about 40% of the Institu te^ total funds. In addition to analysing the organization and operation of the Electro nics Division as a whole, a limited assess ment has also been made of some illustra tive R&D projects carried out by the Elec tronics Division, but touching upon activ ities perf ormed by the Division for Weapons and Equipment. 2 •) Including an allowance of 10 million kroner for rent and 6 million kroner for the salaries of staff engaged in military service who are paid directly by the Ministry of Defence. 2 ) The major R&D projects focussed on in this study concern the development of: (a) laser range-finders; (b) digital electronic computere; (c) the Penguin ship-to-ship missile; (d) naval fire-control systems; (e) Anny weather-radar hardware. Detailed case-studies of (a), (b) and (c) are presented at the end of this appendix, and these provide the basis for much of the illustrative material presented in the main text. The Electronics Division employs a staff of 160 to 170 and has an annual budget of approximately 40 million kroner. This divi sion was created some 15 years ago, follow ing the merger of the divisions for (i) tele communications and (ii) radar. The areas of activity covered by the division have grown markedly over time so that today they in clude radio-geophysics, telecommunications and telecommunications equipment, digital computer development, electro-optics, iner tial navigation and radar systems. 2. Decision-Making and R&D Project Selection. Around 80% of the total FFI budget is provided by a basic block-grant from the Ministry of Defence, whilst the remaining 20% is covered by contract research and special (governmental) R&D project fund ing. The percentage of contract research in the Electronics Division is somewhat higher (25—30%) than that in FFI overall, and in some years up to half of this has come from foreign contracts. The R&D projects and other activities carried out at FFI are selec ted after close collaboration between FFI and the Norwegian military. Main policy directives are set by the Defence Research Policy Board, in which the Chief of Defence and five Inspector-Generals of the forces (Anny, Navy, Air Force, Home Guard, and Medical Corps) are represented, together with f our civilian scientists and the Director of FFI. Detailed selection of tasks for FFI takes place after extensive discussions between FFI and each of the branches of the mili tary, in which ideas and plans from within FFI, on the one hand, and the requirements or needs of the military forces, on the other, are considered. Although no formal criteria for project selection exist, the decision to fund particular programmes in FFI can be seen as the result of f our main f actors: (i) the needs of the military; (ii) longer-term strate gic technological requirements; (iii) existing capability and previous project activities at FFI; and (iv) the manpower and financial resources available. As regards the R&D re quirements for weapon systems, an underlyside 294

activities at FFI; and (iv) the manpower and financial resources available. As regards the R&D re quirements for weapon systems, an underlyside 294

ing policy factor has concerned the option of procuring and perhaps developing equip ment from abroad, as opposed to a national R&D effort; of course, the choice here is limited by the indigenous industrial and technological capability of Norwegian f irms, and partly for this reason FFI stresses the importance of maintaining regular contact with the defence industry community. The majority of projects selected are normally funded out of the basic annual block grants given to FFI by the Ministry of Defence; certain specific projects, however, require the negotiation of additional fund ing (depending on such factors as acqui sition of expensive technology and equip ment, or travel requirements, etc.). Approxi mately 15 to 20% of FFI funds are used for basic research activities and background scientific and technologial research (much of it in the area of toxicology). Because of the relatively large size and length of some R&D projects carried out 3 , there has usually been some scope for channelling sections of allocated project funds within FFI to per ipheral and more basic areas of research and experimental development. This factor, together with flexible project management, has in the past allowed a great deal of «ex ploratory» technological research within and between different project teams. Partly as a consequence, FFI has often been able to embark upon preliminary R&D before of f icial funds are allocated through a Minis try of Defence contract. This process has two implications: (i) it allows a more rapid response both to new technological develop ments (mostly from abroad) and to oppor tunities for follow-up R&D projects based on previous FFI activities; and (ii) it fa cilitates an early formulation of the tech nological and military prospects for certain R&D projects, thereby making the allo cation of development funds in those areas more likely. A powerful feedback loop be tween FFl's current R&D activities and the formulation of f uture military requirements for subsequent R&D project selection is thus created. A significant example of this is the inception and development of part of FFl's opto-electronics activities (starting in the mid 19605), which were based on early R&D on lasers paid for by a combination of 3 ) The largest of these was the Penguin ship-toship missile system. Development of this started in 1962, and has continued up to the present time with two later versions of the system. At its peak, this work occupied about 35% of the total R&D capacity of FFI. FFI internal funds and additional resources allocated within the Penguin missile devel opment programme. On the basis of this early research, the need for, and feasibility of, laser-based systems became apparent, and the Ministry of Defence decided to fund a number of specific military laser projects. A similar example centres on computer de velopment work, where Penguin funds en abled work to be carried out on the SAM computer in the early 19605. Only later did this result in concrete project-funding from the Ministry of Defence in the area of digital computers, as the potential for computer controlled military hardware became clear to policy-makers. Vet another example con cerns the work on fire-control systems, which was carried out for two years using FFI internal funds before the Ministry of Defence started formal funding. 3. Personnel Policy. A particularly prominent feature of FFI appears to be the high quality of its research staff. Around 15% of its 140 researchers hold Ph. D's, and a significant proportion of the remainder have completed the Siv. Ing. de gree at NTH. Most researchers are encour aged to continue their basic science activ ities even while engaged in applied technol ogy projects, and this is reflected in a signi ficant publication output and citation rate (see Table 17 in Section 9). The management of FFI feels that the emphasis on basic re search helps to safeguard against loss of competence and motivation among resear chers, while ensuring that good links with the rest of the Norwegian and international R&D system are maintained and encour aged. In fact, the opportunity at FFI to en gage in state-of-the-art research has been one of the main reasons the institute has been able to attract many of the best stu dents from NTH and Oslo University. Cur rently there is a turnover of around 10% among research staff, 17 new researchers håving been recruited in 1980. 4 The mechanisms for recruitment involve (i) the programme carried out by FFI for the training of Diploma students from NTH — each year some 10 to 15 students write their theses on research carried out at FFI, and on average between 8 and 10 of these are recruited after this work is completed; (ii) recruitment from the group of about 40 4 ) The turnover of engineers in recent years has been much higher — around 15 to 20 pct. per annum — mainly because of the relatively low pay at FPI compared to industry.

in recent years has been much higher — around 15 to 20 pct. per annum — mainly because of the relatively low pay at FPI compared to industry.
