military service personnel tåken on by FFI each year. Rather than undergo an inten sive period of training in the military, many of the academically better qualified opt to do their military service at FFI, and the institute is thus able to select from a large group of applicants. Around 5 of these each year are offered further employment at FFI. Another important feature of FFI is the internal organization of the institute. The Director, Dr. Finn Lied, often stresses that his main role is not to organize but to d i s - organise — emphasising the importance of flexibility and the dangers of ossification. As in many organizations, there have been pressures to structure research activities within well-defined divisions and groups, but FFI has managed to develop and main tain a policy of carrying out its R&D work within f 1 e x i b 1 e teams, newly constituted for each project or major task. In this way, research staff are generally forced to deve lop new skills every few years, and to date this seems to have reduced considerably the eff ects of ageing and rigidity that are often f ound in research organizations. (The aver age age of research staff at FFI is 38, and this has been increasing slowly over time.) It should also be noted in this respect that FFI sees itself as håving been extremely fortu nate (compared with other Norwegian re search institutes) in håving at its disposal, as a result of external contracts, approxima tely 80 temporary positions. These posts are typically allocated to researchers for a period of a year (with the possibility of re newal) without permanent employment håving to be offered, and are frequently used to ensure that those given permanent positions have the requisite competence and commitment to make a successf ul long-term career at FFI. Together these mechanisms ensure flexible research management, which seems to be a particularly important factor in ensuring successful goal-oriented R&D. 4. Technology and Know-How Acquisition. One aspect of the goal-oriented approach within FFI is the recognition of the need to keep up with the most advanced scientific and technological developments relevant for military systems. Perhaps the most eff ective mechanism employed by FFI to maintain state-of-the-art expertise in the institute is its policy of providing extensive periods of overseas employment for its research staff, particularly at American scientific or indus trial centres of excellence. Typically, be tween 6 and 10 FFI employees a year study or carry out research abroad for a period of one year, on full pay from FFI. 5 Researchers sent abroad usually have had at least 2 or 3 years experience at FFI, and are conse quently aware of the areas of advanced R&D most relevant to the work at FFI. On their return, know-how gained abroad is generally used in on-going FFI projects, and has of ten f ormed the basis for new technol ogical research areas at FFI. FFI develop ment of computer technology and lasers are prime examples of areas in the Electronics Division where crucial basic knowledge was imported from the United States in this way. In both cases, know-how from the US proved to be an essential requirement for the early inception and success of R&D pro jects (on the SAM-computer, and laser range-finders, for example), and provided the technological basis for subsequent R&D activities. Visits to overseas research centres, and the personal contacts built up during them, also seem to be a strong element in keeping institute staff informed of overseas develop ments. In addition, contacts resulting from frequent visits to conferences, specialised international meetings (often within the NATO network), and the exchange of papers with international research scientists, help enable FFI to remain well-informed of de velopments in relevant R&D areas abroad. In certain areas of high technology (e.g. space plasma physics and micro-electro nics), FFI perceives its capability to be about the most advanced and well-developed in Norway. For this reason, FFI does not seem to place as much emphasis on monitoring technological developments at other Norwe gian research institutes (although it does occasionally subcontract out tasks to them) as it does on overseas work. The strong extemal contacts of FFI serve to ensure that the institute generally does not inadvertently duplicate previous f oreign R&D activities. FFl's main points of contact are: (i) defence research groups of NATO; (ii) agreements on the exchange of research data with certain foreign military research organizations; and (iii) contacts with specialised research laboratories in the United States and elsewhere, often based on close personal links. Analyses of travel-funds over 1979 and 1980 (these total approximately 1.2 million kroner per year) show that some 45% of 5 ) Often on NTNF-funded fellowships.

travel concerned work related to specific R&D projects, 35% was for NATO-travel, whilst the remaining 20% was used for travel to international symposia, etc. Al though many researchers have criticised the decreasing level of foreign travel-funds, overseas visits (mostly short-term) remain an important aspect of FFl's strategy to wards technology and knowledge acqui sition. In contrast with the acquisition of tech nology and know-how for research and early development, the capability for the later de velopment and industrial production phases of weapon systems in usually sought and acquired within FFI or Norwegian in dustry. The deliberate policy of the Ministry of Defence to develop and maintain a national manufacturing capability for wea pon systems is actively pursued by FFI for those R&D projects which will lead to indus trial production. This policy has frequently required an active role by FFI in the early stages of production. Past FFI R&D projects which have resulted in industrial manufac ture indicate that, in cases where there is a weak (or non-existent) production capability in Norwegian industry, an attempt is first made by FFI to tram people from industry in order to acquire the necessary technical capabilities. Of the major projects surveyed during this study, several examples of this process were f ound, such as in the laser pro duction by Simrad A/S, and the manufac ture of infra-red detector systems. In such cases, the initial technical competence and experience of the firms in certain essential areas of advanced technology production were extremely limited. This require ment of establishing a national industrial capability for the manufacture of weapon systems developed at FFI thus has two im portant implications for the relationship be tween FFI and industry: (i) it encourages the early involvement of an industrial partner in the R&D stage; and (ii) it necessitates considerable involvement on the part of FFI in production-planning and the early stages of the manufacturing process. (See also sec tion 7: Technology Transfer to Industry.) 5. The R&D Process and User Involvement. A typical R&D project carried out at FFI, and f unded by the Material Commands, in volves the definition, research and develop ment of a weapon system, leading in the first instance to the prototype stage. Al though an R&D project may be based on preliminary research work done indepen dently at FFI, the problem-definition and formulation of the military requirements are usually carried out jointly by FFI and the appropriate sections of the military in tending to use the system. Following these discussions, a proposal is formulated by FFI for the development of the system, and pre sented to the appropriate Material Com mand for the award of a contract. Once this has been approved, an advisory committee forms the main link between the work at FFI and the military user. During the R&D phase, there is, however, little involvement on the part of the user — at least not at the working level in most of the projects wc surveyed. (One exception to this was the laser range-finder and the involvement at FFI of the Field Artillery during the R&D phase.) The military user is normally first involved in the prototype stage, when a field-test model can be used for prototype trials. The extensive interactions between FFI researchers and military users allow modifications to be made to the system based on direct knowledge of user-needs. This does not imply that the FFI-military collaboration at this stage is necessarily al ways unproblematic; instances were re ported to us where the military users have experienced difficulties in specifying their needs to FFI. Often these were related to the high degree of technical specialisation in volved in many weapon systems. The more advanced the technology required, the more apparent this practical constraint on the interaction between FFI and the end-users tends to become. The involvement of FFI in the further development and subsequent production of the weapon system and the involvement with the military user does not finish with the prototype stage and field tests. FFI is also in some cases responsible for writing production specifications for the manufac ture of the system, and is usually retained by the military as a technical consultant during the production-planning and pro duction stages. In some projects, bids for industrial production contracts have to be evaluated by the Material Command, and in these cases FFI usually plays an important role too. FFI and the military continue to work closely together during the implementation and production phases of a weapon system; håving carried out the development work, FFI is the only agent that can ensure an ef fective transfer between development and production (see also sections 6 and 7). As the project moves further into the production stage, the role of FFI as an intermediary

development and production (see also sections 6 and 7). As the project moves further into the production stage, the role of FFI as an intermediary

side 297

between the military user and the industrial manufacturer generally starts to diminish. However, FFI is often used as a consultant throughout the entire life-time of the wea pon system, including production, use, and modification. Its role as a permanent con sultant to the military on operational wea pon systems is resented in certain cases by researchers who prefer to devote their time to work on further weapon development. Since FFI is also consulted on technical questions during the operational use of de veloped systems, as well as participating in discussions with military users on subse quent improved versions, involvement of FFI in the formulation of, and response to, user-requirements is virtually continuous. This has a positive effect upon the continu ity and usefulness of in-house R&D activ ities since (i) it enables further modification and development work to be carried out at FFI on the basis of existing project/R&D teams; and (ii) it provides FFI with direct knowledge of user-needs, as well as enhanc ing opportunities for modif ications to exist ing systems and the formulation of future derivative systems or new developments. 6. The Selection of Firms and FFFs Relationship with Industry. The majority of FFI development projects concern weapon systems which are designed to go into industrial production, following research and development work at the insti tute. In most other governemental R&D laboratories, industrial involvement starts after the completion of the prototype lab oratory model. At FFI, however, there is a general belief that earlier industrial involve ment is usually beneficial in ensuring an eff ective transfer to the production stage in industry. At FFI, therefore, industrial parti cipants f requently enter weapon systems de velopment at an earlier stage — the exact timing being dependent on a broad range of factors, including project management, in dustrial competence, technical complexity, interest shown on the part of industrial firms, and the firmness of military produc tion-contract commitments. On the basis of the projects surveyed at FFI, there seem to be four different stages at which intitial in dustrial contacts may be established with respect to specific projects: — after the completion of the early-model (A-model) prototype and field tests; — during the R&D phase at FFI; — at the beginning of the formal project phase; — during the def inition phase of the development project. However, in the sample of FFI Electronics Division projects surveyed during this study, the first two patterns seem to dominate. Generally it seems that the more a particu lar firm has been in contact with FFI on previous projects, the earlier the contact with the finn tends to take place. Personal links play an important role in this respect. Contact between FFI and industry is also structured by definite FFI policy objectives. The stage at which an industrial partner is first sought and involved in a project may depend, for example, on the strategic im portance (for FFI) or complexity of the tech nology involved; FFI may perceive the im portanceofdevelopingan in-housecap ability with respect to an advanced area of technology (for example, the recent work on VLSI microprocessor technology), before an industrial firms is approached for involve ment. In complex weapon systems, similarly, FFI may be reluctant to involve industry before it has demonstrated the equipment internally — especially when it may form the basis of further technical development planned at FFI. As far as the selection of industrial firms is concerned, a formal general request for proposals (for produc tion contracts) is not the norm at FFI; rather, selected industrial firms are directly contacted by FFI on behalf of the Ministry of Defence and invited to take part in a discussion on industrial participation. This rather informal mechanism for selecting firms relates to three background factors specific to the Norwegian defence-techno logy environment: (i) FFI and Ministry of Defence policies aim at selecting Norwe gian industrial contractors for military production whenever possible; (ii) the num ber of Norwegian firms with the technical capability to manuf acture new weapon sys tems is very limited; and (iii) FFI deliber ately performs an active role in increasing technical and industrial capabilities in Nor way (which may sometimes involve promot ing a new manufacturing base). In particu lar, because of the strong links between FFI and the relatively small Norwegian defence industrial sector, the informal nature of the process by which FFI and the Ministry of Defence select their industrial manufactu rers seems to be less problematic than it perhaps would be in larger nations with many advanced defence firms. The relationship between FFI and the

7. Technology Transfer to Industry.
The degree of success in transferring
technology from FFI to an industrial raanu
facturer (as observed from the projects sur
veyed) seems to depend on two inter-related
factors:
(i) the quantity and quality of personnel in
the industrial manufactrer; and
(ii) the degree of involvement of the finn
during the R&D (or definition) phase at
FFI.
An evaluation of the projects covered in
this study clearly indicates that the most
successful ones in terms of transfer of tech
nology to industry have been those where
industry was involved during the R&D
phase or earlier. The extent to which FFI
needed to involve itself in the production
design and production stages was usually
dependent on the competence-level at the
recipient finn and the complexity of the
project involved. Conversely, those projects
where active industrial involvement did not
commence until the final stage of the R&D
phase or after the completion of the proto
type (e.g. Finn A in the Anny Weather
Radar Project — see below), encountered
the largest number of problems and delays

in transferring the technology and the re quired skills to industry. From the projects surveyed, it can be con cluded, however, that the single most im portant factor in enhancing the effective transfer of projects from the R&D phase at FFI to the production phase in industry, is the actual transfer of personnel between FFI and the finn. In theory, such transfer of personnel might have entailed the involvement of industrial employees at FFI during the R&D work on a system; in practice, however, the act i v e partici pation of industrial personnel in develop ment work has been very limited, even in cases where industrial representatives were physically present at FFI for longer periods. The transfer of technical personnel, if any, has been predominantly in one direction: FFI personnel moving to, or working with, industry (for limited periods) after comple tion of the R&D work at FFI, to assist the manuf acturer in the early stages of the pro duction phase. Because experience with past projects has shown that the degree of success in transfer ring technology to industry is directly linked to the extent of involvement of key R&D personnel from FFI in industrial produc tion, FFI, in view of its responsibility for ensuring the successful «industrialisation» of its R&D work, has in some cases actively encouraged the permanent transfer of key technical personnel to industry as a project advances from R&D to production. The more sophisticated and innovative a tech nology, the greater the need for FFI person nel to transfer to industry. Important ex amples of this transfer process are the devel opment and production of the Penguin mis sile (involving transfer of personnel to Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk) and laser range finder technology (involving transfer of per sonnel to Simrad A/S). In both cases, it was recognised early on that the transfer of technical skills through FFI researchers moving to industry would be a crucial factor in the success of the project. The corollary of this is that the absence of transfer of FFI personnel to industry may seriously impair the eff iciency and ef f ective ness of moving a project into industrial pro duction. Particularly in cases where indus trial involvement in the R&D phase has been minimal, the dependence upon FFI for technical skills can become considerable. In one particular case surveyed (involving the production of an IR detector system), sev eral weeks of «training» of industrial person nel at FFI was apparently insufficient to achieve the required degree of transfer of know-how. The complexity of the techno logy involved and the shortage of skilled manpower at the industrial finn forced FFI to remain actively involved in the produc tion of the system in order to meet delivery schedules. In this particular case, the per manent transfer of one or two key people from FFI to industry might well have solved this problem. The absence of such a move seems to have been related to two factors: (i) the lack of qualified manpower in this area of advanced technology; and (ii) the reluct ance of qualified FFI personnel to move to the particular finn involved. In this case, one lesson for the f uture (assording to some) may be the need to employ R&D personnel at FFI for specific projects with the condi tion that the researcher(s) involved will move with the project to the industrial pro ducers, in order to f acilitate the f ollow-up of R&D into production. Another option which has to some extent been exercised before is the creation of a new production unit, staffed by ex-FFI researchers. The opto-electronics division of Simrad A/S, in itially set up for the production of FFI-de veloped laser-range-f inders, is a case in point. The need for an active role by FFI in ensur ing successf ul industrial production in such a manner is closely related to the level of industrial capabilities present in Norway, and the more advanced the technology in volved, the more likely it is that FFI will have to be come involved in this way. In addition to constraints on the pro cess of technology transfer, the co n - t e n t of the technology to be used may be an issue in the relationship between FFI and an industrial manufacturer. Disagree ment on this point usually surf aces in cases where the finn is actually involved in the R&D process, and in discussions on new technological content in particular. When this happens, the FFI-industry relationship can be said to resemble closely that of an internal dispute between the production and R&D sections of a finn about the tech nology to be used. One particular example of this (which involved the development and production of the Penguin II control sys tem) arose because of a difference in prior ities between FFI and industry. On the pro duction side, the finn was more concerned with aspects such as reliability and quality control, therefore preferring to use more «established» technologies for a particular system; FFI researchers, on the other hand, were perhaps more interested in technical advance and sophistication. ces in priorities are best handled as early in the R&D stage as possible, with the impli cation that FFI projects not involving in dustrial participation during the R&D phase are possibly in danger of ending up with an over-sophisticated system, which is sub-optimal from the point of view of indus trial production. As regards the overall technology-transf er process, the greatest FFI-industry interac tion takes place in the period following the completion of the prototype development. The number of man-hours spent with the industrial manufacturer by FFI personnel gradually decreases after the production prototype stage, and during further stages of production. In cases where derivative sys tems (e.g. Mark 11, etc.) are developed and produced by FFI and the finn, there seems to be a trend of diminishing involvement by FFI in the various stages of R&D and pro duction, compared with earlier generations. 8 Outputs and Benefits. A major area of responsibility for FFI con cerns its role in helping to build a strong national capability in strategically import ant areas of technology and industry. In f act, FFI has a dual f unction — attempting to strengthen national capabilities with re spect to both the miliary forces and Norwe gian industry. To this end, FFI performs research and developement tasks both for the military and in support of industrial firms in the defence-related industries. Through successful R&D projects, FFI måkes a contribution to Norwegian techni cal and industrial capability, while on a more direct level the R&D performed by FFI enables Norwegian industry to produce the military systems required for Norwegian defence. Hence FFI plays an active role in provid ing technical assistance and «training» for industry as regards the development and manufacture of weapon systems, working closely with industrial defence contractors. In addition, FFI provides technical consul tancy to both industry and the military, which is another aspect of its role as an «educator» in the Norwegian defence and industrial arena. It is signif icant that in sev eral areas of technology FFI is perhaps the most advanced institute in Norway, and, since a great deal of advanced technology is acquired by FFI from foreign sources, FFI plays a major part in diffusing new know how from abroad into certain sectors of in dustry. To a considerable extent, industrial development in the areas of laser techno logy, computers, and micro-electronics can be traced back to R&D which was first de veloped in Norway by FFI. From our indus trial survey, it is clear that the institute has used its extensive knowledge of advanced technologies to increase the level of techni cal skills in the companies that work with it on development and manufacturing pro jects. The degree of active collaboration at the working level is one important aspect affecting the benefits gained from FFI by the finn. Directly related to the output and trans fer of technology from FFI is its role as supplier of skilled manpower to industry, educational establishments, and govern mental research institutions. As mentioned previously, the supply of skilled manpower can sometimes be temporary in nature, in volving FFI employees working for limited periods with industrial firms engaged in weapon systems development and produc tion. As regards the scientific employees ac tually lea ving FFI, these have numbered ap proximately 20 per year over the last six years, 40 to 50% of whom have tåken up employment in Norwegian industry, and 10% in the education sector. The benef it to Norwegian industry gained through people coming from FFI is depen dent on a range of f actors including acade mic qualifications, the personalities of the researchers involved, and the skills and know-how acquired during the period of working at FFI. In relation to the projects surveyed during this study and the indus trial firms visited, several instances can be cited where ex-FFI personnel have played a central role in the inception and success of new product lines and technical develop ments in industry. More often than not, the move from the R&D environment at FFI to a manufacturer, whether of military or civilian products, seems to have been ac tively encouraged by FFI management and senior research staff . And in most cases the moves have involved areas of advanced technology (computer hardware and soft ware, micro-electronics, lasers, etc.). The most impressive example of new in dustrial activities based on former FFI per sonnel and on R&D and technology from FFI, concerns the development of a fully fledged Norwegian computer industry, with the establishment of Norsk Data A/S. Founded in 1967 by a small group of ex-FFI researchers, Norsk Data drew heavily on ex pertise and technology from FFI in the area of digital electronics, much of which can be traced back to FFI employees acquiring

drew heavily on ex pertise and technology from FFI in the area of digital electronics, much of which can be traced back to FFI employees acquiring

side 301

know-how in the United States in the late 1950 s and early 19605. Since its first com mercial computer (Nord-1), Norsk Data has added several new computer models to its product line, most based largely on R&D at FFI, and has grown to become an interna tional corporation with an annual turnover of 300 million kroner and an average growth rate of over 30% per annum. It is significant that about half of the såles of Norsk Data computers are exports. Two of the three original founders of Norsk Data have since lef t the company, and set up new enterprises in high-technology sectors again related to the work carried out during their time at FFI. Impressive as the «spin-off » of Norsk Data from FFI may be, it is not immediately clear what lessons of relevance today can be learnt from this example of technology transfer from a military context to the civil ian sector of industry. Successes similar to that of Norsk Data (more frequently found in the US in the 1960 s and 19705) seem to have depended on various factors such as the stage of development of the «generic» technology, the scale of operations and hence the resources required, and the acqui sition of a large procurement contract at a crucial early stage of industrial develop ment. Apart from the last, these factors are difficult if not impossible to influence, and hence it must be questioned whether such instances of industrial spin-off do indeed provide a workable «mechanism» for carry ing out military R&D, or whether they should merely be regarded as essentially un predictable «bonuses» from certain R&D ac tivities. Nonetheless, it should be recognised that FFI has been quick to seize and act upon commercial opportunities once they have arisen, and this does highlight the cru cial importance in any high-technology re search organization of developing an aware ness of the mechanisms for translating tech nological opportunities, when they appear, into new commercial products or processes. A somewhat more «typical» example of the industrialisation of FFI development work concern the production of weapon systems rather than civilian products. The case of Simrad A/S opto-electronics division, and its relation to FFI development of laser technology, illustrates that FFI can be an ef f ective instrument for successfully induc ing production-capabilities in industry for military systems. Such a mechanism for the industrialisation of military R&D seems to require the move to industry of key FFI personnel engaged in the R&D work; in this case, the Simrad opto-electronics division was entirely dependent on the innovative activities of former FFI personnel. The sup ply of experienced R&D personnel to indus try is clearly an important output from FFI activities. The impact of this «mechanism» is, however, limited, firstly by the relatively small number of people moving from FFI each year, and, secondly, by the small num ber of high-technology companies in Nor way able to take advantage of the advances provided by FFI development work. As regards the military systems produced by def ence-related f irms on the basis of FFI R&D work, four main ways in which indus trial f irms may benef it can be identif ied: (i) direct såles to Norwegian forces (for whom the project is undertaken); (ii) såles to other customers, including exports; (iii) såles of improved versions of the origmal system; (iv) såles of systems with a similar or related technology base. Again using Simrad laser products as an illustrative example (all four types of benef it were involved here), it is significant to note that, for the first three types of benef it, FFI involvement in the production and further development of the product range has de creased over time, as the degree of new technical inputs has declined. However, in formal links with FFI personnel have been maintained and utilised whenever required, personal contacts and telephone conver sations being particularly important in this respects. When it comes to the development of new (or second-generation) products, where the technology base is similar, FFI involvement seems to intensif y, involving ei ther formal responsibility on the part of FFI for some of the development work, or a direct technical input into the finn's R&D activities. In the case of the Simrad LP7 laser range-finder (a second-generation pro duct), the company collaborated closely with FFI, and the input by FFI personnel on the latest US developments with lasers was a significant factor. This again illustrates FFl's role in transferring foreign techno logy to Norway. A major common feature of firms which have benefited from FBI R&D work in one or more of the ways described above seems to have been the close contact and f requent interaction between their staff and those at FFI. Because of the mutual and interdepen dent interests of def ence industries and mili tary research organizations, there has al ways been close co-operation between the

Moreover, the limited number of de fence-related firms in Norway, as well as the dependence upon the same limited pool of skilled manpower, reinforces these ties. 9 Major Characteristics of the FFI R&D Model. In this section, wc attempt to abstract some of the main features of the FFI «model» for organizing and carrying out ap plied R&D, and transferring the results to industry. The major characteristics of the way in which FFI operates may be described as follows: (a) Management and organization. (1) The organization and management of FFI reflect a clear strategy which is based on an understanding of Norway's needs in the area of defence, and the technology and industrial capability re quired to meet those needs. (2) Senior FFI staff possess a detailed un derstanding both of the industrial struc ture in Norway in the area relevant to FFI work, and of the process of innova tion. They are therefore able to identify and assess fairly accurately the oppor tunities in the area of defence research and technology. FFI is thus strongly placed to make the strategic choices necessary for concentrated efforts when it selects R&D projects and the indus trial partners to help implement the re sults of those projects. (3) FFFs close and regular contact with the military is another essential input to the selection process involved in R&D pro ject definition and in the involvement of industrial partners. The exact formu lation of user-requirements enables FFI to adopt a goal-oriented approach to its R&D projects. (4) FFI projects are managed with a great deal of flexibility, with the non-fixed na ture of project teams allowing resear chers to move between separate but re lated technological areas, and to com bine different tasks whenever required. This organizational flexibility is related to the financial flexibility of FFl's budget allocation. The significant num ber of medium to large sized projects (ty pically involving 8 to 15 million kroner over a three-year period), and the long term existence of a major R&D project (the Penguin programme) linking sev eral different FFI research and develop ment areas, allows relatively flexible fi nancial management. Many FFI projects are interrelated at the technological level, and the R&D management is orga nized in order to capitalise on this. The comparatively large number of short term staff positions, which are not allo cated to one particular division or task group until a specific (job-related) need arises, enhances this capability consider ably. (b) Manpower. (1) Because of the national service system, FFI gains access to some of the best tech nical researchers, and it tries to persuade the most promising to remain at FFI after military service. (2) FFI scientific and technical staff are generally highly qualified, the great ma jority håving received technical training, many at university level, in particular at NTH. (3) It is an established part of manpower training policy to send personnel abroad for a period of about 12 months a few years after they join FFI. This is an ef fective means of making employees aware of developments abroad, both in terms of technology and the organi zational approach to technical and de fence projects. (4) Flexible manpower-planning and project management within FFI ensures that the skills of its technical and scientific staff are fully utilised. (c) Know-how and technology. (1) FFI acknowledges the importance of basic research, and actively enourages its scientific personnel to keep up with recent advances by maintaining contacts with the international scientific com munity. Many staff publish in interna tional journals. (2) FFI researchers have good access to in formation on international defence re search and related technological areas through NATO channels, such as confer ences, and personal contacts with re search centres, particularly in the US. (3) Compared with other Norwegian re search institutes, FFI has a relatively large budget for international travel, and pursues an active policy of sending its employees to f oreign centres of excel lence in order to keep abreast of the lat est scientific and technological ad vances in areas relevant to military sys tems development. In particular, through the one-year visits by FFI per sonnel to foreign research centers, FFI has created an effective mechanism for

development. In particular, through the one-year visits by FFI per sonnel to foreign research centers, FFI has created an effective mechanism for

side 303

transf erring information and know-how on advanced development between over seas countries and Norway. Internatio nal contacts also allow a regular check on possible duplication of R&D efforts at FFI. Given the importance of these links, PFI staff would like the resources available for international travel to be increased. (d) Interaction with military users and in dustry. (1) FFI has direct contact with the military users of the systems it develops both at the level of policies and as regards tech nical programmes, and this enables FFI to establish a clear f ormulation of user requirements. (2) The two-way communication between FFI and the military users creates a po sitive environment for selecting success ful R&D projects, providing a balance between «technology push» and «user de mand» with a minimal degree of risk in the innovation process. User-involve ment in the test-stage of R&D projects allows updating and improvement of de veloped systems prior to production planning. (3) The dual role of FFI as a consultant to the military and technical advisor to the industrial manufacturer, provides the greatest opportunity for achieving a smooth transition between the R&D and production phases of a project. (4) The early involvement of industry in R&D projects and the exchange of per sonnel during R&D and production stages are acknowledged by FFI as cru cial factors influencing a projecfs chance of success. FFl's direct responsi bility for ensuring successf ul industrial isation of its R&D projects is followed up through extensive involvement of FFI personnel in the industrial production stage. If required, FFI will take over part of the production role for military sys tems, and actively assist in building up the technical capability in industry for military systems production. (5) The close contact between FFI and the defence industry, including exchange of personnel, and the rather small number of Norwegian defence-sector firms (and other advanced technology firms), en ables FFI to judge the capabilities of the firms it approaches, and to ensure the continuation of industrial project teams in areas where the long-term defence capability of Norway is judged to be at stake. (6) FFI can act as the R&D laboratory of Norwegian defence industries if the R&D capability within industry is per ceived to be too low. Sometimes indus trial finns rely directly on this, it being generally accepted that in certain areas of advanced technology FFI is ahead of Norwegian industry. (7) FFI is willing to go a long way in helping to create industrial production units for certain military systems, and f eels a con siderable sense of responsibility for safe guarding the national industrial produc tion capability, even when the firms in volved may not be operating as economi cally viable entities in the industrial market system. 10 The Wider Relevance of the FFI «Model» for R&D. There are a number of f eatures of the FFI «model» for R&D and technology transfer to industry, that are likely to be of relevance to an evaluation of the operation of civilian R&D centres, such as the NTNF institutes. Some aspects, on the other hand, may be so specific to military technology and the de fence industry that the potential for trans f erring approaches used by FFI to the civil ian sector is probably rather limited. An important lesson which may be drawn from the FFI experience concerns the ac quisition of technology and know-how, and in particular the great importance of for eign contacts. The success of FFl's policy of sending research staff for one-year periods to North American centres of excellence (be they industrial firms, R&D centres, or uni versities) suggests that this mechanism is worthy of greater consideration for civilian R&D centres in Norway. Even without long-term experience by research staff ab road, frequent foreign visits seem to play a crucial role in keeping abreast of the latest developments in key areas of technology. Such a model also enables research institu tes to ensure that the duplication of previ ous overseas work in their technological ef forts is kept to a minimum, and to foresee when certain areas of competence need to be developed in order to permit the carrying out of future R&D programmes. In connec tion with the latter, the central importance given by FFI to areas of basic research pro vides another aspect of the FFI «model» which could be of relevance to civilian re search institutes. At FFI, however, the areas of basic and exploratory technological reside 304

«model» which could be of relevance to civilian re search institutes. At FFI, however, the areas of basic and exploratory technological reside 304

search are usually directly related to specif ic application-oriented developments. These areas are caref ully selected on the basis of (i) an understanding of the strategic impor tance of certain technologies and (ii) the longer-term requirements for certain wea pon systems. In the case of civilian R&D institutes, the requirements of users may not be so easy to define, so an application oriented approach in NTNF institutes would require important strategic choices to be made and clear policies f ormulated as to which areas of application or industrial sec tors deserve special attention. Concen tration of R&D efforts at FFI is clearly re flected in the Institute's «project profile»: a relatively small number of medium to large projects, together with at least one very large project, which together utilise most of the Institute's resources. The relatively large size of most R&D projects compared with those in NTNF institutes has clearly enhanced project-management flexibility, and contributed to the success of projects, because of the scale of resources which could be brought to bear on particular problems. Concentration of efforts obvi ously requires careful selection procedures and clearly formulated policies as to which projects deserve priority. The well-defined aims of the defence sector are clearly an advantage in this respect compared with the civilian economy, where policy choices are often less clear-cut. One area where FFl's experience may have definite implications for other applied R&D centres is the importance of transfer ring people during the transition from the R&D stage at the Institute to the produc tion stage in industry. There appears to have been a strong relationship between the success of a project in industry and the de gree of interchange between FFI resear chers and industrial staff . Particularly im portant has been the involvement of FFI staff in production activities in industry. This has had benefits for both FFI and in dustry, but again it must be noted that this close co-operation is made much easier by the relatively small number of Norwegian defence firms. In civilian areas where there are a large number of competing firms, in terdependence such as that which exists be tween FFI and certain firms may be far more difficult to attain — for practical or political reasons. Hence, there may be less scope for civilian research institutes to carry out the R&D associated with industry in the way that FFI has managed to do. Another key factor in the way FFI oper ates is its close and regular contact with the users of its weapon-systems. A clear under standing of the requirements of users is known to be one of the major factors deter mining the success or failure of R&D pro jects, but in the civilian sector it is generally not possible to obtain as precise a knowledge of user needs as PFI is able to achieve through its close contact with the military. A knowledge of user-requirements also has implications for the selection of techno logies and the estimation of the resources required to develop them. FFI has always attempted to use the most advanced tech nology available whenever it can. This has encouraged the development of high level technical expertise within FFI, one conse quence of which seems to have been a cer tain amount of «technology push» from the Institute. However, the close contact with the military user on the one hand and the producer on the other has generally ensured that this «technology-push» is restrained by the needs of users and producers, thereby minimizing any tendency towards undirec ted technology. Even though the import ance of establishing contacts between users in the civilian economy and R&D centres has been widely recognized by governmental policy-makers, the mechanisms for achiev ing this have inevitably been less effective than in the military sector. And because the contact between researchers and users in the civilian sector is unlikely to be as strong as in the military sector, this limits the ex tent to which the FFI «model» for the per formance and transfer of R&D to industry can be applied to the civilian economy. The dual function of FFI, serving both military users and the industrial producers, is unique. Its specific function in relation to Norway's defence needs provides FFI with the background to take certain reponsibil ities, such as performing R&D for the de fence industry, and playing an active role in the promotion and creation of production capabilities in industry. These f unctions can only be performed effectively because of a very close interdependency between mili tary users, defence manuf acturers and FFI. Whilst these are perhaps the central featu res of the FFI «model» of research, develop ment, and technology transfer to industry, translating them to the civilian economy would require substantial political changes, in particular with respect to the traditional government-industry relationship. Without such changes, the relevance of the FFI model to the civilian R&D system must re main limited.

capability in Norway for the production of
laser-based systems. FFI was aware of this
situation, and at an early stage — before
formal funding by the Anny began — ac
tively sought industrial participation.
Through informal discussions, it was even
tually agreed that Simrad A/S would estab
lish a new electro-optics division, built
around certain individuals who had been
working on the laser project at FFI. As a
result, three FFI researchers lef t for Simrad
in 1969.
It should be noted that Simrad personnel
were heavily involved in the R&D phase of
the project, which was completed in 1971 at
FFl.However, it was the migration (both
temporary and permanent) of personnel to
industry that was the crucial factor in
transf erring the know-how on laser technol
ogy from FFI to Simrad, once it became
f ormally reponsible for f urther development
work and eventual production. At no stage
was the involvement of a foreign firm con
sidered since official policy specified that
major parts of national defence systems
should be developed and produced in Nor
way.
(d) Outputs and benefits.
By transferring skilled personnel and
technology to Simrad A/S, the laser range
finder project enabled the finn to develop an
industrial production capability in electro
optics products. During the early develop
ment phase of the project, three Simrad per
sonnel worked for about half a year at FFI,
where they received extensive training. This
factor, together with the core group of exFFI researchers working at Simrad, contri
buted to the successful production of laser
range-finders, for which there were initital
såles of 250 units (LP 3) to the Norwegian
Anny and around 200 units to the British
Ministry of Defence (LP 6). These two pro
duction contracts generated såles of ap
proximately 40 million kroner, and the Brit
ish contract in particular seems to have
been important in enabling the company, to
reach the economic «threshold» required for
successful industrial exploitation.
On the basis of the R&D for the original
laser range-finders, Simrad was able to de
velop derivatives of the system, including
more advanced versions and a range-finder
for armoured fighting vehicles (LV 2 and LV
3). A second generation of laser range-finside 306

ders (LP 7) — developed by the group which was formed around the ex-FFI researchers — has so far generated contracts totalling about 40 million kroner. FFI remains in close contact with Simrad, even today. Over the last 5 years, several people from FFI have been involved for va rying periods in work on lasers at the com pany. In 1980 the electro-optics division split off to form a separate firm: Simrad Optro nics. It remains the only Norwegian finn with a capability in laser products. FFI, on the other hand, is continuing work in the area of laser technology with an Anny pro ject to develop a laser spectroscopic system for the early detection of toxic gases. (e) Lessons. The success of the laser range-finder pro jects has depended upon the following fac tors: — technology was acquired from abroad and subsequently developed at FFI with internal f unds; — there was a clear understanding at FFI of user-needs and continuing close invol vement of the military during the R&D phase; — industrial involvement started early in the R&D phase; — there was a transfer of key FFI resear chers to the industrial producer; — industrial personnel were involved in R&D work at FFI and received extensive training; — there was a foreign procurement contract at an early stage of industrialisation, in addition to såles to the Norwe gian military; — as the first development of laser range finders in Norwegian industry, the potential for follow-up was great; — the continued collaboration between the industrial producer and FFI has streng thened the finn's technological base, and enhanced its opportunities for obtaining future development and procurement contracts from the Norwegian military for derivative systems; — foreign producers of laser range-finders did not recognize early enough that the weight of the instrument would prove such an important factor; they therefore produced a product that could not easily be reduced in size, thus leaving certain sections of the market open to Simrad, even though the development of their product took longer than initially plan ned. (ii) Digital C omputers . (a) Initiation and early research. FFI started work on digital computers in the late 19505, using technology and know how originally developed in the USA — in particular at MIT. The early research at FFI, which was funded from internal funds, was triggered by an awareness of develop ments abroad and of the potential appli cation of digital computers to military fire control systems. FFI was given funds to pur chase the first production model of the early Figure 1 Main Developments in Computing at FFI and the Spin-Off to Industry Military Projects 51RWA| PENGUIN- 5L G JI-!: CESAR DATANETT WERA g»«jj»»- p ROS ESSERING TROMSØ TELEMETRERING DAF Spin-Off to Industry

Ferranti computer range, at the time one of most advanced electronic computers in the world, and this was a key factor in building up expertise at the Institute. FFFs mainstream activities on digital computers commenced with the develop ment of the SAM-computer, on which re search began in the early 19605, with money from the Penguin missile project. The SAM f amily of digital computers was to form the basis of further developments at FFI in this area, as can be seen from Figure 1, which presents a pictorial history of computing de velopments at FFI. (b) Technology acquisition. Competence in the area of digital compu ters was built up in the late 1950 s and early 1960 s around a small number of FFI resear chers who had spent some time in the United States, many at MIT. Therefore, much of the FFI work on digital computers can be directly traced back to developments at MIT. In the late 19505, MIT completed its first transistorised computer, the TX-O, and visiting FFI personnel were instrumental in transferring this technology to FFI. Several basic technological concepts of the TX-O were incorporated within the development of the SAM-O at FFI (in 1961 and 1962), just as they were in the American DEC series of computers (the firm, DEC, being set up by researchers from MIT who had worked on the TX-O). In the early sixties, FFI was the only place in Norway working on computer hardware. FFI kept up its close contact with MIT, and all through the 1960 s FFI researchers were sent to work at MIT for periods of one to two years, making use of the links built up in the late 19505. Consequently, FFI was able to keep up with the latest computer develop ments, and to incorporate new technological concepts, such as time-sharing, in its own digital computer work. (c) The FFI «line» of digital computer developments and subsequent industrialisation. The first signif icant digital computer de veloped at FFI was the SAM computer in 1961. This subsequently led to SAM-2, the first working computer in the world using TTL technology, which was completed in April 1967. It was these developments at FFI that led to the first Norwegian industrial activities in digital computers, both for mili tary and civil purposes. (1) Military computers: Kongsberg Våpen fabrikk. Production of the military version of the SAM computer was tåken up by Kongsberg Våpenfabrikk, and this formed the basis of the finn's future digital computer activities. Kongsberg's first use of the computer tech nology developed by FFI concerned the ODIN Field Artillery Control System and the SM-3 Computer System produced at Kongsberg (between 1967 and 1969). The SM-3 computer was subsequently incorpor ated in a range of Kongsberg's military pro ducts, including the MSI-70U and MSI-80S control systems. Further derivatives of this computer system, developed by FFI and Kongsberg and produced by the latter, in cluded the SM-4 and SM-5, used along with other systems in the various Penguin mis siles. At the heart of Kongsberg's computer ac tivities was a small group of people who had worked at FFI on the development of the SAM computer, and who moved to Kongs berg in 1967. Follo wing this move, Kongs berg was given the development and produc tion contract for the military version of SAM (for ODIN), and this provided the basis for much of Kongsberg's successful military export business during the 19705. Although Kongsberg has recently decided to termin ate construction of its own computer hard ware, the experience gained in the past will continue to prove useful in incorporating outside computers in the finn's product lines. (2) Civilian computers : Norsk Data. A few months bef ore the Kongsberg com puter division was formed to produce a mili tary version of SAM, several prominent FFI researchers (from the group which had de veloped the ODIN computer) took the initi ative to set up a new company to produce the computer. One of the senior staf f mem bers at FFI had recognised the possibilities for commercialising the technology devel oped at the Institute, and was instrumental in initiating discussion among researchers as to the possibilities of setting up a new company. Although such a move was encouraged by some FFI staff, others were less positive, feeling that FFI should remain loyal to Kongsberg. In the event, Norsk Data was founded in 1967 by three FFI researchers (together with a technician), who put up approximately 200,000 kroner of their own money. The share capital was increased to 800,000 kroner a year later, with a shipping

who put up approximately 200,000 kroner of their own money. The share capital was increased to 800,000 kroner a year later, with a shipping

side 308

company, Moswold, taking a stake of over 50% in the company. Moswold still retains control today, with most of the remaining shares owned by employees. The new company initially hoped to pro duce the military version of the SAM-2 for the Fire Control System, but, as it became clear that Kongsberg would be given this production contract (after much fierce de bate at FFI), the founder memers rapidly changed the focus of the company to the production of computers for civilian use. With hindsight, Norsk Data recognises that the SAM-2 project would in fact have put an extremely heavy load on the young company, that, coupled with the extra problems involved in establishing links with the user, Kongsberg, might well have held back Norsk Data's later, very rapid growth. By drawing on the FFI R&D work on digital computers, Norsk Data was able to develop and produce the first commercial Norwegian computer, the NORD 1, which was completed in 1968. It is significant to note that much of the funding for the NORD 1 came from a procurement contract issued by NTNF for three computers at the central research institutes — SI, SINTEF and CMI. The extent to which senior FFI staff were involved in persuading NTNF of the merits of supporting Norsk Data, is not certain, but there is no disputing that this contract proved crucially important in giv ing the new company early support (com pensating for the failure to obtain the mili tary contract). Thus NTNF can take some credit for helping to establish what soon became a major Norwegian company, as can the Development Fund, which was also an important source of loans to the finn. Direct derivatives of the NORD 1 compu ter system came with the NORD 10 (1973), NORD 105 (1977) and NORD 100 (1978) com puters which, in relation to their basic tech nological f eatures, can all be traced back to earlier R&D work carried out at FFI. In total, over ten people have moved from FFI to Norsk Data since its formation in 1967, migration on a scale that was envisaged by senior staff at FFI even before the resear chers took the decision to leave and found the company. Since 1967, Norsk Data has expanded its activities rapidly, particularly in the area of time-sharing minicomputers (as has its his torical rival, DEC), and has now grown into an international company with an annual turnover of more than 300 million kroner, and an average growth rate of 30% per an num. It should be noted that Norsk Data's breakthrough into the international market came with a crucial contract in 1972, when CERN, the European Nuclear Research Centre, ordered 24 NORD 10 computers from Norsk Data. Won under strict com mercial conditions against fierce compe tition from major American producers (in cluding DEC), this established the technol ogical reputation of Norsk Data interna tionally. Since the mid-19705, Norsk Data has itself become the source of further industrial spin-off. Two of the three founding mem bers left to establish their own advanced technology companies (Mycron and Simex) in specialised areas of computing, while other former Norsk Data staff have also been instrumental in setting up various Norwegian software companies. The devel opment of the core sectors of the Norwegian computing industry, is summarised in Fig ure 2, below. (d) Lessons. This evolution of work on digital compu ters at FFI and in Norwegian industry high lights several important f eatures of the pro cess by which technology is acquired at FFI and transferred to industry. The main aspects can be summarised as follows: — the single most important factor in transferring digital-computer techno logy and know-how from MIT to FFI was the long-term visits by FFI personnel to MIT; — the opportunity to take up digital com puter work and to exploit advanced tech nology from overseas was made possible by the flexible financial and organi zational approach at FFI, and by the ability of senior staff at FFI to foresee the long-term strategic importance of the new technology; — in the case of both military and civilian computers, the transfer from FFI of the technology for the production of digital computers took place through the move ment of FFI personnel to industry; — senior staff at FFI actively encouraged the more entrepreneurially minded of their colleagues to set up a new com pany, and hence to establish a Norwe gian capability for manufacturing digi tal computers; — a few very active individuals, some basic new concepts in computer technology (like time-sharing), and a procurement contract from NTNF, were all crucial in the early success of Norsk Data; — the breakthrough of Norsk Data into the

time-sharing), and a procurement contract from NTNF, were all crucial in the early success of Norsk Data; — the breakthrough of Norsk Data into the

(iii) Anny Weather Radar. (a) Initiation and development. Out of the modernisation programme for the Norwegian field-artillery system, which began in the mid-19605, came, in the early 19705, the requirement for a weather radar. The weather radar system was intended as one of the input-sensors for the field-artil lery fire-control system, and was the last element in the overall modernisation pro gramme. Given the toplogy of Norway, wind speeds vary immensely, and because of this the hardware available on the world market was not considered suitable for local conditions. FPI was asked by the Military Require ments Board to develop a small, relatively portable, weather radar unit using any tech nology they thought appropriate. FFI had already developed an expertise in radar during the period 1969—72 while working on another aspect of the fire control system, the muzzle velocity radar — by all accounts an extremely successf ul pro ject that was finished on time and (unusu ally for such a project) cost less than expec ted. A pre-study on weather radar was therefore carried out during 1973/74 at a cost of about 2 million kroner. Because of the rather diffuse nature of the problem, this pre-project was carried out by FFI in close collaboration with both government meterologists (who provided basic know ledge on how air density, temperature, wind, etc., affect ballistic behaviour), and the School of Field Artillery and the Artillery Inspectorate (who provided the necessary input on user-problems and requirements). Initially the idea was to measure wind speed by sending up a small rocket to a height of around 2 kilometres, which would then disperse chaff — the drift average be ing measured by radar. Very early on, this system had been preferred «for inituitive reasons» (in part because of the technology involved) over such alternatives as a bal loon-based system. However, when the Anny changed its requirements during the pre-project to a system that would be suit able for new artillery firing shells with a

side 310

trajectory of up to 6 kilometres the possibil ity of using rockets seemed prohibitively ex pensive. It was decided to opt for a balloon borne radar reflector, and development of this began in 1975. In giving the go-ahead, Anny Material Command asked that the radar system be built for manual operation. The Anny had wanted an automated sys tem, but the extra costs (an additional 30%) were not seen as warranted. So instead of a relatively sophisticated system, using adv anced rocketry and automated tracking, Materials Command pressed FFI to develop a «lower technology» balloon-based unit, with manual tracking f acilities. Development of the A-model was carried out during 1975—76, and then tested by the f ield artillery, who had the final decision as to whether or not the project should con tinue. After detailed consideration, the Anny decided they liked the concept, but required that the range of the system be increased, a decision which meant that a larger reflector had to be used and the scan system changed. As researchers at FFI themselves now re alise, the costs of making such a design change were seriously underestimated. 1 This was not helped by the fact that the «B-mo del», finished in late 1978, experienced a number of major technical problems. The result was that another year had to be spent on redesigning the system, and it was only in 1979 that the hardware was finally ready for operational field-testing. Total staff involve ment in the project was around 50 man years, with an overall cost (including exter nal costs) of approximately 11.5 million kroner. It should be stressed that the level of technology required in this project was high, mainly because of the use of microprocessor technology. (b) Industrial selection and early involve ment. Industrial selection had actully tåken place at a relatively early stage in the pro ject: the finn, referred to here as Finn A, was chosen as the main industrial partner by FFI, because of its previous work with the Institute on solid-state radar technol ogy. According to FFI staff, it was the only finn which had the capability for successful industrialisation, although the Anny Mate rial Command had wanted to use a larger ') The cost of a weather-radar unit was initially estimated at appromiximately 300,000 kroner. The final cost was around 1 million kroner, i.e. about three times the expected price. finn. In addition, Finn B was chosen to sup ply a hybrid microprocessor. Despite the early discussions between FFI and the industrial partner, Finn A did not actively involve itself in the project until mid-1980, when the official production con tract was finally awarded. Up to this time, the finn had not assigned any personnel to work actively with FFI during the R&D phase. In part, this may have been due to the failure to give a definite development contract to Finn A, which in turn seems to have been related to the concentration of military expenditure on the F 16 contract. (c) Industrialisation. The lack of early industrial involvement seems to have had certain implications for the transfer of technology to the finn. Ac cording to FFI personnel, many of the later problems in taking up the project at Finn A could have been overcome had there been some involvement of the finn's staff in the early stages of R&D. It was estimated that earlier involvement might have saved around 6 months. The relative lack of contact between FFI and Finn A was a particular constraint in building up the level of specialised techno logical capability within the finn. The ex perience of Finn A with digital electronic equipment had been limited, and their shortage of skilled personnel made the re lationship between FFI and the finn crucial. This was particularly apparent when it was realized that Finn B did not have the digital competence to provide the microprocessor technology (a version of the MIPROC devel oped at FFI and licensed to Plessey of Brit ain). In the event, FFI had to pay a third finn, Finn C, to redevelop Finn B's micro processor, the final costs being far greater than they would have been had FFI opted for the Plessey chip instead of trying to im plant the technology in a Norwegian finn. With the pressure on development costs increasing, it was decided to construct only one «B-model» prototype. This has created interface problems between FFI and indus try because two finns (several hundred kilo metres apart) are now involved in the pro duction phase. In an attempt to reduce the costs, FFI off ered to produce the mechanical part of the system (using their new work shop), leaving the digital part to Finn A. Overall, the researchers at FFI feel this is not the way that a defence research insti tute should «industrialise» its technology, and attempts have been made to learn and

at FFI feel this is not the way that a defence research insti tute should «industrialise» its technology, and attempts have been made to learn and

side 311

absorb the lessons from this particular ex perience. (d) Potential industrial benefits. Although it may be too early to assess the industrial spin-off and benefits of the weather radar project to the finns involved, FFI staff expressed conf idence that, despite the problems, the experience will be benefi cial to Firm A. As with other projects, FFI researchers feel a high degree of responsibil ity for ensuring the transfer of technologi cal know-how to Norwegian industry. They believe that, through this project, FFI has tåken an active and positive role in creating the technological capability in industry for using microprocessors. The project was the first major attempt by Finn A to employ microprocessor technology, and, although there were problems in transferring the technology, the finn has developed a great deal of useful competence for the f uture (as has Finn C). Finn B has meanwhile decided to diversif y into other areas of microprocessor technology. (e) Lessons. The main f eatures of the Weather Radar project in relation to FFI and to the transfer of technology to Norwegian industry can be summarised as follows: — the formulation of the project was lar gely carried out by FFI and military users, with minimal involvement of in dustry; — the R&D work was performed by FFI with no active industrial participation; — the lack of a development contract resul ted in the f inn being reluctant to commit scarce resources, particularly highly skilled engineers, to the project; -r- the lack of industrial involvement and transfer of personnel during the R&D phase hindered the transition from de velopment to production work; — the transfer of new (electronic) techno logy was highly constrained by the late involvement of one industrial partner; — additional efforts by FFI were required to ensure a successful transition to the production phase and to establish an adequate technological capability in industry.

! Depotbiblioteket STORTINGETS OG REGJERINGENS PUBLIKASJONER Stortingsproposisjoner Forslag til vedtak fra Regjeringen i saker som Stor tinget skal ta stilling til. Abonnement: kr. 105, — pr. sesjon fritt tilsendt. Stortingsmeldinger Inneholder bl. a.: Statsregnskapet, meldinger til Stor tinget om arbeidet i statens bedrifter, meldinger om planer som Regjeringen vil sette i verk i framtida osv. Abonnement: kr. 115, — pr. sesjon fritt tilsendt. Odelstingsproposisjoner Regjeringens lovforslag. Abonnement: kr. 70, — pr. sesjon fritt tilsendt. Dokumenter Omfatter bl. a.: Riksrevisjonens antegnelser. Grunnlov forslag. Private lovforslag. Svar til Regjeringen på for slag og henvendelser oversendt av Stortinget. Sivil ombudsmannen og Ombudsmannsnemndas innberet ninger m.m. Abonnement kr. 18, — pr. sesjon fritt tilsendt. Innstillinger til Stortinget Stortingskomitéenes vurderinger av de enkelte propo sisjoner og meldinger, og komiteenes forslag til vedtak i Stortinget (innst. S.). .mm .a. _ _m_ _ _ Abonnement: kr. 24, — pr. sesjon fritt tilsendt, Innstillinger til Odelstinget Stortingskomitéenes vurderinger av lovforslag og odelstingsmeldinger samt komiteenes forslag til ved tak I Odelstinget (innst. O.). Abonnement: kr. 24, — pr. sesjon fritt tilsendt Stortingstidende Stenografiske referater fra møtene i Stortinget, Odels tinget og Lagtinget. Abonnement: kr. 20, — pr. sesjon fritt tilsendt. Saksregister Omfatter register for alle ovennevnte trykksaker. Ut arbeides etter endt sesjon. Abonnement: kr. 12, — pr. sesjon fritt tilsendt Lover Etter endt sesjon samles de i sesjonen vedtatte lover i ett hefte. Pris: kr. 12,— fritt tilsendt. «Publikasjonsliste fra Storting og Regjering» Liste over offentlige publikasjoner som foreligger trykt. Kommer ut ca. hver 14. dag under stortingssesjonen. Abonnementpris kr. 15, — pr. sesjon. Statsinstitusjoner får listen fra Statens trykksakekspedisjon. Abonnement kan tegnes hos Universitetsforlaget, Offentlige publika sjoner, Tollbugt. 31, Boks 8134 Dep., Oslo 1. Postgiro konto 2 09 75 58. Abonnenter som tegner abonnement etter 1. oktober får tilsendt de dokumenter som utkommer etter teg ningsdagen. Statsinstitusjoner bestiller i Statens trykksakekspedisjon, Boks 81 69 Dep., Oslo 1. Enkeltbøstillinger Nye og eldre proposisjoner, meldinger m.v., samt utredninger kan bestilles gjennom bokhandelen. Prisen fastsettes etter trykksakens sidetall. UNIVERSITETSFORLAGET
